units.la: HABES Lector quæ de Crucè scripsimus, sed germana. Antea atque alibi quæ edita (credas hoc nobis) non sunt nostra. Quid ergo? non illa dictavimus? Fortasse. sed o imperitiam! quasi edendi illo fine. Reverentior posteritatis sum: & aliud scio esse Schedia, aliud Opera; nec subitaria hæc nostra dedicanda in Memoriæ templo. Quid, quòd alii graviùs etiam peccant? qui excipiunt aut intercipiunt dicta aut oratiunculas nostras, & in contumeliam mei divulgant. Aliter non accipio. Ævum hoc ut multis deliciis fibulam, ita petulantiæ & licentiæ laxat: & quod avet procacissimus quisque, id etiam audet. Ego femel & ferio teslor, audite qui in Europâ. NIHIL MEVM EST, AVT ERIT, QVOD NON DE AVTOGRAPHO MEO, ET ME VOLENTE, SIT EXPRESSVM. Quicumque aliter, mihi injuriam facit, vobis fucum. Deus bone, hæc monenda publicè esse? Ecce in bona opesque externas jus est non vivo mihi solùm sed mortuo, & solatium fati est voluntas ultra fatum: in istis animi & ingenii verè bonis non idem erit? Reprimite Principes qui poteslis, & vos lectores quâ poteslis: illi puniendo, vos spernendo. Ego præter teslari nihil habeo, & hoc etiam addo, Siquid usquam præter religionem moresque veterum, non agnosco: & tibi adhæreo. Statu felix Ecclesia,
units.tr: You have here, reader, what we have written about the Cross, but genuinely ours. Earlier and elsewhere, whatever has been published (believe us) is not ours. What then? Did we never dictate those things? Perhaps we did. But oh, what inexperience, as if they were written with publication in view! I am more respectful of posterity. I know that a Schedia is one thing and a Work another, and these hasty pieces of mine should not be dedicated in the temple of Memory. And what of the fact that others sin even more grievously, who catch up or intercept my sayings or little speeches and spread them abroad to my disgrace? I cannot take it otherwise. This age loosens the clasp of many pleasures, and likewise of wantonness and license, and whatever the most shameless man desires, he also dares. I testify once and again, hear it, you who are in Europe. NOTHING IS OR WILL BE MINE THAT HAS NOT BEEN PRINTED FROM MY OWN AUTOGRAPH AND WITH MY CONSENT. Whoever does otherwise does me an injury and you a deception. Good God, must these things be announced publicly? Behold, over goods and external wealth the right belongs not only to me while living but to me dead, and a will that outlasts fate is a consolation for fate. In those truly good things of the mind and genius, will it not be the same? Restrain them, Princes, as far as you can, and you readers as far as you can: they by punishing, you by scorning. I have nothing beyond testifying, and this too I add: if anything anywhere goes beyond the religion and morals of the ancients, I do not acknowledge it, and I cling to you. Happy in its condition is the Church,
TO THE READER.

units.la: ENtibi Lector benevole Illustrissimi Viri Justi Lipsii de Cruce libellum, in quo edendo eâ curâ usi sumus, quâ uti vel diligenti vel diligentissimus quisque poterat: nam & menda nonnulla, quæ occurrebant, sustulimus, & rerum simul verborumque, & auctorum catalogum adjecimus: ac ne quid desiderari à nobis ulla ratione posset, notas quæ ad calcem operis aut nullo aut obscuro discrimine subjectæ erant paginarum & numerorum titulis insignivimus, ut quo quæque pertineant haud difficulter, & uno quasi intuitu perspici posšit, ac jam præter favorem tuum nihil desideretur amplius, quem si adesse nobis perspexerimus, brevi Niquetus de Titulo Crucis, & Curtius de Clavis Dominicis pari diligentia & editionis nitore subsequentur.
units.tr: To you, kind reader, we present this little book of the most illustrious man Justus Lipsius, On the Cross. In printing it we have taken such care as any diligent, or most diligent, person could take. We have removed several errors that came to light, and we have added an index of matters and words as well as of authors. And so that nothing could be found wanting on our part, we have marked with the titles of pages and numbers the notes that were placed at the end of the work either without distinction or with an unclear one, so that what each refers to can be grasped without difficulty and at a single glance. Now, apart from your favour, nothing more is needed; if we perceive that it is present with us, the Niquetus on the Title of the Cross and the Curtius on the Nails of the Lord will shortly follow, with equal care and elegance of printing.
Farewell.
THE PRINTER TO THE READER.

units.tr: Kind reader, we have put into your hands this little book of the most illustrious man Justus Lipsius, De Cruce, and in printing it we have taken such care as the most diligent of printers could take. For we have removed some errors that were found in it, and we have added an index of things and words as well as of authors. And so that nothing could be thought to be lacking on our part, we have marked the notes, which at the foot of the work were set down either without any distinction or with an obscure one, with the titles of pages and numbers, so that where each belongs may be seen without difficulty and at a single glance. Now, apart from your goodwill, nothing more is lacking; and if we perceive that you are giving it to us, the Niquetus on the Title of the Cross and Curtius on the Nails of the Lord will follow shortly, with the same care and elegance of printing.
Farewell.

units.la: IVSTI LIPSII DE CRVCE LIBER I.
units.tr: Justus Lipsius, On the Cross, Book I.
Chapter I.
A short prayer. The subject matter and plan of the work.

units.la: AGgredior de CRVCE scribere, sed tuam priùs opem auxiliumque invocans qui eam confecrasti, & infame illud lignum instrumentum fecisti publicæ salutis. Tu Deus à Deo genite, homo ex homine genite, hominibus genite, da mihi vera, da recta scribere, tibi in honorem, Cruci in splendorem, nobis in fructum. Materies & ordo mei operis iste. Quid Crux, & Cujusmodi fuerit: Ubi, Quare, Quomodo, & Quatenus usurpata. Hæc omnia non distinctè solùm, sed diffusè dicam: nec displicebit accuratio illi, cui salutare hoc signum placebit.
units.tr: I am about to write about the CROSS, but first I call upon your help and aid, you who consecrated it and made that infamous wood the instrument of public salvation. O God begotten of God, man begotten of man, begotten for men, grant that I may write true and right things: to your honour, to the splendour of the Cross, and to the profit of us all. This is the subject matter and plan of my work: what the Cross is and what kind of thing it was; where, why, how, and to what extent it was used. I shall say all of these things not only distinctly but at length, and that thoroughness will not displease anyone who takes pleasure in this saving sign.
CHAPTER II.

units.la: Crucis nomen polysemon. Hac nostra Gabalus etiam dicta, item Infelix lignum, & Infame. Sed & Crux non in ligno.
units.tr: The name cross has several meanings. This cross of ours is also called gabalus, and likewise an unlucky wood, and an infamous one. But the cross is not wood.

units.la: CRVX significatione duplici, Laxa & Adstricta. Illa est, cum pro omni angore, tormento, atque etiam interitu sumunt, ut Comici passim, qui Abire jubent in malam Crucem: ut Gracchus, qui dixit (alio etiam genere) Malo Cruce perire: ut Plautus de homine merso aquis, Abstractum in maximam malam Crucem. Sed & Terentius a cruciando, Meretrices dixit Cruces: nec dissimiliter Plautus, Aliqua mala Crux semper est, quae aliquid petat. Paullo diversius illud ejusdem:
units.tr: The word CRUX has two meanings, a loose one and a strict one. The loose meaning is when people take it for any anguish, torment, or even death. The comic poets everywhere do this, bidding people go to a bad cross. So Gracchus said (in another form) to perish by a bad cross, and Plautus of a man drowned in water: dragged off to the greatest bad cross. Terence also used "crosses" for prostitutes, from the torment they cause, and Plautus says similarly: there is always some bad cross that seeks something. The same author has a slightly different phrase: what bad cross is driving you?, close to what ghosts, or what storms?

units.la: ¹ Menæch. Prolog. ² Aulular. dem: Quæ te mala Crux agitat?1 quod adfine istis, Quæ larvæ, aut quæ intemperiæ? At Adstricta significatio est hæc mea, & vulgò receptissima, cùm peculiariter cruciatum & interitum notamus in ligno. Quid ita? credo, quia eximius ille, mors tarda & planè cum sensu. Dixerunt & alio nomine Gabalum. Nonius 2 ex Varrone citat: Nos barbari quòd nocentes in Gabalum suffigimus homines, vos non barbari noxios absolvitis. Quæ vox etiam in priscís Glossis, sed vocali mediâ mutante: Gabulum, βάσαν@, explicatque laxè, ut vides, & pro quocumque tormento. Dixerunt aliter, Infelicem arborem, lignum, stipitem. In carmine horrendo apud Livium 3: Caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito.
units.tr: ¹ Menaechmi, Prologue. ² Aulularia. Seven other items here. The strict meaning, which is mine and most generally accepted, is when we mark out especially torment and death on wood. Why so? I believe because that is a remarkable death, slow and clearly with feeling. They also called it by another name, gabalus. Nonius cites from Varro: We barbarians, because we fix guilty men on a gabalus, you non-barbarians acquit the guilty. The word also appears in old glossaries, with the middle vowel changed: gabulum, [βάσανον], and it explains it loosely, as you see, as any torment at all. They also called it an unlucky tree, wood, or post. In the dreadful song in Livy: cover his head, hang him on the unlucky tree.

units.la: ¹ Aulular. ² In Gabalum. ³ Lib. 1. to. De Cruce accipi res docet, & Cicero, qui in eâ pro Rabirio palàm sic interpretatur. & Seneca 1: Invenitur qui velit adaēus ad infelix illud lignum trahere animam tot tormenta traſturam. Minutius Felix 2: Deus ligneus, rogi fortasse vel infelicis stipitis portio: id est, Crucis. Dixit & Infamem Poëta 3 incertus.
units.tr: ¹ Aulularia. ² On Gabalus. ³ Book 1. That the thing is to be understood of the cross is shown also by Cicero, who in his speech for Rabirius explains it openly in this way; and Seneca: there is found someone who would be willing to drag his breath to that unlucky wood, which will bring so many torments. Minucius Felix: a wooden god, perhaps a piece of the pyre or of the unlucky post, that is, of the cross. An unknown poet also called it infamous.

units.la: Noxius infami districtus stipite membra, Sperat & àfixâ posse redire Cruce.
units.tr: A guilty man, bound by his limbs to the infamous post, hopes too that he may return, though fixed to the cross.

units.la: ¹ Epist. c. 1. ² In Octavio. ³ In Catalect. Virg. ⁴ Lib. 1. de Asin. ta, inquit, jam crucis candidatus : bene, & pro hoc sensu. Etsi autem Crux proprie in ligno : tamen adnoto, similitudine etiam ita dictam suspensionem aut fixionem in alia paratura. puta in monte aut petra. Sic Tertulliano fuint Cruces Caucasorum, alludenti ad Promethea illic affixum : quem ipsum Lucianus describit & appellat τραγοσκιλα. Sic & Manilius de Andromeda, quae in scopulo vincta & ceto exposita :
units.tr: ¹ Epist. c. 1. ² In Octavio. ³ In Catalecta Virgilii. ⁴ Book 1, On the Ass. ta, he says, now a candidate for the cross: well said, and in this sense. Although the cross properly means wood, I note that by a similarity a suspension or fixing on some other structure, for example on a mountain or a rock, was also so called. So Tertullian speaks of the crosses of the Caucasus, alluding to Prometheus fixed there, whom Lucian also describes and calls tragoskila [τραγοσκιλα]. So too Manilius of Andromeda, who was bound to a rock and exposed to a sea monster:
And the maiden, doomed to die, hung on a virgin cross.
