Juba Numidas eos, qui loco amisso fugâ se receperant, in cruce omnes suffixit. Item Cruci affigere, & Cruci figere, crebra in libris. Illud minùs, Figere ἀπλῶς & sine additione. Tertullianus 2 sic utitur: Taceo quod figitur (Christus:) in hoc enim venerat. Quod idem Confige re Paulinus 3 Nolanus Episcopus dixit:
units.tr: These are the names of the cross and of the punishment that is carried out by it: Cruci suffigere, as Velleius says of the pirates whom Caesar, he says, Cruci suffixit. In cruce suffigere, as Hirtius says in book 1: Juba fastened all those Numidians, who had fled to safety after losing their position, in cruce omnes suffixit. Likewise Cruci affigere and Cruci figere are common in the books. The shorter form Figere, used absolutely and without any addition, is less common. Tertullian, in book 2, uses it thus: I say nothing of how he was figitur (Christ), for he had come for this. Paulinus of Nola, bishop, in his ninth Natalis of Felix, used the same word, Configere, when he said:

units.la: 1 De bello Africo. 2 De patientiâ, cap. 111. 3 Natali ix. Felic. Agnoscant trepidi, quem confixere rebelles:
units.tr: (1) On the African War. (2) On Patience, ch. 111. (3) Natalis 9 of Felix. Let the trembling recognize him whom the rebels pierced through:

units.la: de Christo ad judicium venturo. Etsi Tertullianus paullò aliter, veterem hominem confixum esse Christo dicit: quod vulgò, unà crucifixum. Suo etiam & proprio verbo appellarunt, Cruciare . Aufonius: —— Cruciaverat illic Spreta olim, memorem Veneris, Proserpina Adonim.
units.tr: of Christ, who is to come to judgment. Although Tertullian says in a slightly different way that the old man is fastened with Christ, which is commonly rendered crucified together with him. They also used a word of their own and proper to the purpose, Cruciare. Ausonius: Proserpina, once scorned, mindful of Venus, had tormented Adonis there.

units.la: Hegesippus : Capiebantur innumeri (Judæi,) quingenti fermè ad diem cruciabantur. quod est in crucem agebantur: atque Josephus in istâ ipsâ re dixerat, ἀνεσταυρωθησαν. Paulinus : —— Cruciatâ in carne corusçum Agnoscant trepidi.
units.tr: Hegesippus: Countless Jews were seized, and about five hundred were tormented almost daily, that is, were led off to the cross. Josephus, in this very matter, had said were crucified [ἀνεσταυρωθησαν]. Paulinus: The trembling recognize the flashing one whose flesh was tormented on the cross.

units.la: 1 De Resur. carn. cap. XLVII. 2 In Cupidine crucif. 3 Lib. v. cap. XVIII. 4 Lib. VI. Excid. cap. XII. 5 Natal. IX. Fel.
units.tr: (1) On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 47. (2) On Cupid Crucified. (3) Book 5, ch. 18. (4) Book 6, On the Destruction, ch. 12. (5) Natalis 9 of Felix.

units.la: Glossæ veteres: Cruciat, crucificat, σταυροῖ. Nota ibidem & Crucificat, quod in iisdem glossis alibi: Crucificatus, σταυρωμένος. A Crucio sive & Cruce ipsâ Cruciarius dictus is qui in cruce, vel qui eâ dignus. In ipsâ, ut Petronius 1: Cruciarii unius parentes ut viderunt noctu laxatam custodiam, detraxêre pendentem. Et in Declamationibus Calpurnii Flacci 2 inscriptio: Pædagogus cruciarius: & Peregrinus cruciarius. de his qui appensi jam in cruce. At qui eâ digni, per convicium aut minas quoque sic nominati. Isidorus: Cruciarius, Cru-cio quod sit cruce dignus. Apuleius 3: Nec tantillum cruciarius ille deterritus. Ammianus 4: Longum est, qua cruciarius ille conflavit.
units.tr: The ancient glosses: Cruciat, crucificat, σταυροῖ [he crucifies]. Note also in the same glosses, elsewhere, Crucificat, and Crucificatus, σταυρωμένος [crucified]. Cruciarius is named from crucio, or from the cross itself, and means one who is on the cross, or one who deserves it. Of one on the cross, as in Petronius: When the parents of one cruciarius saw that the guard had been relaxed at night, they took down the hanging body. And in the Declamations of Calpurnius Flaccus there are the titles Pedagogue cruciarius and Foreigner cruciarius, referring to those already hung on the cross. But those who deserve it are also so named by way of abuse or threat. Isidore: Cruciarius, from crucio, because he is worthy of the cross. Apuleius, in book 3: That cruciarius was not frightened even a little. Ammianus, in book 13: It would be long to tell by what means that cruciarius brought it about.

units.la: ¹ In Satyr. ² Declamat. xvii. & xxix. ³ Lib x. ⁴ Lib. xiii.
units.tr: (1) In the Satyricon. (2) Declamations 17 and 29. (3) Book 10. (4) Book 13.
CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Graecorum verba ad Crucem & crucifixionem. Hesychius & Ovidius emendati, iste etiam explicatus.
units.tr: The Greek words for the cross and crucifixion. Hesychius and Ovid emended, and this one also explained.

units.la: ISta Latinis : Græcis duo fere Crucis nomina, Σταυρὸς & Σκόλοψ. Illud frequentius: quod tamen proprie non nisi stipitem signat singularem & erectum. Latinè dixeris Palum sive Vallum. Eustathius : Σταυ-ροὶ δὲ δξὰ καὶ ἀπωξυμένα ξύλα· τὰ καὶ σανίσες πρὸς τοῖς μὴ λαλῆσιν ἐνχῶς· γίνονται ὁ πρὸς τὴν εἰς ἀέρα στάσιν, ἢ πρὸς τὸ εἰς ἀέρα ἵσταῖς. Οἱ δ' ἀνθρωποι Σκόλοπες λέγουσι: Staturi sunt ligna recta & praacuta: qua & Stavara dicuntur ab iis qui minùs ingenuè loquuntur. facta vox, vel quòd ad aërem stent, vel quòd in latum. Hi ipsi & Scolopes dicuntur.
units.tr: In Latin there are almost two names for the cross, and in Greek there are two as well: Stauros [Σταυρὸς] and Skolops [Σκόλοψ]. The first is the more common, though properly it means only a single upright stake. In Latin you may call it palus or vallum. Eustathius says: "Stauroi [Σταυροί] are sharp, pointed pieces of wood, which are also called planks by those who do not speak elegantly. The word is formed either because they stand upright toward the air, or because they are set up toward the air. But men call them Skolopes [Σκόλοπες]." The Latin gloss reads: "Stauri are straight and sharp-pointed timbers, which are also called stavara by those who speak less elegantly. The word is formed either because they stand upright in the air, or because they are set up on high. They are also called Scolopes."

units.la: {1} In Odyss. ξ. initio. tur. Quod ait, ὡς σὺξ© vel in latum, de pluribus junctis verum est, ut solet in castrorum vallo. Neque immuto; etsi ex Hesychio, paullo aliter derivante, possim. Ille sic: Σταυροί, οἱ καλα-πεπηγότες σκόλοπες, χάρακες, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἑστῶτα ξύλα. ἀπὸ τῆς ἑστῶσης σταυροί, ἢ ἐν τῇ εἰς τὴν αὐγὴν ἱστασθαι·
units.tr: {1} On the Odyssey, book 14, at the beginning. tur. What he says, ὡς σὺξ [garbled; apparently 'as a stake'], or 'sideways', holds true of several stakes joined together, as is usual in the rampart of a camp. I do not change it, though I could follow Hesychius, who derives the word a little differently. He writes: Σταυροί, οἱ καλαπεπηγότες σκόλοπες, χάρακες, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἑστῶτα ξύλα. ἀπὸ τῆς ἑστῶσης σταυροί, ἢ ἐν τῇ εἰς τὴν αὐγὴν ἱστασθαι· [Stauroi: the fixed stakes, palisades, and all standing timbers. Stauroi from the standing (hestōsēs), or from standing up into the air (eis tēn augēn histasthai).]

units.la: Stauri, defixi stipites sunt, valli, & omnia ligna recta stantia: ab eo quòd stent Stauri, vel quòd ad auraм consistant. Allusisse ad postremum hoc etymon Prudentius videatur:
units.tr: Stauri are fixed stakes, palisades, and all upright wooden posts standing firm: so called from their standing (stent) firm, or because they stand (consistant) up into the air. Prudentius seems to have alluded to this last derivation:

units.la: Crux ipsum tollat in auras, Viventesque oculos offerat alitibus.
units.tr: Let the cross lift itself up into the air, and offer its living eyes to the birds.

units.la: Hæc Grammatici. sed Lucianus ingeniosè & pro argumento, in Judicio vocalium, derivat à Tau litterâ, quæ figurâ crucem refert. Ait ἀπὸ τύτε (τῆς Ταῦ) καὶ
units.tr: These are the views of the grammarians. But Lucian, cleverly and to suit his argument in the Judgement of the Vowels, derives the word from the letter Tau, which in its shape represents a cross. He says: "from that Tau [ἀπὸ τῆς Ταῦ]…"

units.la: ¹ Περὶ σχ. Hymn. IV. τῆ τιχνήματι τῆ πονηρῷ τὴν πονηρὰν ὑπαωμρίων σωεληθὲν: ab ista etiam, instrumento pessimo (cruci) pessimum nomen venisse. Atque hoc in fine etiam dialogi iterat. Jam Σκόλοψ proprie, vallum, sudemque significat acutam. Hesychius: Σκόλοπες, ὀξέα ξύλα, ὀρθά: Scolopes, acuta ligna, recta. Homerus a:
units.tr: ¹ On the Schemata. Hymn IV. "…by that wicked contrivance, the wicked…" He says that the most wicked name came from that most wicked instrument, the cross. And he repeats this at the end of the dialogue too. Now Skolops [Σκόλοψ] properly means a rampart and a sharp stake. Hesychius: "Skolopes [Σκόλοπες]: sharp timbers, upright": Scolopes, acuta ligna, recta. Homer, a:

units.la: — Σκόλοπες ᾗ ἐν αὐτῇ [τάφρῳ] Ὀξέες ἑσταςιν.
units.tr: "…Within it [the trench] sharp stakes [σκόλοπες] stand [ὀξέες ἕστασιν]."

units.la: Ibi Eustathius: Σκόλοπες, ὀρθὰ ξύλα ἐ ὀξέα, ἃ ᾗ σαφῶς σκάλοων. ἐφ' οὓς ἀνεμορφιότης ἀνεσταυρωμένους ἐλέγονται: Scolopes recta ligna & acuta, quae & Stauros vocabant: in quibus appensi, cruci aut vallo figi dicebantur. Et bene, quòd duo illa verba suggerit, quibus ipsam crucifixionem significabant, Ἀνασταυρῶν & Ἀνασκολοπίζειν. Ita enim plerumque com-
units.tr: There Eustathius says: "Skolopes are straight and sharp timbers, which were also called stauroi, and on which, through cruelty, those crucified were said to be impaled." The Latin reads: "Scolopes are straight and sharp timbers, which they also called stauroi. Those who were hanged on them were said to be fixed to the cross or the stake." He is right, since he suggests those two words by which they signified crucifixion itself: anastaurōn [Ἀνασταυρῶν] and anaskolopizein [Ἀνασκολοπίζειν]. For these are usually compounded in this way, namely to mark the raising up and fixing on high; though elsewhere they also occur simply, stauroō [Σταυρῶ] and skolopizein [Σκολοπίζειν].

units.la: ¹ Iliad. μ. verb. 63. compositè, ad elationem scilicet fixionemque in alto notandam: etsi alias etiam simpliciter, Σταυρῆ & Σκολοπίζειν. Sunt & alia duo verba, quibus vulgò valdè usi, Προσηλῶν & Κρεμάζειν sive Ἀνασταυρῶν. quorum illud clavationem ipsam in ligno proprie notat, hoc suspensionem. In illo, scriptoris aliquis error videtur apud Hesychium: Προσηλωτή, ἀνίσταυτή. atque ego rescribam, ἀνασταυρῶ. In isto, saepe interpretum, qui ad suspensionem vulgariam & in laqueo aptant. Ita quod Arrianus narrat de Musicano: Τῆτον κρεμάσαι Ἀλέξανδρος ... ξύλου ἐν τῇ ἀυλῇ γῇ: aliter versum legi, cùm sic debuerit: Hunc Alexander crucifigi in suâ regione jubet. Curtius satis praexit, qui scribit in crucem sublatum. Ita quod Diodorus Siculus ejus-
units.tr: ¹ Iliad μ, verse 63. There are two other verbs, which were commonly used: prosēloun [Προσηλοῦν] and kremazein [Κρεμάζειν], or anastaurōn. Of these the former properly denotes the nailing itself to the wood, the latter the suspension. In the former there seems to be an error of some copyist in Hesychius: "Prosēlōtē [Προσηλωτή]: anistaurē [ἀνίσταυτή]." I would correct it to anastaurō [ἀνασταυρῶ]. In the latter, the translators often apply it to ordinary hanging and to hanging by a noose. So what Arrian tells of Musicanus, "Touton kremasai Alexandros … xylou en tē aulē gē" [Τῆτον κρεμάσαι Ἀλέξανδρος … ξύλου ἐν τῇ ἀυλῇ γῇ], is read otherwise than it should be. The sentence ought to read: "Alexander orders him to be crucified in his own land." Curtius expresses it quite well, when he writes that he was "lifted up onto the cross."
1. Book VI. 2. Book XIII.

units.la: ejusdem Alexandri rebus de Tyro capta: Τὴς ἢ νέας πόλεως, ὅνλας ἐν ἰλάδης ἢ διχαλίων, ἐκξίμακτιν. idem Curtius recte: Duo millia cruci-bus affixa, per ingens litoris spatium pependerunt. Et exempla plusucula. Tale apud Latinos ipsum Suspendere, quod ad Crucem referendum moneo juventutem. Ut in Silio :
units.tr: …the same Alexander's affairs concerning the capture of Tyre: "Tas de neas poleōs, hōs chilias ē dischiliōn, ekxiphēmaktin" [Τὰς ἢ νέας πόλεως, ὅνλας ἐν ἰλάδης ἢ διχαλίων, ἐκξίμακτιν]: he impaled the men of the new city, about two thousand. Curtius likewise rightly: "Two thousand men, fixed to crosses, hung along a vast stretch of the shore." And there are quite a few examples. Among the Latins, the verb suspendere itself is of this kind, and I advise young readers to refer it to the cross. As in Silius:
"When he saw him hanging from the cruel timber…"

units.la: In Seneca Latrocinium fecit aliquis. quid ergo meruit? ut suspendatur. In Ovidio :
units.tr: In Seneca: "Someone committed robbery. What then did he deserve? To be hanged."

units.la: More vel interea capti suspensus Achai, Qui miser auriferâ teste pendit aquâ.
units.tr: In Ovid: "Likewise, meanwhile, Achaeus, taken captive and hanging, who wretchedly hangs with the gold-bearing water as his witness."

units.la: ¹ Quibus versibus vera historia & sensus è Polybio reddatur iste. Antiochus rex per fraudem Achæum
units.tr: These verses render the true history and meaning from Polybius, as follows. King Antiochus, by treachery, led Achaeus down from the citadel of Sardis and took him by ambush.

units.la: ¹ Lib. I. ² Epist. VII. ³ In Ibin. ⁴ Lib. VIII.
units.tr: ¹ Book I. ² Epistle VII. ³ On the Ibis. ⁴ Book VIII.

units.la: Achæum ex arce Sardium deduxit, & per insidias cepit. καὶ ἰδὼξι, addit, πρῶτον μὲν ἀκρωτηριάσαντ᾽ αὐτὸν τὰ ταλαίπωρον, εἶτ᾽ ἢ ταῦτα τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀπολιμψάμενος ἀνὴρ, καὶ πολλὰ ψυχὰς ἐξ ὄνου ἄσκων, ἀναστρωννύσα τὸ σῶμα: Et visum est, primò admutilare illum miserum & extremas partes succidere, deinde capite ejus resecto & in asininum culleum conjecto, reliquum corpus crucifigere. Hæc res: sperne aliorum inanes logos. Sed & mecum lege, teste pependit aquâ: non triste aut rectè, quod vulgatur. Vult enim, eum non in ipsâ aurifera aquâ, id est Pactolo, suspensum: quî potuit? sed juxta eam, atque illâ quasi arbitrâ & inspectante. Pactolus autem haud longè Sardes, ubi hæc gesta.
units.tr: He took Achaeus by ambush. Polybius adds: "And when they had seen it, first they maimed that wretch and cut off his extremities; then, having cut off his head and put it into an ass's skin, they crucified the rest of the body" [καὶ ἰδόντες … ἀναστρωννύσα τὸ σῶμα]. The Latin reads: "And it was decided, first to mutilate that wretched man and cut off his extremities, then, with his head cut off and placed in an ass's hide, to crucify the rest of the body." That is the account; do not rely on the empty tales of others. But read with me also teste pependit aquā, not triste or recte, as is commonly printed. For he means that Achaeus was hanged not in the gold-bearing water itself, that is the Pactolus (how could he be?), but close beside it, with the river as witness and spectator. The Pactolus is not far from Sardis, where these things happened.
CAP. V.

units.la: Divisio prima Crucium: & de specie vetustissimâ dictum, Assi- xione. Tertullianus per occasio- nem correctus, atque Isis eadem cum Cerere existimata.
units.tr: The first division of crosses: the most ancient form, called assixion (fastening). Tertullian, corrected by an occasion, and Isis thought to be the same as Ceres.

units.la: VErba non ultrà me tenent: rem ordiâmur, cui illustrandæ duplex genus Crucium statuo, Simplex & Compactum. Illud voco, cùm in uno simplicique ligno fit affixio, aut infixio. Quæ crux, meo judicio, prima fuit, & in aliam speciem à rudi hac ventum. Sed ea quoque duplex, ut tetigi: altera ad Affixionem, altera ad Infixionem. Nam alias ad arborem sive stipitem alligabant figebantve hominem, ut in Cupidine Crucifixo Ausonii, quem sic describit:
units.tr: I will not hold myself back any longer; let us begin the matter. To illustrate it I establish a twofold kind of cross: simple and compound. I call the first that in which the fastening or infixing is made on one simple piece of wood. In my judgment this cross was the first, and from this rough form came the other kinds. But this too is twofold, as I touched on: one kind for affixion, the other for infixion. For they sometimes bound or fixed a man to a tree or a stake, as in Ausonius's Cupid Crucified, which he describes thus:
Eli-

units.la: Eligitur mœsto myrtus notissima luco, Invidiosa Deum pœnis. Cruciaverat illic, Spreta olim, memorem Veneris, Proserpina Adonim. Hujus in excelso suspensum stipite Amorem, Devinctum post terga manus, substrictaque plantis Vincula mœrentem, nullo moderamine pœnæ Adsigunt.
units.tr: The myrtle, most famous, is chosen from a grove of mourning, hateful to the gods for its punishments. There once Proserpina, scorned by Adonis, who remembered Venus, had tormented him. Love, hung high on the trunk of this tree, his hands bound behind his back and cords fastened to his feet, they fix to the stake, grieving, with no measure of punishment.

units.la: Verba omnia nota : videbis & in arboris stipite appensum, nec manibus expansis, sed à tergo devinctis, denique nec clavis sed funibus substrictum : nisi forte in pedibus. Simile in Tertulliano, de Tiberio : qui Saturni sacerdotes, ut inquit, in eisdem arboribus templi sui, obumbra-
units.tr: All these words are familiar. You will see that he is hung on the trunk of a tree, not with his hands outstretched but bound behind his back, and finally fastened not with nails but with cords, unless perhaps at the feet. Similar is Tertullian on Tiberius, who, as he says, exposed the priests of Saturn on votive crosses, on the very trees of his own temple, shadowy accomplices of crimes.

units.la: ¹ Apolog. cap. VIII. bratricibus scelerum, votivis Crucibus exposuit. In Martyrologio 1, de Paphnutio: Ipse palmæ arbori affigitur, ceteri autem ferro necantur. Nec ambigimus arbores plerumque huic rei servisse, præsertim in grandi numero cruciandorum, sive recisas leviter & ad Crucem aptatas, sive etiam comantes. Sed & in stipite simplici idem fuit. Ex Tertulliano 2: Quanto distinguitur à Crucis stipite Pallas Attica, vel Ceres Farrea, quæ sine effigie, rudi palo & informi ligno prostant? Nam rudem ecce palum componit & assimilat cum Cruce. Sed in ejus verbis menda de Cerere Farrea. Cur enim sic appellet? an quia far invenerit? esto. atqui non omnis Ceres sic efficta, sed certa aliqua, & in loco quem voluit ex-
units.tr: ¹ Apolog. cap. VIII. In the Martyrology 1, on Paphnutius: He himself is fastened to a palm tree, while the others are put to death with the sword. Nor do we doubt that trees were mostly used for this purpose, especially where there was a great number to be tormented, whether they were lightly trimmed and fitted for the cross, or even left with their foliage. But the same was also true of a plain stake. From Tertullian 2: How far is the Attic Pallas, or the Ceres of the Farrea, distinguished from the stake of the cross, which stand without an image, on a rough post and a shapeless piece of wood? For look, he puts a rough post side by side with the cross and likens them. But there is a fault in his words concerning Ceres Farrea. Why does he call her that? Because she discovered grain? Granted. Yet not every Ceres was made in this way, but a certain one, and in the place he meant, as with Pallas, who is at Athens. I think we should read Faria or Pharia, as if he had said the Ceres who is in Egypt. And I believe Isis is meant, who differs from Ceres in name but shares her divinity.

units.la: ¹ XXIV. Septembr. ² Apolog. cap. XVI. expressum : sicut de Pallade, quæ Athenis. Legendum arbitror, Faria sive Pharia: quasi dixerit Cererem, quæ in Ægypto. Et intelligi credam Isidem : quæ nomine divertit à Cerere, numine communicat.
units.tr: ¹ XXIV. Septembr. ² Apolog. cap. XVI. So Herodotus: Demeter [Δημήτηρ], Isis [Ἴσις]. (The Greek here is corrupt; the sense is Demeter and Isis.)
So Herodotus: Demeter [Ἀημήτης ϡ, Ι″σις], Isis.

units.la: In Apuleio , ipsa de se Isis: Me primigenii Phryges Pessinuntiam matrem nominant, me Eleusinii vetustam deam Cererem.
units.tr: In Apuleius, Isis herself says of herself: The first-born Phrygians call me the Mother of Pessinus; the Eleusinians call me the ancient goddess Ceres.

units.la: Eusebius de Præparatione : Φασὶ τοίνυν Αἰγύπτιοι τ̀ μὲν Ὀσίριν εἶναι τ̀ Διόνυσον, τὴν δὲ Ἴσιν τὴν Δήμη-τρα: Aiunt Ægyptii Osirim esse Bacchum, Isidem vero Cererem.
units.tr: Eusebius, in the Preparation: The Egyptians, then, say that Osiris is Bacchus, and Isis is Demeter [Φασὶ τοίνυν Αἰγύπτιοι τὸν μὲν Ὀσίριν εἶναι τὸν Διόνυσον, τὴν δὲ Ἴσιν τὴν Δήμητρα].

units.la: ¹ Lib. xi. de Asin. ² Lib. ii. cap. i.
units.tr: ¹ Lib. xi. de Asin. ² Lib. ii. cap. i.
CAP. VI.

units.la: Altera Simplicis Crucis species, Infixio. Seneca, Hesychius, Plato, Plinius, illustrati.
units.tr: Another species of the simple cross: impalement. Illustrated from Seneca, Hesychius, Plato and Pliny.

units.la: ATque hæc fuit in Simplici Cruce Affixio : est & in eâdem Infixio. qualis ? cum nudum hominem erecto acutoque stipiti infigebant, eâ formâ & facie quam exempla hæc docebunt. Seneca ¹: Video illic Cruces nec unius generis, sed aliter ab aliis fabricatas. Alii capite converso in terram suspendere, alii per obscœna stipitem egerunt. Duo in iis verbis observes, & Cruces varias fuisse, quod nunc diducimus: & inter eas, Infixionem. Quam magis etiam aperit idem Seneca ²: Cogita hoc loco carcerem & Cruces, & ada-
units.tr: This, then, was the affixion in the simple cross. There is also an impalement in the same kind of cross. What was it like? They fixed a naked man to an upright, sharp stake, in the shape and form which the following examples will show. Seneca¹: I see crosses there, not of one kind but made differently from one another. Some suspended the head turned towards the ground; others drove a stake through the private parts. In these words you may observe that there were various crosses, which we now distinguish, and among them impalement. Seneca himself explains this more clearly²: Think here of a prison and crosses, and a stake driven up through the middle of a man, coming out through his mouth.

units.la: ¹ Consolat. ad Mart. c. xx. ²Epist. xiv. adactum per medium hominem, qui per os emergat, stipitem. Viden' clarè medium hominem scissum & transfossum? Atque id imagine etiam illustrat Hesychius: Σκόλοψιν, ὡς ὀπλησιν· τὸ γὰρ παλαιὸν τὰς κακουργοῦντας ἀνεσκολόπιζον, ὀξύροπος ξύλον διὰ ῥάχεως καὶ τῆς ῥάχης, καθάπερ τῆς ὀπταμένης ἰχθῦς ἐπὶ ὀβελίσκων: Sudifixionem dixeris, quasi Affationem. Nam antiquitus maleficos fudi infigebant, acuto ligno penetrantes spinam & dorsum, sicuti assos in verubus pisces. Vbi amplius disco, proprie hoc esse Σκόλοψιν; & Σκολοπίζειν ubi legitur, plerumque referendum ad hanc formam. Ista Crux nescio an Mæcenati etiam descripta: cuius versus apud Senecam jam olim sic legimus:
units.tr: ¹ Consolation to Marcia, ch. 20. ²Letter 14. Do you see clearly the man split and pierced through the middle? Hesychius also illustrates this with a picture. Hesychius: Skolopsin, that is, impaling: for in ancient times they impaled wrongdoers, driving a sharp-pointed piece of wood through the back and the spine, just as fish are roasted on spits [Σκόλοψιν, ὡς ὀπλησιν· τὸ γὰρ παλαιὸν τὰς κακουργοῦντας ἀνεσκολόπιζον, ὀξύροπος ξύλον διὰ ῥάχεως καὶ τῆς ῥάχης, καθάπερ τῆς ὀπταμένης ἰχθῦς ἐπὶ ὀβελίσκων]. You might call it sudifixion, as if it were affation. For in antiquity they fixed malefactors on stakes, piercing the spine and back with a sharp piece of wood, like fish roasted on spits. Here I learn more clearly that this is properly skolopsis, and where we read skolopizein it should mostly be referred to this form. I am not sure whether this cross was also described by Maecenas, whose verses we have long read in Seneca as follows:
¹ Letter 101.

units.la: Hanc mihi, vel acutâ Si sedeam Cruce, sustine. Vita dum superest, bene est.
units.tr: Bear this for me, even if I sit upon the sharp cross. While life remains, all is well.

units.la: Vult miser & adsuspirat vivere, etiam inter tormenta, & in istâ maximè cruciante Cruce, quam signanter dixit Acutam. Sed ait etiam Sedere: benè. Nam ille profectò habitus hominis ab infero in superum sic transfixi. Hoc ipsum genus Ἀναστανρωθῆναι, dictum Græcis, quasi diffindere & dissecare. Hesychius: Ἀναστανρωθῆναι, ἀναστανρολογισθῆναι. Plato eo verbo usus: Μαστιγούσθαι, σταυρωθῆναι, τυλάς τῶν ἡ πάντα ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν: Flagellabitur, distorquebitur, denique omnia mala passus Cruce diffindetur. Plinii 2 etiam verba huc referam narrantis, Polybium cum Scipione in Africa leones homicidas crucifixos vidisse, quia ceteri metu pœnæ similis B abster-
units.tr: The wretch wishes and sighs to live even amid the torments, and especially on this most agonizing cross, which he rightly called sharp. But he also says sit: all is well. For that was surely the posture of a man transfixed from below upwards. This very kind of punishment the Greeks called anastaurōthēnai [Ἀναστανρωθῆναι], as if to split and cut apart. Hesychius: anastaurōthēnai [Ἀναστανρωθῆναι], that is, anastaurologisthēnai [ἀναστανρολογισθῆναι]. Plato used the word: mastigousthai, staurōthēnai [Μαστιγούσθαι, σταυρωθῆναι] and the rest, as if of sinners who suffer everything from their own deeds: He will be flogged, racked, and finally, having suffered every evil, will be split on the cross [τυλάς τῶν ἡ πάντα ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν]. I will also cite the words of Pliny, who tells that Polybius, in Africa with Scipio, saw man-killing lions crucified, because the others were frightened by the same punishment as the crime deterred. For who would believe that this was an elaborate and composed crucifixion? Not I. I will take it of this ready and chance impalement on a stake, or indeed affixion.

units.la: ¹ II. De Repub. ² Lib. VIII. cap. XVI. absterrerentur eâdem noxâ. Quis enim credat operosam & compositam crucifixionem illam fuisse? non ego : & accipiam de hac promptâ & fortuitâ in stipite infixione, sive etiam affixione.
units.tr: ¹ On the Republic, book 2. ² Book 8, ch. 16. They were deterred by the same offence. Who would believe that this was an elaborate and composed crucifixion? Not I. I will take it of this ready and chance impalement on a stake, or indeed affixion.
CAP. VII.

units.la: In genere de Cruce Compaƈtâ : tum de primâ ejus specie, Decussatâ. & an hæc sit Andreana?
units.tr: On the compacted cross in general; then its first kind, the decussate cross; and whether this is the St Andrew's cross?

units.la: AT Compaƈta Crux est, quæ manu facta, idque è duplici ligno. Ita septuaginta Interpretes Ptolemæani, libro Josuæ quâ vulgò est, lignum, & Chaldæo paraphraste, Crux, ipsi verterunt ＊ξύλον δίδυμον : benè sanè, ad hanc formam. Hæc est plena & vera Crux, in quâ brachia etiam explicantur, atque ideò Patibulum non semel dicta. Hujus species triplex, ut distinctè imò curiosè edisseram, & semel tollam dubitationes aut lites. Est Decussata, est Commissa, est Immissa. Illa prima mihi dicitur, in quâ duo ligna directa & æquabilia, inter se obliquantur. Decussare hoc enim Romani dixerunt. Hieronymus 1: Decussare, est per medium secare, veluti si duæ regulæ concurrant ad speciem litteræ X quæ figura est Crucis. Nec minùs clarè Isidorus 2: X littera, & in figurâ Crucem, & in numero decem demonstrat. Obscuriùs paullò alii Patres & Doctores nostri, ut Iustinus Martyr 3: qui illud Platonis in Timæo, E'χ(ασεν αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ παντί: Decussavit eum in universo: adseveranter ad Christum & Crucem tm nostram retulit, quo nisi hoc aspectu? Iam cùm transversis obliquatisque manibus benedictionem Iacobi eôdem aptant: quid nisi hæc forma in oculis?
units.tr: A compacted cross is one that is made by hand, and made of two pieces of wood. So the Seventy interpreters of Ptolemy's time, in the book of Joshua where the common text has wood, and the Chaldee paraphrast, with cross, rendered it, calling it a double wood [ξύλον δίδυμον]. This was certainly right, for this is the shape in question. This is the full and true cross, in which the arms are also extended, and for this reason it is also called the patibulum. It has three kinds. I shall set them out clearly, indeed with care, and settle doubts and disputes once for all. There is the decussate, the joined, and the fixed. The first I take to be that in which two straight and even pieces of wood cross each other obliquely. For the Romans called this decussare. Jerome says: To decussate is to cut through the middle, as when two rules meet in the shape of the letter X, which is the figure of the cross. Isidore is no less clear: The letter X signifies both a cross in its shape and ten in its number. Our other Fathers and teachers are somewhat more obscure, as Justin Martyr, who, applying to Christ and to our cross Plato's words in the Timaeus, Decussated him in the universe [ἐχίασεν αὐτὸν ἐν τῷ παντί], confidently referred them to Christ and the cross. What else could he have had in view? Again, when Jacob with crossed and twisted hands applies the same to the blessing, what else but this shape is before their eyes?

units.la: 1 In Hierem. cap. xxxi. 2 Lib. 1. Orig. c. iii. 3 Advers. Triph.
units.tr: 1 On Jeremiah, chap. 31. 2 Book 1 of Origen, chap. 3. 3 Against Trypho.

units.la: +Damascenus 1: Ἰακὼβ ἀσπαζόμενος τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου, συνηλαγμένως ταῖς χερσὶ τὰς υἱὰς Ἰωσὴφ εὐλογήσας, καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ σταυροῦ διαγράφει σαφέστατα: Iacob adorans extremum virga, alternantibus manibus liberos Ioseph benedicens, etiam signum hoc Crucis describit manifestissimè. Quid χεῖρες ἱσταὶ συνηλαγμέναι etsi non ambiguum, tamen audiamus Cedrenum commodè explicantem. Ἰσραὴλ (idem cum Iacobo) τὰς χεῖρας ἀμφοτέρας, τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν ἐπὶ τὴν νεώτερον, τὴν ἀριστερὰν δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν πρεσβυτέραν τὴν κεφαλὴν τιθεὶς: Israël manus permutans, dextram quidem in junioris, sinistram vero in senioris caput imponens. Et Tertullianum 2 in ipsâ re: Impositis & intermutatis manibus benedixit, & quidem ita transversim obliquatis inter se, ut Christum deformantes, jam tunc portenderent bene-
units.tr: +Damascenus 1: "Jacob, kissing the tip of the staff, blessing the sons of Joseph with crossed hands [Ἰακὼβ ἀσπαζόμενος τὸ ἄκρον τῆς ῥάβδου, συνηλαγμένως ταῖς χερσὶ τὰς υἱὰς Ἰωσὴφ εὐλογήσας], also marks out the sign of the cross most clearly [καὶ τὸ σημεῖον τοῦ σταυροῦ διαγράφει σαφέστατα]." What "crossed hands" [χεῖρες ἱσταὶ συνηλαγμέναι] means is not ambiguous, but let us hear Cedrenus explain it aptly: "Israel, who is the same as Jacob, placing both hands crosswise, the right on the head of the younger and the left on the head of the elder." And Tertullian, speaking of the act itself: "He blessed with his hands laid on and crossed over, and indeed so slantwise crossed over one another that, by forming the figure of Christ, they already then foreshadowed the blessing that was to come upon Christ."

units.la: ¹ Lib. iv. de Orth. cap. xii. ² De Baptis. cap. viii. benedictionem in Christum futuram.
units.tr: ¹ Book 4 of On Orthodoxy, chap. 12. ² On Baptism, chap. 8. that the blessing was to come upon Christ.

units.la: Quomodo Christum deformarunt illæ manus? imò Crucem: & sic mihi libido aliquando legere: sed refræno, & accipio Christum crucifixum. Hæc illa est quam Andreanam hodie dicimus, validâ & satis veteri famâ divum istum in eâ cruciatum. Anne verâ? facit me ut ambigam Martyrologium Romanum: in quo vt & hoc saltem legas,in Cruce suspensum. & magis Hippolytus , qui scribit Crucifixum Patris in Achaiâ, ad arborem oliuæ rectum. Quid magis contra famam? Atque hæc fixio ad Simplicem nostram potiùs abeat, longè à Decussatâ.
units.tr: How did those hands deform Christ? Rather, the cross. So sometimes I am tempted to read it that way, but I restrain myself and take it to mean Christ crucified. This is the cross that we today call St Andrew's, supported by a strong and fairly old tradition that the saint was tortured on it. Is the tradition true? The Roman Martyrology makes me doubt it, in which you may at least read this, hung on a cross. Even more so Hippolytus, who writes that Andrew was crucified at Patras in Achaia, straight on an olive tree. What could be more contrary to the tradition? And this fixing would rather be taken to our simple cross, far from the decussate.
¹ In the Greek commentary.
CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Commissa Crux quid nobis sit? exemplis testibusque asserta, tum etiam vestigio nostra lingua.
units.tr: What is the crux commissa for us? It is asserted by examples and witnesses, and also by a trace in our own language.

units.la: IAm Commissam Crucem, appello, cum ligno erecto brevius alterum superne, & de ipso capite committitur, sic ut nihil exstet. ea forma examussim est in T litterâ, quam uno ore omnes cum Cruce componunt. Lucianus ubi Tau accusatur: Τῷ γὰρ τότε σωμάτι φασι τὰς τυχέντας ἀκολουθήσαντας καὶ μιμησαμένης αὐτῆς τὸ πλάσμα, ἐπειτα χήματι τετάγῳ ξύλα τεκτήναντας, ἀνθρώπως ἀπακολουθεῖζειν ἐπ' αὐτά: Hujus enim corporis filum tyrannos ajunt secutos, ejusque speciem imitatos, simili deinde figurâ ligna fabricasse, & homines in iis fixisse. Palàm est Crucem intelligi. Tertullianus : Ipsa enim littera Graecorum Tau,
units.tr: Now I call the crux commissa a cross made of an upright beam with a shorter beam fastened across the top, joined to the head itself, so that nothing projects beyond it. This shape corresponds exactly to the letter T, and everyone agrees in comparing it to the cross. Lucian, where he accuses the Tau, says: "For they say that the men of that time, following the body and imitating its form, then made wood in the shape of a crossbeam and fixed men to it" [Τῷ γὰρ τότε σωμάτι φασι τοὺς τυχόντας ἀκολουθήσαντας καὶ μιμησαμένους αὐτοῦ τὸ πλάσμα, ἔπειτα σχήματι τετάγῳ ξύλα τεκτήναντας, ἀνθρώπους ἀπακολουθεῖζειν ἐπ' αὐτά]. Clearly the cross is meant. Tertullian: "For the Greek letter Tau itself,

units.la: 1 III adver. Marcion. Tau, nostra autem T, species Crucis. Isidorus1: Tau littera speciem Crucis demonstrat. Hieronymus2: Antiquis Hebraorum litteris, quibus usque hodie Samarita utuntur, extrema Tau Crucis habet similitudinem. Paulinus Nolanus3: Christus non multitudine nec virtute legionum, sed jam tunc in sacramento Crucis, cujus figura per litteram Graecam Tau numero trecentorum exprimitur, adversarios Principes debellavit. Adstruunt etiam picturae, & nostra lingua. In illis quidem, passim hodie videas D. Antonii vetustissimi monachi penulae & manui assui aut imponi hanc crucem. An quia Ægyptius ille vir, quibus jam olim notum, & inter sacra hoc signum? Certe in obeliscis, qui inde Romam vecti, sculptum sic vidimus
units.tr: Tau, but our T, is the form of the cross. Isidore: "The letter Tau shows the form of the cross." Jerome: "In the ancient letters of the Hebrews, which the Samaritans still use today, the final Tau has the likeness of a cross." Paulinus of Nola: "Christ defeated the adversary princes not by a multitude or the strength of legions, but already then by the sacrament of the cross, whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter Tau, which has the number three hundred." Pictures also support this, and so does our own language. In the pictures, you may see everywhere today the cross placed on the cloak and hand of the very ancient monk St Anthony. Was this because that Egyptian man knew it long ago, and this sign was among their sacred things? Certainly on the obelisks, which were carried from there to Rome, we have seen it carved in this way

units.la: 1 De vocat. gent. 2 In Ezech. cap. ix. 3 Epist. ad Scu. mus (woodcut mark) : cum anulo tamen vel (cross mark) ansulâ superne, nec satis solidè scio ad quam rem aut usum. Sed de præcipuâ ipsâ notâ, dignum aliquid notâ Ecclesiasticæ nostræ historiæ prodiderunt. Ruffinus : Signum hoc dominica Crucis, inter illas quas dicunt ἱεϱογλυφικὰς id est Sacerdotales litteras, habere Ægyptii dicuntur, velut unum ex iis quæ apud illos sunt litterarum elementis. Cujus litteræ seu vocabuli hanc asserunt esse interpretationem, VITA VENTVRA. Sozomenus : Φασὶ δὲ Ϝ ταῦ καθ' αὐτὸ ... γεμίνε τύτε (τὸ Σαραπιδῶν) τινὰς τῶν ἀναγλυφικῶν ἱερογλυφικῶν χαρακτήρων ... ἐμφερεῖς ἐγχειχαραγμένας τοῖς λίθοις ἀναφανῆναι. Adjunt templo isto (Sarapidis) diruto & disjecto, quasdam ex iis, quas vocant Hieroglyphicas notas, similes signo Crucis inscriptas lapidibus apparuisse. Ab iis autem, qui docti haec talia, explicatam eam notam, significare vitam venturam. In Suidâ etiam historiola haec breviter: E'πὶ Θεοδοσίου τῆ μεγάλῳ βασιλείᾳ κατὰ μερυμένην τ' Ἑλλη- νικῶν ἱερῶν, ἐυρέθησαν ἐν τῷ Σαραπίδι ἱερογλυφικὰ γράμματα σὺν ἕχον- τα τύπους. ὅτις Χριστιανίστες, ἔφασαν σημαίνειν τ' σαυτὸν παρὰ τοῖς ἱερογλυφικὰ γινώ- σκοντες γράμματα ζωὴν ἐπιεχομένην.
units.tr: (woodcut mark), but with a ring, or (cross mark) a loop, above. I do not know with enough certainty for what purpose or use. But as to this very mark itself, the writers of our ecclesiastical history have handed down something worth noting. Rufinus: "The Egyptians are said to have this sign of the Lord's cross among those characters which they call hieroglyphic, that is, sacred letters, as one of the elements of their writing. They assert that this is the interpretation of that letter or word: VITA VENTURA (the coming life). Sozomen: [Φασὶ δὲ τὸ ταῦ καθ' αὐτὸ ... γεμίνε τύτε (τὸ Σαραπιδῶν) τινὰς τῶν ἀναγλυφικῶν ἱερογλυφικῶν χαρακτήρων ... ἐμφερεῖς ἐγχειχαραγμένας τοῖς λίθοις ἀναφανῆναι.] They add that when that temple of Serapis was torn down and thrown into ruin, some of those characters which they call hieroglyphic, like the sign of the cross, appeared carved on the stones. Those who were learned in such matters explained that this mark signifies the coming life. Also in the Suda there is a short little story: [Ἐπὶ Θεοδοσίου τοῦ μεγάλου βασιλείᾳ κατὰ μερυμένην τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἱερῶν, εὑρέθησαν ἐν τῷ Σαραπίδι ἱερογλυφικὰ γράμματα σὺν ἔχοντα τύπους, ὅτι Χριστιανίζοντες ἔφασαν σημαίνειν τὸν σταυρὸν παρὰ τοῖς ἱερογλυφικὰ γινώσκοντες γράμματα ζωὴν ἐπερχομένην.]

units.la: Theodosio magno regnante, cum fana Gentilium diruerentur, inventa sunt in Serapidis templo Hieroglyphica littera, habentes Crucis formas, quas videntes ii gentilium qui Christo jam addicti erant, ajebant significare Crucem apud peritos Hieroglyphicarum notarum Vitam venturam. Atqui & à linguâ argumentum petii, sed nostrâ. Nos inquam Belgæ hodie, bacillos in hanc formam, quos ægrorum brachiis sustentaculum subjicimus, vocamus ipsâ Latinâ voce Cruckas.
units.tr: In the reign of the great Theodosius, when the temples of the Gentiles were being demolished, hieroglyphic letters were found in the temple of Serapis, having the shape of the cross. Those of the Gentiles who had already come over to Christ, seeing them, said that the cross, among those skilled in hieroglyphic letters, signifies the coming life. But I have also drawn evidence from language, our own. We Belgians today call those little sticks, which we place under the arms of the sick as a support, by the very Latin word cruckas.
CAP. IX.

units.la: Affirmata Crux Immissa e scriptis maximè Patrum : ipsi alii per alios, & imaginibus per nos etiam, explicati.
units.tr: The Immissa cross affirmed, chiefly from the writings of the Fathers; the same Fathers explained by one another, and also by images, by us.

units.la: DEnique Immissa crux est, cum ligno erecto transversum alterum injungitur atque immittitur, sed sic ut ipsum secet. Ita eminentia hic semper aliqua & capitellum, aliter quàm in Commissa. Etiam anguli hic sive fines quaterni, illic terni. Quis de istâ ambiget? Ingerunt eam oculis Pictura pariter & Scripturæ priscæ. Sed illas omitto aut differo : hæ variæ & obviæ sunt, atque ex iis eligam non colligam, nostro more. Iustinus signanter in primis deformat adverExplicat vetus illud vaticinium de Unicorni, & ad Crucem sic aptat:
units.tr: Finally, the Immissa cross is one in which a second beam is laid across an upright one and driven into it, but in such a way that it cuts through it. So here there is always some projection, and a little head, unlike the Commissa. Also, the angles or ends here are four, and there three. Who would doubt this? Both painting and the ancient inscriptions present it to the eyes. But I set those aside or defer them: they are many and easy to find, and from them I will choose rather than collect, as is my custom. Justin, in particular and above all, sets out and explains that old prophecy about the unicorn, and fits it to the cross thus:

units.la: Μονοκέρωλος γὰρ κέρατα ἔδειξεν ἄμα πρέ-γματ' ἢ χρήματ' ἔχοι αὐτῆς ἐπεῖν ἢ πρὸς ἀπ' ἀδέξαι, ἐπὶ μὴ τοῦ τόπου ὡς τὸν Σῶζοντα δέκτυσιν. ἐξ ἴου γὰρ ἐν ἱστὶ τὸ ξύλον, ἀφ' ἧς ἐστὶ τὸ ἀνώτατον μέγα ὡς κέρας ἐπηγε-μένον, ὅταν τὸ ἄλλο ξύλον σταυρωμένον ᾖ, καὶ ἑκατέρωθεν ὡς κέρατα τῷ ἑνὶ κέρατι παραξευγμένα τὰ ἄκρα φαίνεται, καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ὡς κέρας καὶ αὐτὸ ἐξέχον ἐστὶν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπανοχῆται οἱ σταυρού-μενοι:
units.tr: Μονόκερως γὰρ κέρατα ἔδειξεν ἅμα πράγματα ἢ χρήματα ἔχοι αὐτῆς ἐπεῖν ἢ πρὸς ἀπ' ἀδέξαι, ἐπὶ μὴ τοῦ τόπου ὡς τὸν Σῶζοντα δέκτυσιν. (The unicorn's horns show that the thing has... the place where the Saviour is received; for the wood is one, from which the upper part rises like a great horn, when the other wood is crossed, and on either side the ends appear joined to the one horn like horns, and the piece fixed in the middle stands out like a horn, on which the crucified rest and lean.)

units.la: Unicornis enim cornua alteri rei aut figura haud quispiam similia dixerit aut ostenderit, quam illi quae Crucem refert. Rectum enim unum est lignum a quo est suprema pars in cornu sublata, cum alterum lignum aptatum est: & utrimque tamquam cornua illi uni cornu conjuncta, extrema apparent: & illud in medio defixum, & ipsum tamquam cornu eminet, in quo requiescunt & innituntur crucifixi.
units.tr: The unicorn's horns could not be said or shown to be like anything else except that which represents the cross. For one beam is upright, and from it the upper part rises like a horn, when the other beam is fitted on; and on either side the ends appear, joined to that one horn like horns; and the piece fixed in the middle also projects like a horn, on which the crucified rest and lean.
Ob-

units.la: Obscuriuscula alibi verba, sed hac parte liquidissima, quòd eminens unum cornu facit à vertice crucis. Iam alii Patrum, variâ imagine, non sine lasciviâ quâdam ingeniorum & stili eam describunt & notificant. Ut Hieronymus 1 : Ipsa species Crucis, quid est nisi forma quadrata mundi? Aves quando volant ad æthera, formam Crucis assumunt. Homo natans per aquas, vel orans, formâ Crucis visitur. Ut Tertullianus2 : Victorias adoratis, cum in Tropæis Cruces intestina sint tropæorum. Omnes illi imaginum suggestus in signis, monilia crucium sunt. Sipara illa vexillorum & cantabrorum stola crucium sunt. Laudo diligentiam, noluistis incultas Cruces confecrare. Ut Minutius Felix3 : Cruces nec colimus, nec optamus. Vos plane, qui ligneos Deos consecratis, cratis, cruces ligneas, ut deorum vestrorum partes, forsitan adoratis. nam & signa ipsa, & cantabra, & vexilla castrorum quid aliud quàm inaurata Cruces sunt & ornata? Trophaa vestra victricia non tantùm simplicis Crucis faciem, verùm & affixi hominis imitantur. Signum sanè Crucis naturaliter visimus in navi, cùm velis tumentibus vehitur, cùm expansis palmulis labitur: & cùm erigitur jugum, Crucis signum est: & cùm homo porrectis manibus Deum purâ mente vener/ atur. Ita signo Crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur, aut vestra religio formatur. Ut Maximus Taurinensis : Grande est Crucis sacramentum, &, si intelligamus, per hoc signum mundus ipse salvatur. Nam cùm à nautis scinditur mare, prius arbor erigitur, velum distenditur, ut Cruce Domini factâ aquarum fluenta rumpantur. Sed & bonus
units.tr: His words elsewhere are somewhat obscure, but in this part they are quite clear, since the projecting horn makes the top of the cross. Other Fathers, with varied imagery, describe and point out the cross not without a certain playfulness of wit and style. Thus Jerome: "What is the very shape of the cross, if not the square form of the world? Birds, when they fly up to the heavens, take the form of the cross. A man swimming through the waters, or praying, is seen in the form of the cross." Thus Tertullian: "You worship victories, since the crosses are the inner parts of the trophies. All those supports for images on your standards are crosses; those little banners and the stoles of your heralds are crosses. I praise your diligence; you would not consecrate crosses unadorned." Thus Minucius Felix: "We neither worship crosses nor desire them. You certainly, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as parts of your gods; for your standards, your heralds' staves, and the banners of your camps are nothing else than gilded and decorated crosses. Your victorious trophies imitate not only the shape of a simple cross but also that of a man fixed to it. Surely we see the sign of the cross naturally in a ship, when it is carried with swelling sails, when it glides with its little sails spread; and when the yard is raised, it is the sign of the cross; and when a man prays to God with pure mind, his hands stretched out. So either natural reason rests on the sign of the cross, or your religion is formed by it." Thus Maximus of Turin: "Great is the sacrament of the cross, and, if we understand, the world itself is saved by this sign." For when the sea is cut by sailors, first the mast is raised and the sail stretched, so that by the making of the Lord's cross the flow of the waters is broken. But also the good

units.la: {¶} De Cruce Dom. Homil. II. bonus agricola, cùm parat terra solum vertere, non nisi per signum Crucis id facere conatur. Dum enim aratro dentale subjicit, afficit (lege affigit) aures, stivam inserit, figuram Crucis imitatur. Calum quoque ipsum hujus signi figurâ dispositum est. Nam cùm quatuor partibus distinguitur, Oriente, Occidente, Meridiano, ac Septentrione, quatuor quasi Crucis angulis continetur. Ipsius etiam incessus hominis, cùm manus levaverit, Crucem pingit. atque ideò elevatis manibus orare praecipimur, ut ipso quoque membrorum gestu passionem Domini fateamur. Et diffusissimè omnium Justinus 1 : Καὶ κοσμοῦ διὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ χρήματι τὰ ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ διοικεῖται, ἡ κοινωνίαν ἔχειν δύναται. Θάλασσα μὲν γὰρ ἡ τίμιος τὸ πᾶν, ἂν μὴ τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα ἢ τὸ ἴσον, ἐν τῇ γῇ σῶον μένει. γῆ γὰρ ἀγρὸς ἄνευ ἀνθρώπου. Σκαπτῆς δ᾽ ἐργασίαν ἡ ποιοῦντος,
units.tr: {¶} On the Lord's Cross, Homily 2: "The good farmer, when he prepares to turn over the soil, does not attempt it except by the sign of the cross. For when he fits the share to the plough, he fastens the ears (read: fastens), he inserts the handle, he imitates the figure of the cross. The heaven itself too is arranged in the figure of this sign. For when it is divided into four parts, East, West, South, and North, it is contained by four angles, as it were, of the cross. Also the very gait of a man, when he has raised his hands, paints a cross; and therefore we are commanded to pray with raised hands, so that by the very gesture of our limbs we may confess the Lord's passion." And most fully of all, Justin: [Καὶ κοσμοῦ διὰ πάντα τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ χρήματι τὰ ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ διοικεῖται, ἡ κοινωνίαν ἔχειν δύναται. Θάλασσα μὲν γὰρ ἡ τίμιος τὸ πᾶν, ἂν μὴ τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα ἢ τὸ ἴσον, ἐν τῇ γῇ σῶον μένει. γῆ γὰρ ἀγρὸς ἄνευ ἀνθρώπου. Σκαπτῆς δ᾽ ἐργασίαν ἡ ποιοῦντος] (Justin: "Nothing in the world can be administered or have fellowship without this sign on the cross..." — for the sea, the precious thing, does not stay safe on land unless this shape is present; for land is a field without a man, and the labour of the digger...)

units.la: 1 Apolog. 11. τὰς, ὧδὲ βαυαυσκεφοὶ ὁμοίως, ἐ μὴ διὰ τ' τὸ κῆμα τοῦτο ἐχόντων ἐγκαλέων. Τὸ δ' ἀνθρώπειον κῆμα ἔδιν ἄλλο τ' ἀλόγων ζώων διαφέρει, ἢ τῷ ὀρθόν τι ἔχειν, ᾧ ἐπλα-τιν χαριζῶν ἔχειν, ἐ ἐν τῷ ἀπεγεώπῳ ἀπὸ τῆς μέσης τιτιμένον τ' λεγόμενον μυξωτή-ῃ Φέρειν, διὸ ὃ ἡ τι ἀναπνοὴ ἔτι τῷ ζῴῳ, καὶ ἐδὲν ἄλλο δέιχνυσιν ἡ τὸ κῆμα τῆς Στωϊκῆς. καὶ τὰ παρ' ὑμῖν ὁ σύμβολα τὴν τοῦ κήματος τῦτο δύναμιν δηλοῖ. * * * ἀν μὴ ... ἡμῶν παντα-χῶ γίνονται, ἐ ἐχ-ῆς καὶ δυνάμεως τὰ σημεῖα ἐν τύτοις δεικνύντες, ἐν ᾧ μὴ νοῦντες τῦτο παρὰτῆι. καὶ τῶν παρ' ὑμῖν ἀπολογιζόντων Αὐτοκρατόρων τὰς εἰκόνας ἐπὶ τύτῳ τῷ κήματι ἀνατίθετε, καὶ Ἰησοῦς διὰ γραμμάτων ἱστορομάζετε.
units.tr: Apol. 11. [Justin, First Apology, ch. 11, in the Greek as printed, which is garbled.] The human form differs from those of the irrational animals only in having something upright, so that it can stand erect and not bend forward, with the nose projecting from the middle of the face, through which the living creature breathes; and it shows nothing other than the sign of the cross [σταυρός]. Your symbols too declare the power of this sign. Wherever our people are found, the signs of the cross, which they display without strength and power, are present in these things, though they do not recognise it. You also set the images of your emperors on this very sign, and you name Jesus by letters.

units.la: Confiderate omnia qua in mundo sunt, an sine signo hoc Crucis gubernentur, aut possint prabere sui usum. Mare enim non scinditur, nisi tropæum istud, quod malus appellatur, salvum in navi maneat. Terra non aratur sine eo. Fossores vero opus non absolvunt, neque
units.tr: Consider all the things in the world: whether they are governed without this sign of the Cross, or can offer their use without it. For the sea is not parted unless that trophy, which is called the mast, remains safe in the ship. The land is not ploughed without it. Diggers do not finish their work, nor

units.la: alij item operarij Mechanici, nisi per instrumenta quæ formam hanc referant. At humana figura non aliâ re belluis differt, quàm quòd, & recta sit, & manuum extensionem habeat, & in facie à fronte protensum nasum, per quem & respiratio animalibus est, neque aliud demonstrat quàm signum hoc Crucis. Sed & apud vos notæ hujus signi potentiam declarant: cùm alia quædam, tum tropæa, ob quæ progressus & expeditiones ubique vobis siunt imperii & potentiæ signa in istis præferentes, etsi ignorantes hoc facitis. Et Imperatorum qui apud vos mortui sunt imagines in hac figurâ ponitis, & Deos per litteras appellatis. Quæ pluscula posui, quia me quoque inter exscribendum delectarunt inventiunculæ istæ Patrum. Spero & te, si plenè intelliges: atque adminiculum, figuras istas, habe.
units.tr: other craftsmen likewise, unless by instruments which bear this shape. But the human figure differs from the beasts in nothing other than that it is upright, has its arms extended, and has its nose projecting from the face, through which animals also breathe; and it shows nothing other than this sign of the Cross. But also among you the marks of this sign declare its power: certain other things, and trophies, on account of which your advances and expeditions are made everywhere, you carry as signs of empire and power, though you do so without knowing it. And you place the images of your emperors who have died in this figure, and you call the gods by letters. I have set out these rather many things, because those little inventions of the Fathers delighted me too while I was copying them. I hope you too will be pleased, if you understand them fully; and keep these figures as an aid.
* See the Note at this chapter.
CAP. X.

units.la: In quâ Crucium formâ Christus mortem tulerit : videri in ultimâ, argumento è Patribus & picturis. Ruffini non bona fides notata in verbis Pauli citandis sive explicandis.
units.tr: In what form of cross Christ bore death: that the last form is the one to be seen, argued from the Fathers and from pictures. The bad faith of Ruffinus noted in citing and explaining the words of Paul.

units.la: HAbes omnes Crucium species. In quâ earum ille mortuus, qui morte suâ nobis vita? Ne quærendum quidem censcam, nisi dubitasse & disputasse viderem viros graves & sacrorum peritos, ego arbitror & pronuncio, in hac postremâ, in illâ inquam, quæ quatuor finibus universum orbem complexa est, non sine mysterio, quod toti orbi mortuus, Salvator noster pependit. Tangit hoc & docet Sedulius1:
units.tr: You have all the kinds of cross. Of these, on which one did he die who gives us life by his death? I would not even ask, were I not to see learned men skilled in sacred things doubting and disputing. I hold and affirm that it was on this last one, I mean the one that embraces the whole world with four ends, and that our Saviour hung on it, not without mystery, because he died for the whole world. Sedulius touches on this and teaches it:<sup>1</sup>
1 Book iii.

units.la: Néve quis ignoret speciem Crucis esse colendam, Quæ Dominum portavit ovans, ratione * potenti, Quatuor inde plagas quadrati colligit orbis. Splendidus auctoris de vertice fulget Eous, Occiduo sacra labuntur sidere planta, Arctᴏn dextra tenet, medium lava erigit axem.
units.tr: Lest anyone fail to know that the figure of the Cross is to be honoured, which in triumph carried the Lord by its mighty power, from it the four corners of the square world gather. The bright East shines from the top of the author, the sacred soles slide down on the western star, the right hand holds the North, the left raises the middle axis.

units.la: Et auctoritas etiam firma à D. Paulo . cujus hæc verba, Vt possitis comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis, qua sit latitudo & longitudo, & sublimitas & profundum, plerique Doctorum veterum referunt ad Crucem. Augustinus : Erat latitudo, in quâ porrecta sunt manus; longitudo à terrâ surgens, in quâ erat corpus infixum; altitudo, ab illo innexo ligno sursum quod eminet;
units.tr: Paul's authority also supports this. His words, That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length, and height and depth, are referred by most of the ancient teachers to the Cross. Augustine: The breadth was where the hands were stretched out; the length was rising from the earth, where the body was fixed; the height was what projects upward from the wood joined to it;

units.la: 1 Ad Eph. c. iii. 2 In Psal. cxii. & alibi. eminet; profundum, ubi fixa erat Crux, & ibi omnis spes vita nostra. Damascenus ¹ : Ω˝αντις τὰ τίςσαςσ ὰχξα τοῦ Σταυροῦ διὰ τοῦ μίσυ κίντξυ κςατουῦτιυ καὶ συσφίγγοντας, ὥστε διὰ τ̃ς τοῦ Θεὸς δωάμεως τό, τι ὕψ@ καὶ τὸ βάθ@, μῆκ@ καὶ πλάτ@, ὅτι πᾶσα ὀςατὴ τι καὶ ἀόςατ@ κτίσις συνίςτατ.
units.tr: 1 On Eph. ch. iii. 2 On Ps. cxii. and elsewhere. projects; the depth was where the Cross was fixed, and there is all our hope of life. Damascene: In the same way the four extremities of the Cross are held and bound together through the middle centre, so that by the power of God the height and depth, length and breadth, that is, every visible and invisible creature, is held together. [Ὡσαύτως τὰ τέσσαρα ἄκρα τοῦ Σταυροῦ διὰ τοῦ μέσου κέντρου κρατούμενα καὶ συσφιγγόμενα, ὥστε διὰ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ δυνάμεως τὸ ὕψος καὶ τὸ βάθος, μῆκος καὶ πλάτος, ὅτι πᾶσα ὁρατὴ καὶ ἀόρατος κτίσις συνίσταται.]

units.la: Sicut quatuor extrema Crucis per medium centrum vinciuntur & junguntur : sic per divinam potentiam Sublimitas & Profunditas, Longitudo & Latitudo, sive omnis conspicua & inconspicua creatura continetur. Palàm & ipse quatuor fines nominat, & verba Pauli huc adaptat. Ruffinus ² cur diffentit? qui tres modò agnoscit, & ipsa. Apostoli verba (nefas!) admutilat & detruncat. Docet, inquit, Apostolus Paulus illuminatos esse debere oculos cordis ad intelligendum quae sit altitudo, latitudo, & profundum. Descriptio Crucis est,
units.tr: Just as the four extremities of the Cross are bound and joined through the middle centre, so by divine power height and depth, length and breadth, that is, every visible and invisible creature, is held together. Clearly he too names the four ends and applies Paul's words to them. Why does Ruffinus2 disagree? He recognises only three, and mutilates and truncates the Apostle's words (an outrage!). He says: The Apostle Paul teaches that the eyes of the heart must be enlightened to understand what is the height, breadth and depth. It is a description of the Cross:

units.la: ¹ De Orth. lib. iv. cap. xi i. ² In Symbol. est, cujus eam partem quae in terram defixa est, profundum appellavit: altitudinem vero illam, quae in aërem porrecta sublimis erigitur: latitudinem quoque illam, quae distenta in dextram lævamque protenditur. Mirum, & in verbis Pauli, & in eorum sensu longitudinem ubique improvidè omisit, an de industriâ ejecit? Culpa, si illud: crimen, si iştud. Sed ad rem. Poëtae quoque & Pictores sunt à formâ istâ. Nonnus diserte scribit, Christum sublatum ις διὰ τἰτρεάπαλιυξον: in lignum quadrilaterum. Et in priscis sculpturis (illis merito fides) quadrata conspicitur hæc forma. Constantinus Imp. in Labaro suo expressit: & Deus ipse in aëre ei deformarat. In columnis ejusdem Principis, quae nunc in cognomine urbe (heu, quò ea recidit?) Crux ejusmodi insculpta visitur, & utrimque ab alatis Geniis sus-ten-
units.tr: 1 On Orthodoxy, book iv, ch. xii. 2 In the Creed. the part that is fixed in the earth he called the depth; that height which is stretched up into the air and rises aloft he called the height; and the breadth is that which is extended to the right and left. It is strange that he has carelessly omitted the length everywhere, both in Paul's words and in their sense. Did he do it on purpose? If so, it is a fault; if not, it is a crime. But to the point. Poets and painters too have this shape. Nonnus clearly writes that Christ was lifted up on a four-sided wood, εἰς τετράπλευρον ξύλον: on a quadrangular wood. And in ancient carvings (to which faith is rightly given) this square form is seen. The Emperor Constantine expressed it on his standard, and God himself had shaped it for him in the air. On the columns of the same Prince, now in the city that bears his name (alas, into what has it fallen?), a Cross of this kind is seen carved, and it is held up on both sides by winged Genii, who sup-port it

units.la: ften- (rendered as the running word at the foot of the page) stentatur. Quid, quòd in Nummis plurifariam sic apparet ? quorum alibi damus typos. Nec meo sensu, ambigi profecto potest, in tam veteri Christianorum sensu. Tamen sunt qui de Commissâ sive de Tau forma contendunt. nec damno, etsi dissideo: quia & illi si Titulum supernè addis, efficere atque imaginari possis quaternos istos fines.
units.tr: port (the word running at the foot of the page) it. What of the fact that it appears in many ways on coins, of which we give pictures elsewhere? Surely there can be no doubt in my mind about this, given the ancient sense of the Christians. Yet there are those who contend for the form of the Committee or Tau. I do not condemn them, though I disagree, because if you add a Title above, you can make and imagine these four ends.
CAP. XI.

units.la: Apud plerasque gentium Cruces ferè usitatas. Apud Syros, Iudæos, Ægyptios, Persas, Afros, Græcos, maximè Romanos. Quando apud eos cœperit? An & apud Germanos?
units.tr: Crosses were widely used among most peoples. Among the Syrians, Jews, Egyptians, Persians, Africans, Greeks, and especially the Romans. When did it begin among them? And among the Germans too?

units.la: CRuces satis vidimus: ubi gentium eæ in usu fuerint, addam. Etsi uno verbo pænè dixerim, ubique gentium receptas. Oriens quidem plerosque
units.tr: I have seen enough crosses. I will add where in the world they were in use. I could almost say in a single word that they were received everywhere. The East indeed used them for the most part, and that long ago.

units.la: usurpavit, idque jam olim. De Syris in Esthère 1 scriptum : Suspensus est Aman in patibulo, quod paraverat Mardochaeo. De Judaeis, in Josua 2 : qui regem ejus (Hai) suspendit in patibulo usque ad vesperam. Item in Numeris 3 : Tolle cunctos Principes populi, & suspende eos contra Solem in patibulis. Atque in sacris libris saepius. Ægyptios etiam usos reperio. ut Thucydides 4 de rege Inaro : προδοσίᾳ ληφθεὶς ἀνεσταυρώθη : proditione captus, in crucem est actus. Et Justinus 5, in eadem Ægypto : Agathocles occiditur, & mulieres in ultionem Eurydices patibulis suffiguntur. Et Persas crebrò. Herodotus 6 de Polycrate : Ἀποκτείνας δὲ μιν ἐκ ἀξίως ἀνεσταύρωσε : Interficiens eum (quod indignum relatu fit) Orætes in Cruce suffixit. Ammianus 7 de suo aevo ; Ælianus Comes
units.tr: Among the Syrians, Esther 1 records: Haman was hanged on the gibbet which he had prepared for Mordecai. Among the Jews, Joshua 2: who hanged their king (of Ai) on a gibbet until evening. Likewise Numbers 3: Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gibbets facing the sun. And this is found often in the sacred books. I find the Egyptians also used it, as Thucydides 4 says of King Inaros: captured by treachery, he was crucified [προδοσίᾳ ληφθεὶς ἀνεσταυρώθη]: captured by betrayal, he was put on the cross. And Justin 5, of the same Egypt: Agathocles is killed, and women, in revenge for Eurydice, are fixed on gibbets. And the Persians often. Herodotus 6, of Polycrates: Having killed him unworthily [Ἀποκτείνας δὲ μιν ἐκ ἀξίως ἀνεσταύρωσε]: Oroetes, having killed him (a thing unworthy to relate), fixed him on a cross. Ammianus 7, on his own age: Ælianus Comes

units.la: ¹ Cap.vii. ² Cap.viii. ³ Cap.xxv. ⁴ Lib.i. ⁵ Lib. xxx. ⁶ In Thalia. ⁷ Lib. xix. Comes & Tribuni patibulis scelestè suffixi: capti nempe à Persis. Sed Afros vel omnium creberrimè: qui non in viles modò, sed illustrissimas personas adhibebant. Atque à Senatu Carthaginiensium etiam Duces, (Valerii verba sunt) bella pravo consilio gerentes, etsi prospera fortuna subsecuta esset, Cruci suffigebantur : Video & Græcos usitasse. Certè Alexander Macedo Glaucum medicum, & Tyrios, & plures crucifixit 1. Etiam Xantippus Atheniensis Artaÿctam Persam, de quo apud Herodotum in Calliope extremâ leges. Iam Romanis vetus veterrimumque, & (verba Victoris 3 usurpabo) supplicium patibulorum. Si 4 Livio fides, statim sub primis regibus usurparunt: & exemplum in Horatio, cui id sub Tullo C para-
units.tr: ¹ Chap. vii. ² Chap. viii. ³ Chap. xxv. ⁴ Book i. ⁵ Book xxx. ⁶ In Thalia. ⁷ Book xix. A count and tribunes, wickedly hanged on gibbets: taken, of course, by the Persians. But the Africans most of all, most frequently of all: they used it not only on base persons but on the most illustrious. Indeed, by the Senate of Carthage even generals, (Valerius's words) conducting wars with bad policy, were fixed to the cross, even if fortune had followed them favourably. I see the Greeks also used it. Certainly Alexander the Macedonian crucified the physician Glaucus, and the Tyrians, and many more 1. Also Xanthippus the Athenian crucified Artayctes the Persian, of whom you will read at the end of Herodotus in Calliope. Now among the Romans it is old, and most old, and (I shall use the words of Victor 3) the punishment of gibbets. If we trust Livy 4, they took it up straight away under the first kings, and there is an example in Horatius, for whom this was prepared under Tullus C para-

units.la: ¹ Lib. II. c. VII. ² Plutarch. in Alexan. ³ In Constantino. ⁴ Lib. I. parabatur. Etsi Cicero dissentire videtur, & horridum illud Carmen ad Tarquinium Superbum auctorem referre. I lictor, inquit, colliga manus. quae non modo hujus libertatis mansuetudinisque non sunt, sed ne Romuli quidem, aut Numae, sed Tarquinii, superbissimi ac crudelissimi regis ista sunt cruciatus carmina, Caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito. Quae tamen aut populariter & ad causam Cicero dixerit; aut hoc sentiens, non ab auctore illa Tarquinio fuisse, sed illo maxime digna, & apud eum crebra. Utrum horum est, video etiam liberâ republicâ statim in usu cruces. Dionysius 2 de servis conjuratis: Καὶ αὐτίκα οἱ μὲν ἐκ οἰκιῶν συλληφθέντες, οἱ δὲ ἐκ τῶν ἀγορῶν ἀχθέντες, ἀνεστραλοπίσθησαν ἄπαντες. Et ilico alii quidem e domibus extracti, alii e foris abducti, omnes in Crucem acti sunt. & dein-
units.tr: ¹ Book II, ch. vii. ² Plutarch, in Alexander. ³ In Constantine. ⁴ Book I. being prepared. Yet Cicero seems to disagree, and refers that dreadful song to Tarquin the Proud as its author. Go, lictor, he says, bind his hands. These are not the marks of this liberty and gentleness, nor even of Romulus or Numa, but of Tarquin, the proudest and cruellest king; these are the songs of torture: cover his head, hang him on the unlucky tree. Cicero may have said this for effect, to serve his cause; or, feeling it himself, he may have meant that these things were not from Tarquin as their author, but that they were most worthy of him and common in his time. Whichever of these is true, I see that crosses were in use at once even in a free republic. Dionysius5 says of the slaves who conspired: And straightway some were seized in their houses, others led from the marketplaces, and all were crucified. And then all were led to the Cross. And afterwards

units.la: ¹ Orat. pro Rabir. ² Lib. v. Antiq. & deinceps * ψαμμοκονίστι, ut *Infi-cum Græcis dicam, testes. Quid Germani? numquid & illi usi? distrahor. Tacitus videtur dicere: Proditores & transfugas arboribus suspendunt. sed fortassis ad laqueum & suffocationem hoc aliquis trahat. Tamen idem Patibula etiam attribuit: Quot patibula captivis, quæ scrobes: quo nisi suo & Romano sensu?
units.tr: ¹ Speech for Rabirius. ² Book v of the Antiquities. And afterwards (I shall call it, in Greek, as the witnesses do). What of the Germans? Did they too use them? I am torn. Tacitus seems to say: They hang traitors and deserters on trees. But perhaps someone might take this to refer to the noose and strangling. Yet the same author also ascribes gibbets to them: How many gibbets for the captives, what pits, which surely has only his own Roman sense.
CAP. XII.

units.la: Apud Romanos vile fuisse hoc supplicium, & plurimum ser- vorum. Quas ob causas ii affecti.
units.tr: Among the Romans this punishment was cheap and was inflicted on very many slaves. The causes for which such people were punished.

units.la: PLurifariam igitur receptæ Cruces, sed vix tamen nisi in homines viliores, Romano quidem ritu. Atque apud eos servorum ferè hoc supplicium, aut plebeiorum qui juxta servos.
units.tr: Crosses were therefore used in many ways, but scarcely ever except on the baser sort of men, and in the Roman manner. Among the Romans this punishment was almost always reserved for slaves, or for common people who ranked close to slaves.
1 On the Manners of the Germans. 2 Annals, book 1.
A woman in Juvenal speaks of a slave:
Put the cross on the slave.

units.la: Et alia apud Petronium : Nec dii sinant, ut amplexus meos in Crucem mittam. Ita enim venustè servum cruciarium appellat, quâ facie sermonis Scelus pro scelesto. Servis ipse apud Plautum comiter fatetur:
units.tr: And elsewhere in Petronius: May the gods not allow me to send my embraces to the cross. For so he elegantly calls the slave a man for the cross, using a figure of speech that puts "crime" for "criminal".

units.la: Noli minitari, scio crucem futuram mihi sepulcrum,
units.tr: In Plautus the slave himself candidly says to the others: Do not threaten me; I know the cross will be my tomb,

units.la: Ibi majores mei siti sunt, pater, avus, proavus, abavus.
units.tr: There my ancestors lie buried: father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather.

units.la: Atque adeò peculiare hoc servis, ut nomine Servilis supplicii Crux veniat capienda. In Tacito : Asiaticus (enim is libertus) malam potentiam servili supplicio expiavit. Iterum : Sumptum de eo supplicium in servilem modum, In Vulcatio explicatiùs: Centuriones rapi jussit & in crucem tolli, servilique supplicio affici. In Capitolino : Nam & in crucem milites tulit, & servilibus suppliciis semper affecit. Ergo Livium sic evolves: De captivis, ut quisque liber, aut servus, sua fortuna a quoque sumptum supplicium est. Suae fortunae: nempe Crux servo reposita, gladius aut securis libero. Ipsum hoc ita in Hirtio legas: Prehensi servi tres, & unus e legione vernacula. Servi sunt in crucem sublati, militi cervices abscisae. Servile igitur hoc supplicium, sed non ob levem aut cottidianam noxam. Horatius indicat: Si quis eum servum, patinam qui tollere jussus Semesos pisces, tepidumque ligurrierit jus, In cruce suffigat; Labeone infanior inter Sanos dicatur.
units.tr: So peculiar to slaves was this punishment that the cross came to be called by the name of "servile punishment". In Tacitus: Asiaticus (for he was a freedman) atoned for his wicked power with servile punishment. Again: Punishment was taken from him in the servile manner. In Vulcatius more fully: He ordered the centurions seized, lifted onto the cross, and subjected to servile punishment. In Capitolinus: For he both raised soldiers onto the cross and always subjected them to servile punishments. So read Livy in this way: Concerning the captives, each was punished according to his fortune, whether he was free or a slave. "According to his fortune" means that the cross was kept for the slave, and the sword or axe for the free man. You may read this very thing in Hirtius: Three slaves were seized, and one from the native legion. The slaves were lifted onto the cross, and the soldier's neck was cut off. This punishment, then, was servile, but it was not inflicted for a slight or everyday offence. Horace indicates this: If anyone, ordered to carry the dish, licked the half-cooked fish and the warm broth, let him be fixed to a cross; he would be called more mad than Labeo among the sane.

units.la: 1 In Macrino. 2 Lib. III. 3 De bello Hispan. 4 Lib. I. Serm. III. Indicat, inquam, graves fuisse & in extremo supplicio extremas caussas. Sed quas illas? ægrè universas dixerim: quasdam adnumerabo. Delatura domini. Pertinax apud Capitolinum ¹, eos qui calumniis appetiti per servos fuerant, damnatis fervis delatoribus, liberavit, in Crucem sublatis talibus fervis. Sic Macrino ² jam Principe, συνωφά) τι ἡ δἔλοι, ὅσοι διαστταις ηγητηγυλοι, ἀνσκολωπισθησαν: Sycophantæ, aut fervi, quicumque dominos detulerant, in crucem sunt ffi. Et in genere, omnis machina contra dominicam salutem.
units.tr: 1 In Macrinus. 2 Book 3. 3 On the Spanish War. 4 Book 1, Satire 3. It indicates, I say, that the offences were grave, and that for the extreme punishment there were extreme causes. But what were those? I would hardly say all of them; I will list some. The first is informing against masters. Pertinax, in Capitolinus, freed those who had been assailed by false accusations through their slaves, the slave informers having been condemned and such slaves lifted onto the cross. Likewise under Macrinus, already emperor: [συκοφάνται ἢ δοῦλοι, ὅσοι δεσπότας ἐμήνυσαν, ἀνεσκολοπίσθησαν]: sycophants, or slaves, whoever had informed against their masters, were impaled on the cross. And in general, every plot against the master's safety.

units.la: Paulus ³: Si servi de domini salute consuluerint (Mathematicos intellige:) summo supplicio, id est Cruce, afficiuntur. Item Fuga, sed (ut opinor) diuturna, aut repetita. Cicero ⁴ tangit: Qua Crux huic fugitivo potest satis sup-
units.tr: Paulus says: If slaves have consulted about their master's safety (understand: by the mathematicians), they are subjected to the supreme punishment, that is the cross. Likewise flight, but (I think) prolonged or repeated flight. Cicero touches on this: What punishment of the cross can be enough

units.la: ¹ In Pertin. ² Herodian. lib. v. ³ Lib. v. Sent. Tit. xxi. ⁴ Pro Dejotaro. supplicii adferre ? Et Valerius {1}: Cruce dignissimi fugitivi. Quin Scipio, apud eumdem {2}, transfugas Romanos, tamquam patriæ fugitivos, Crucibus affixit. Simile sub Augusto, in Sexti milite puniendo, qui ferè è fugitivis: τὸ μὲν διδασκαλικὸς, ait Dio, τοῖς διαστάσεις πρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπιδόθη· εἰ δέ τις μηδεὶς νόμῳ [?] ἐυφόρηθο, ἀντεκολωπίζετο [?]: Servitia dominis reddita ad pœnam; quorum domini non exstarent, Cruci sunt fixa. Quamquam hîc & alia caussa suberat, Hostilitas in rem Romanam. Hæc & plura in servis: quos mitiores duriorésve domini, graviùs, mitiùs, pro arbitrio sunt puniti.
units.tr: ¹ In Pertinax. ² Herodian, book 5. ³ Book 5 of the Sentences, title 21. ⁴ For Deiotarus. for this fugitive? And Valerius {1}: a fugitive most worthy of the cross. Indeed Scipio, in the same author {2}, fixed Roman deserters to crosses as fugitives from their country. Something similar happened under Augustus, in the punishment of a soldier of Sextus, who was mostly drawn from fugitives. Dio says: [τοὺς μὲν δούλους τοῖς δεσπόταις πρὸς τιμωρίαν ἀπεδόθη· εἰ δέ τινες μηδενὸς ... ἀνεσκολοπίζοντο]: the slaves were handed back to their masters for punishment; those whose masters could not be found were fixed to crosses. Although another cause also lay beneath this, namely hostility toward the Roman state. These and more examples concern slaves, whom harsher or milder masters punished more severely or more leniently, as they pleased.

Chapter XIII.

units.la: Etiam liberi quidam in Crucem data, sed viliores aut nocentiores : ut Latrones, Sicarii, Falsarii, atque alibi & Fures.
units.tr: Some free men too were put on the cross, but the baser or more guilty ones: such as robbers, assassins, forgers, and elsewhere thieves.

units.la: {a}QVid autem in liberis? Rara crux, ut prædixi. Quin removere prorsus ab hoc genere Lactantius videatur, ubi de Christo : Cur si Deus fuit, & mori voluit, non saltem aliquo honesto genere mortis affectus est? cur potissimum Cruce? cur infami genere supplicii? quod etiam homine libero, quamvis nocente, videatur indignum. Sed frænanda ea assertio est : & cive quidem indigna Crux, nec credo usurpatam in eos nisi præter leges, & per sævitiam. viliores liberi, & provinciales, non ab ea profecto immunes. Atque hæc crimina in
units.tr: But what of free men? The cross was rare, as I said before. Indeed Lactantius seems to exclude this class altogether when he speaks of Christ: Why, if he was God and wished to die, was he not at least afflicted with some honourable kind of death? Why the cross above all? Why a shameful kind of punishment? Which seems unworthy even of a free man, however guilty. But that assertion must be qualified. The cross was unworthy of a citizen, and I do not believe it was used on citizens except contrary to the laws and out of cruelty. The baser free men and the provincials were certainly not exempt from it. And these crimes in
1 Lib. iv. Inst. cap. xxvi.

units.la: in iis cruciaria : primùm, Latrocinium. Seneca : Latrocinium fe-cit aliquis. quid ergo meruit? ut sufpendatur. Cave de alio suspendio interpretêre. Petronius : Imperator provinciæ jussit Latrones Crucibus affigi. Apuleius : Latronem iflum, miserorum pignorum meorum peremptorem, Cruci affigatis. Calliftratus Iurisconsultus : Famosos latrones, in his locis ubi grassati sunt, furcâ figendos compluribus placuit. Scripserat ille, Cruce, ut post docemus. Cum ipso Servatore utrimque secus latrones duo fixi: quos duo Euangelistæ diserte λῃστὰς appellant, Lucas paullò communius κακούργους. Deinde Sicariatus. Paulus : Inhonestiores (sicarios) pœnâ capitis vindicari placuit, humiliores verò in Crucem tolluntur, aut bestiis subjiciuntur. Tertiò, crimen Falsi, Firmicus:
units.tr: those cases of crucifixion: first, robbery. Seneca: Someone committed robbery. What then did he deserve? To be hanged. Beware of taking this as some other kind of hanging. Petronius: The governor of the province ordered robbers to be fixed to crosses. Apuleius: Fix to a cross that robber, the destroyer of my wretched children. Callistratus the jurist: It has been decided by many that notorious robbers are to be fixed to the gallows in the places where they have raged. He had written crux, as we shall show later. Two robbers were fixed on either side of the Saviour himself. The two Evangelists plainly call them λῃστάς, though Luke more commonly calls them κακούργους. Next, assassins. Paulus: It has been decided that the more distinguished assassins are punished by capital punishment, but the humbler ones are raised on the cross or thrown to the beasts. Thirdly, the crime of forgery. Firmicus: They shall have those caught in the crime of forgery raised on the cross. And theft too? Yes, but not at Rome. Lampridius: When kings were asked what they suffered thieves to undergo among them, they answered: the cross. It would be no wonder if those kings were Gauls or Germans, whose customs even now send thieves to the gallows.

Aliam etiam crimina in hanc poenam, ne ambigas: sed ego sileo, quæ testibus aut tabulis non consigno.
