units.la: CAP. XIV. Quæ causa falsò assignata in Cruce Christi? videri Innovationem & Seditionem esse.
units.tr: Chapter XIV. What cause was falsely assigned for the cross of Christ? That it seemed to be innovation and sedition.

units.la: CUm hæc vidimus, piè non curiosè quæro, in Servatore nostro quis prætextus (nam causa nunquam fuit) ad Crucem? Blasphemiam aliquis dixerit, ex voci-
units.tr: Having seen these things, I ask piously, not curiously, what pretext (for there was never any cause) there was in our Saviour for the cross. Someone might say blasphemy, from the words or the judgments of the Jews.

units.la: ¹ Lib. VI. Matth. cap. XXVI. ² In Alexand. vocibus aut judiciis Iudæorum. Atque ipsi sanè ita apud Pontificem accusant, & huic noxæ testes quæruntur, & ipse denique Pontifex ejus damnat. Attamen, si legem spectes, hi tales lapidibus, non cruce puniti. An non verius ac simpliciùs, totum illud judicium, etsi judicii dissimile, Romanis moribus legibusque directum? Mihi videatur. & respondeam damnatum innocentium nostrum agnum, quasi Seditionis nomine & Regni afsectati. Certè Romanâ lege , auctores seditionis aut tumultus, pro qualitate dignitate, aut in Crucem tolluntur, aut bestiis objiciuntur. Quòd autem sic etiam apud Pilatum accusatus, Lucas clarè: Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram, & prohibentem tributa dare Cæsari, & dicentem se Christum regem esse. Credidit,
units.tr: ¹ Lib. vi. Matth. cap. xxvi. ² In Alexand. And indeed they accuse him in this way before the High Priest, witnesses are sought for this offence, and the High Priest himself condemns him. Yet if you look to the law, such people were punished by stoning, not by the cross. Is it not truer and simpler that the whole proceeding, though unlike a proper trial, was conducted according to Roman custom and law? That is how it seems to me, and I would answer that our innocent lamb was condemned in the name of sedition and of aspiring to kingship. Certainly by Roman law, the authors of sedition or tumult, according to their rank and standing, are either raised on the cross or thrown to the beasts. That he was also accused in this way before Pilate, Luke states clearly: We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ the king. They believed it

units.la: 1 Lib. v. Paulus, Tit. xxxi. 2 Cap. xxiii. dit, nec credidit Pilatus: & Titulum tamen caussamque mortis inscripsit, Rex Iudaorum. Ex Iudaeorum quidem libris si rem decidimus, intricamur: nec usquam traditum clarè quae noxa ad crucem, nisi quod Philo {1} prodidit de Homicidis. contra quos ait Legislatorem mille mortis genera, si post ruisset, dilecturum fuisse: cum non potuit, τιμωρίαν ἄλλην ἀντιδικαστικὴν; κτλ.: poenam aliam adjunxit, jubens homicidas & sicarios crucifigi. Sed tua pace Philo, ubi hoc Legislator? nusquam expressè. hoc tantum universè{2}: Quando peccaverit homo, quod morte plectendum est, & adjudicatus morti appensus fuerit in patibulo. Peccatum non designat: & frustrà credo fore, si quis nunc quaerat. Tamen Theologi videntó, ego ἐν ἀλλοτρίᾳ χορῷ πόδα ἐ τίθημι. {1} Libello de speciali lege. {2} Deuteron. cap. xxi.
units.tr: 1 Lib. v. Paulus, Tit. xxxi. 2 Cap. xxiii. ...and Pilate did not believe it; yet he nonetheless inscribed the title and cause of death: The King of the Jews. If we settle the matter from Jewish books, we become entangled, and nowhere is it clearly handed down what offence merited the cross, except what Philo reports about murderers: against whom he says the Lawgiver, had he gone further, would have chosen a thousand kinds of death; since he could not, he added another penalty [τιμωρίαν ἄλλην ἀντιδικαστικὴν], etc., ordering murderers and assassins to be crucified. But with all respect to you, Philo, where does the Lawgiver say this? Nowhere expressly. Only this in general: When a man has sinned in a way that deserves death, and has been condemned to death and hung on a gibbet. It does not name the sin, and I think it would be in vain if anyone now asked. Let the theologians see to that; I do not set my foot in another's dance [ἐν ἀλλοτρίᾳ χορῷ πόδα οὐ τίθημι]. {1} In the treatise On the Special Laws. {2} Deuteronomy chap. xxi.
CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Crux interdum libere & laxè vagata : in hostes, in seditiosos, in Christianos, in faeminas denique.
units.tr: The cross sometimes wandered freely and loosely: against enemies, against rebels, against Christians, and finally against women.

units.la: IN hos ergo tales ex ordine more Crux usurpata. Interdum regnum ei largius, & praefertim apud reges. Nam hi ex libidine saepe ita saevierunt in hostes aut rebelles, & uno tempore multos. Alexander Magnus, ut supra tetigi, duo millia Tyriorum, capta eorum urbe, crucifixit1. Alius Minutus Alexander in Iudaea, ἐξιόμενον ἐν ἀπόστροφῃ μετὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἀπολωλότων, ἀνασταυροῦσθαι Ιουδαίων ὡς ὁ: ὁ: Convivans in publico & conspicuo loco una cum pellicibus, jussit in Crucem dari Iudaeorum ad octingentos. Quinctilius etiam Varus 2, ex eadem gente,
units.tr: Thus the cross was customarily applied to such persons in the usual order. Sometimes it had freer rein, especially among kings, for they often raged so savagely out of lust against enemies or rebels, and against many at one time. Alexander the Great, as I touched on above, after taking their city, crucified two thousand Tyrians.[1] Another Alexander, Minutus, in Judaea, feasting in a public and conspicuous place along with his concubines, ordered about eight hundred Jews to be put on crosses [ἐξιόμενον ἐν ἀπόστροφῃ μετὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἀπολωλότων, ἀνασταυροῦσθαι Ιουδαίων ὡς ὁ]. Quinctilius Varus too, from the same nation,

units.la: 1 Ioseph. lib. XIII. Antiq. cap. XXII. 2 Ioseph. lib. II. Excid. cap. III. te, ob nescio quem motum, ἀνεσάνεσαν πιεὶ διχιλίας: crucifixit circiter bis mille. At Titus 1 in obsidione illâ exitiali, quingenos, & plures, in singulos dies Crucibus affixit: Καὶ διὰ τὸ πλῆθος χώρας τι ἐπι-λείπειν τοῖς Σταυροῖς, καὶ Σταυροὶ τοῖς σώμασι: & ob multitudinem terra Crucibus, & Cruces corporibus deerant. Nota, nota. historicâ hæc fide, non attollendi causâ dicuntur, & ab eo qui vidit Josepho. Nec ego miseror. abi pessima natio, hæc præmia Crucis illius, quam impie posuisti nostro & tuo (voluisses modò) Servatori. Iam & Augustus confecto bello Siculo, * sex millia servorum, quorum domini non exstabant, in Crucem egit 2. Et in Christianos Tyranni crebrò adhibuerunt, atque eos numerosos. Lego uno tempore, uno loco, ad millia decem sic
units.tr: 1 Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book XIII, ch. 22. 2 Josephus, Jewish War, book II, ch. 3. on account of some uprising I know not what, [ἀνεσάνεσαν πιεὶ δι]χιλίας: crucified about two thousand. But Titus, in that deadly siege, put up five hundred and more on crosses every day, and [Καὶ διὰ τὸ πλῆθος χώρας τι ἐπιλείπειν τοῖς Σταυροῖς, καὶ Σταυροὶ τοῖς σώμασι]: and because of the multitude there was a lack of ground for the crosses, and of crosses for the bodies. Note, note. These things are related on historical authority, not to exalt him, and by Josephus, who saw them. Nor do I pity them. Begone, most wicked nation! These are the rewards of that cross which you impiously set up against our Saviour and yours (if only you had wished it). Again, when Augustus had finished the Sicilian war, he sent six thousand slaves, whose masters could not be found, to the cross.[2] And tyrants often used it against Christians, and in large numbers. I read that at one time, in one place, about ten thousand were thus [slain].

E Christianis etiam Beata Eulalia, ungulas flammasque perpessa, demum cruci affixa martyrii coronam accepit3. Sed & in Corsica, sancta Iulia virgo crucis supplicio coronata est4. Plura in Martyrum historiis exempla reperies, &, si voles, addes.
units.tr: 2 Orosius, so slain.[1] Yet they did not refrain from this punishment even against women. Tiberius, because of Paulina's adultery in the temple of Isis, [τὸς τε ἱερέας ἀνιερακότας, ἡ τ' Ῥώμη ...] crucified the priests,[2] and Ida (the name of a maidservant), who had been the cause of the corruption. Among Christians too, Saint Eulalia, having suffered the claws and the flames, was at last fastened to a cross and received the crown of martyrdom.[3] And in Corsica the holy virgin Julia was crowned with the punishment of the cross.[4] You will find more examples in the histories of the martyrs, and, if you wish, you may add to them.

LIBER II.
CAPVT I.

units.la: Transitio ad Modum figendi, prae- missum de atrocitate hujus sup- plicii, quod Summum & Ex- tremum dictum.
units.tr: Transition to the mode of fixing, preceded by a account of the atrocity of this punishment, which was called the highest and extreme.

units.la: DIxi satis Quid Crux & Cujusmodi fuerit, Vbi & Quare usurpata: pergo longius, & universum hoc poenale aedificium exstruo; per singula etiam membra. Dicam enim Quomodo usurpata: & non animis solum, sed paene oculis subjiciam saevitiam & foeditatem ejus supplicii: quae sane magna. Nec temere Cicero crudelissimum teterrimumque appellavit: & poëta Nonnus
units.tr: I have said enough about what the cross was and what kind of thing it was, and where and why it was used. I now go further and build up this whole penal structure, taking its individual parts one by one too. For I will say how it was used, and I will set before the eyes, almost, the savagery and foulness of that punishment, which is indeed great. Nor did Cicero call it "most cruel and most loathsome" without thought, and the poet Nonnus [wrote of it] as

units.la: ¹ In Verr. ² In cap. xix. Ioan. — ἰλέγχισέν τινα πῶτμον : damnatissimum quoddam fatum.
units.tr: ¹ In Verr. ² In cap. xix. Ioan. — ἐλέγχισέν τινα πότμον: a certain most condemned fate.

units.la: Quin etiam Iurisconsulti, nomine Summi supplicii, velut ob eminentiam, designant istud. Paulus 1: Summo supplicio, id est Cruce, afficiuntur. Ab eadem mente Supremum Ulpianus 2 dixit: Si liberi sint, ad bestias dari; si servi, supremo supplicio affici. cum enim aliud non exprimat, & de servis responsum sit, jure capio Crucem. cur non ignem? inquies: cum Tertullianus 3 etiam dixerit & censuerit, Summam ignium poenam? Quia ex Iurisconsultorum mente, Crux etiam supra ignem. Certè Paulus 4 hoc ordine Summi supplicii tria genera recensent: Crucem, Cremationem, Decollationem. Praeit, ut vides, Crux: & cum causa, si infamiam, magnitudi-
units.tr: Indeed even the jurists, using the name "highest punishment" as if by way of eminence, designate this. Paulus, book 1: They are punished with the highest punishment, that is, the cross. In the same sense Ulpian 2 said "supreme": If they are free, they are given to the beasts; if slaves, they are subjected to the supreme punishment. Since he expresses nothing else, and the answer concerns slaves, I rightly take it as the cross. "Why not fire?" you will ask, since Tertullian 3 also called fire the highest punishment and judged it so. Because in the jurists' mind the cross stands even above fire. Certainly Paulus 4 lists the three kinds of highest punishment in this order: the cross, burning, beheading. As you see, the cross comes first, and with reason, if you consider the infamy, the magnitude, and above all the long duration of the pains in it.

units.la: 1 Lib. v. Sent. tit. xxi. 2 Lib. viii. Ad leg. Corn. Falsi. 3 Ad Martyr. c. iv. 4 Lib. v. Sent. tit. xvi i. tudinem, & præsertim diuturnitatem pœnarum in eâ attendis. Dicta hæc ipsa Extrema pœna. ut in Apuleio de servo cruciando: Certum extrema pœna, quæ more majorum in eum competit. An & sic Arnobius? Crucem mereatur extremam, quisquis vobis dominis supplicarit. Quod tamen etiam laxè, & de peste aut pernicie capit interpretari.
units.tr: 1 Book 5 of the Sentences, title 21. 2 Book 8, On the Cornelian law on forgery. 3 To the Martyrs, ch. 4. 4 Book 5 of the Sentences, title 17. These very words are called extreme punishment, as in Apuleius on torturing a slave: Certainly the extreme punishment, which by the custom of our ancestors belongs to him. Does Arnobius say so too? Whoever has supplicated you masters deserves the extreme cross. Which, however, one may also take loosely, and interpret of plague or destruction.

units.la: CAP. II. Duplex figendi Modus, Vulgaris & Rarus. In illo Flagellatio ex more semper anteivit.
units.tr: CHAP. II. The twofold mode of fixing, the common and the rare. In the former, flogging always preceded, by custom.

units.la: SEd sævi fœdiqueque quid in hoc supplicio fuerit, Modus ipse dixerit: quem graphicè imus repræsentatum. Ut magis possit; partimur, & duplicem eum facimus: Vulgarem, & Rarum. Illum, qui receptissimus, & quo vulgo
units.tr: But what was cruel and foul in this punishment the mode itself will tell, which we have set out vividly. So that it may be easier to treat, we divide it and make it twofold: the common and the rare. The former is the most usual, and the one commonly

units.la: 1 Lib. I. 2 Lib. I. Adver. Gent. vulgò utebantur. Alterum, qui magis sepositus, nec in tam assiduo usu. De illo prius: & quidem ordine hæc tria, Quæ ante fixionem, Quæ in ipsâ, Quæ post ipsam. Ante fixionem duo adhibita: Flagellatio & Deductio. Flagellatio quidem sollennis antecessor, & raro in crucem dati nisi sic purpurati. Apud Livium , de servis conjuratis: Multi occisi, multi capti, alii verberati crucibus affixi. Verberatos ecce prædixit. Alexander apud Curtium , moris hujus retinens, eos qui Petram obstinatè defenderant, omnes verberibus affectos, sub ipsis radicibus Petræ crucibus jussit affigi. Iudæi, apud Iosephum , μαστιγού- ... flagellati & pracruciati ante mortem omne genus verberibus, crucifigebantur.
units.tr: 1 Book 1. 2 Book 1, Against the Gentiles. used. The other is more set apart and not in such constant use. Of the first, let us speak first, and in order these three: what precedes fixing, what occurs in the fixing itself, and what follows it. Before fixing two things were used: flogging and the leading out. Flogging was the solemn forerunner, and a man was rarely given to the cross unless so scourged. In Livy, of slaves who conspired: Many were killed, many captured, others flogged and fixed to crosses. See, he foretold the flogging. Alexander in Curtius, keeping this custom, ordered those who had stubbornly defended the Rock, all subjected to beatings, to be fixed to crosses beneath the very roots of the Rock. The Jews, in Josephus, flogged and tortured with every kind of lash before death, were crucified.

units.la: Philo {1} item narrans Iudæos Alexandriæ in crucem actos à Flacco, hoc addit: μετὰ τὸ αἰκίσασθαι ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ : postquam flagellati fuissent in theatro. Sollennis ergo mos, imò lex: & horrendum Carmen diserte canebat {2}: Verbera intra aut extra pomœrium: & tum denique succinebat: Arbori infelici suspendito.
units.tr: Philo, also relating that the Jews at Alexandria were led to the cross by Flaccus, adds this: after they had been tortured in the theatre [μετὰ τὸ αἰκίσασθαι ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ]. The custom was therefore solemn, indeed a law, and a horrible song was openly sung: Beatings inside or outside the pomerium; and then at last the refrain answered: Hang him on the unlucky tree.
CHAP. III.

units.la: Flagellorum & Virgarum discri- men. Illa magis vilia, & magis acerba esse. solere & talis aspe- rari.
units.tr: The difference between whips and rods. That the former are baser and more cruel, and are commonly roughened with knucklebones like these.

units.la: Verberati igitur: sed utrùm virgis an flagellis? Illas interdum reperio: sed magis crebrò ista. Discrimen enim esse scimus: & quia Virgæ honestiores, inhonestissimo huic supplicio adtributa Flagra. Cicero
units.tr: Were they beaten, then, with rods or with whips? I find both at times, but whips far more often. For we know there is a difference, and rods were considered more honourable, while whips were assigned to this most dishonourable punishment. Cicero
{1} Against Flaccus.

units.la: {2} Apud Liv. lib. r. cero illudens & cavillans in Labienum : Porcia lex virgas ab omnium civium corpore amovit; hic misericors flagella retulit. Quomodo retulit ? una cum Cruce scilicet, cui haec adjuncta. Dixi inhonestiora fuisse. Ita, & proprie servorum. Sic apud Terentium 1, ——— ad necem operiere loris. SAN. loris liber ?
units.tr: {2} Cicero, mocking and jeering at Labienus in Livy, book 10: "The Porcian law removed rods from the bodies of all citizens; this man, merciful, has brought back the whips." How did he bring them back? Together with the cross, of course, to which they were attached. I have said they were more degrading, and this was especially so for slaves. Thus in Terence: "...you will wait to be killed with thongs." SAN. "A free man with thongs?" He cries out and is indignant, as at something unheard of, that thongs were threatened against a free man.

units.la: Exclamat & indignatur, ut in re insolenti, quod libero intentata lora. Et ab hac nota servilem conditionem Menae Horatius 3 approbat : Sectus flagellis hic triumviralibus Praeconis ad fastidium.
units.tr: And Horace confirms that this mark of servile status belonged to Menas: "Here he is, cut with the triumviral whips, to the herald's disgust."

units.la: Significat a Triumviris (Imperium iis & animadversio in servos 4) caesum flagris publice, idque sub praeconis voce. Itaque & Ma-
units.tr: He means that he was publicly flogged on the orders of the triumvirs (they held power and the right of punishment over slaves), with the herald calling out the sentence. And so Macer, the jurist, also wrote:

units.la: 1 Orat pro Rabir. perd. 2 Adelph. 3 Epod. Od. IV. 4 Vide Fabr. in Semestr.
units.tr: 1 Pro Rabirio Perduellionis. 2 Terence, Adelphi. 3 Horace, Epodes and Odes, book 4. 4 See Fabricius on the Semestria.

units.la: & Macer 1 Iurisconsultus scripfit, Ex quibus caussis liber fustibus, ex hisservum flagellis cædi. Et Imperatores 2 rescripserunt, mulierem habere justas divortii causas, si se verberibus, quæ ingenuo aliena sunt, afficientem maritum probaverit. Flagra hæc ipsa intelligunt: quæ cùm ab ingenuis, tum à fœminis remota maximè. Atque ut novum & severum in Licinio Pontifice narrat Valerius 3: quòd ei virgo Vestalis, quia parum diligens ignis æterni custos suisset, digna visa est, quæ flagro admoneretur. Flagella autem hæc aspera. adeò ut Vlpianus 4 scripserit, ministrorum immanitate, multos sub ejusmodi flagellis interiisse. Et Horribile etiam id Horatio 5 visum agnominare:
units.tr: "For which causes a free man is beaten with clubs, for these a slave with whips." And the emperors rescripted that a wife has just grounds for divorce if she proves that her husband inflicts blows that are foreign to a free man. They understand these very whips, which are most remote from free men and women. And as a novel and harsh act concerning Licinius the Pontiff, Valerius relates that a Vestal virgin, because she had been rather careless as guardian of the eternal fire, was thought worthy to be admonished with a whip. Moreover these whips were harsh, so much so that Ulpian wrote that many had died under such whips through the savagery of the attendants. Horace also thought it worth calling this "horrible":

units.la: 1 Lib. x. de pœnis. 2 Lib. viii. c. 1. de repud. 3 Lib. i. cap. 1. 4 Lib. viii. de pœnis 5 Lib. i. Ser. iii.
units.tr: 1 Book 10, on punishments. 2 Book 8, chapter 1, on repudiation. 3 Book 1, chapter 1. 4 Book 8, on punishments. 5 Satires, book 1, satire 3.

units.la: Nec scutica dignum, horribili sectere flagello.
units.tr: "Not worthy of the lash, you cut with a horrible whip."

units.la: Quod magis fuit, cùm ea insitis aut officiulis exasperabant. Factum Romae, atque alibi. Eustathius dici notat : ἀτεφυαλω-τὰς μαςιγας, τὰς ἐξ ἀτεφυάλων σπειρο-μένας καλαχεοτερμένας : Flagra talaria, quae talis insertis involutisque confecta sunt. Apud Athenaeum quispiam recenset, in Parthis optimates quoque & Satrapas, ubi visum Regi, ψιλθοις ἡ ἱμάσιν ἀτεφυαλωθεὶς μαςιγᾶς : virgis & loris taxillatis cadi. Apuleius agnoscit, & Flagrum pecuinis ossibus cathenatum, scitè appellat. Ille idem Gallis Matrisdeum adscribit: Arrepto flagro, inquit, quod semiviris illis proprium gestamen est, contortis taniis lanosi velleris prolixè fimbriatum, & multijugis talis ovium tesellatum, in-didem
units.tr: This was more so when they made them harsher with inserted or small knucklebones. This was done at Rome and elsewhere. Eustathius notes the term: "talaria whips, made from knucklebones spun and tied together." Athenaeus records that among the Parthians even the nobles and satraps, when the king so wills, are beaten with whips and thongs studded with knucklebones [ψιλθοις ἡ ἱμάσιν ἀτεφυαλωθεὶς μαςιγᾶς]. Apuleius acknowledges this and aptly calls it "a whip chained with sheep's bones." The same writer ascribes to the Galli of the Mother of the gods a whip: "Having seized the whip, which is the proper implement of those half-men, fringed thickly with long twisted thongs of woolly fleece and checkered with many knucklebones of sheep, they lash themselves."

units.la: ¹ Lib. iv. ² Lib. viii. didem sese multinodis commulcant illibus. Et Plutarchus appositè ad ejus lucem: Ο᾽ υδὲ μάστιγ᾽ ἰλισ-θέρας διόμεν᾽, ἀλλὰ τ᾽ ἀτερ-γαλεῖνς ἐκέινης ἢ τὰς Γέλλας πλημμελοῦντας ἐν τοῖς μυστεῖοις κολάζεσι: Nec qui libera verberationis egeat, sed flagri illius taxillati, quo Gallos aliquid offendentes in sacris Magnae matris coërcent. An tale aliquod flagri genus, quo Christus etiam noster cæsus? imaginantur aut pingunt per pietatem nonnulli. Haud ego affero: sed illud Evangelistæ, cæsum esse & quidem flagro. Sic enim Matthæus, corruptà ipsâ Latinâ voce: Τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ. Iesum cum flagellasset, tradidit ut crucifigeretur. Ἰμάσθλω, id est, loreum flagellum appellat Nonnus
units.tr: Plutarch also, aptly, in this same light: "Not one who needs a free beating, but of that knucklebone-studded whip with which they punish the Galli who offend in the mysteries" [Ο᾽ υδὲ μάστιγ᾽ ἰλισ-θέρας διόμεν᾽, ἀλλὰ τ᾽ ἀτερ-γαλεῖνς ἐκέινης]. Is there perhaps some such kind of whip with which our Christ too was struck? Some people, out of piety, imagine or paint it so. I do not assert this, but the Evangelist's words that he was struck, and indeed with a whip. For Matthew, with the Latin word itself corrupted, writes: "Having flogged Jesus, he handed him over to be crucified" [Τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ]. Nonnus calls a leather whip "ἰμάσθλω", that is, a whip of thongs.

units.la: † Contra Color. Γ'ιγιδανὴ Χριστοῖο δέμας φοίνιξι ἰμά- ἅλῃ, Horribili Christi corpus rubefecit habena.
units.tr: † Against Color. "Christ's body he reddened with the horrible thong" [Γ'ιγιδανὴ Χριστοῖο δέμας φοίνιξι ἰμά-ἅλῃ].
Chapter IV.

units.la: Solitos ad Columnam verberari; atque aliàs per viam. De ipsâ columnâ cui sacrum corpus annexum.
units.tr: That they were accustomed to be scourged at the Column, and at other times along the way. Concerning the column itself to which the sacred body was bound.

units.la: SEd observa. Flagellatio hæc non uno semper loco, aut tempore. Aut enim ante Deductionem utebantur, idque domi, aut in prætorio: quod in Servatore factum. aut in ipsâ Deductione, per viam: quod moris fuit magis prisci. Si domi, ligabant interdum ad columnam. Firmamenta huic ritui non tam multa reperio, reperio tamen. Artemidorus ubi somnium narrat servi, qui visus sibi ab hero δἰφιϑἀρ, deglubi & turpiter tangi:
units.tr: But observe. This scourging did not always take place in one place or at one time. For they used it either before the Deduction (the leading out to execution), and then at home or in the praetorium, which is what happened to our Saviour; or during the Deduction itself, along the way, which was more the custom of earlier times. If it was done at home, they sometimes bound the victim to a column. I do not find many proofs for this practice, but I do find some. Artemidorus, in relating the dream of a slave who seemed to his master to be a hide [διφθέρα], to be flayed and shamefully handled,

units.la: D tangi : addit ἀναστάσεις χιονι πολλὰς ἐλαύνεις πληγάς : columna alligatus, multas accepit plagas. Phileas etiam apud Eusebium , saevitiam in Martyres, qui Alexandriae, referens : Ἀλλοι δὲ πρὸς τοῖς κίοσιν ἀντιπρόσωποι ἐδέοντο : Alii autem ad columnas vultibus inter se adversis, astringebantur: & de flagellatione sentit. An & Plautum sic accipimus ?
units.tr: touched shamefully, adds: "you are driving many blows [ἀναστάσεις χιονι πολλὰς ἐλαύνεις πληγάς]": "bound to a column, he received many blows." Phileas also, in Eusebius, recounting the cruelty toward the martyrs at Alexandria, says: "Others, however, were bound to the columns, facing one another [Ἄλλοι δὲ πρὸς τοῖς κίοσιν ἀντιπρόσωποι ἐδέοντο]," and he means the scourging by this. Or do we also understand Plautus in this way?

units.la: — Abducite hunc Intro, atque adstringite ad columnam fortiter.
units.tr: "Take this man inside, and bind him fast to the column."

units.la: Ego quidem : etsi ad custodiam modo id factum aliquis pertendat. Sed de Servatore nostro non ambiguum, piis quidem & in religione antiquis. Etsi enim Euangelia non exprimunt : tamen secuti Patres. Prudentius clarè, & cum ritus quoque prisci attestatione :
units.tr: I, for my part, though someone may maintain that it was done merely for custody. But concerning our Saviour there is no doubt, at least for the pious and those ancient in religion. For although the Gospels do not express it, the Fathers followed it. Prudentius clearly does so, and with the testimony of the ancient ritual as well:
and

units.la: 1 Lib. viii. Eccl. Hist. cap. x. 2 Bacchid. 3 Novo Testam. atque columna Annexus, tergum dedit, ut servile, flagellis.
units.tr: 1 Eccl. Hist. book 8, chap. 10. 2 Bacchides. 3 New Testament. "And bound to the column, he gave his back, like a slave, to the scourges."

units.la: Hieronymus & suo ævo exstitisse commemorat. Ostendebatur illi (Paulæ) Columna, Ecclesiæ porticum sustinens infecta cruore Domini, ad quam vinctus dicitur & flagellatus. Indicat fulcri usum habuisse in ædificio templi : quod ipsum Prudentius . Perstat adhuc, templumque gerit veneranda columna. Etsi Bedæ tempore in medio Ecclesiæ fuisse, ipse testatur. Meminit hujus quoque, & miraculorum per eam, Gregorius Turonensis . Hæc domi flagellatio, & ad columnam : quid per viam? sub furcâ id factum, de quâ in * loco dicam.
units.tr: Jerome also records that it existed in his own age: "A column was shown to Paula, supporting the portico of the Church, stained with the blood of the Lord, to which he is said to have been bound and scourged." He indicates that it served as a support in the building of the temple, which Prudentius himself also says: "The venerable column still stands and bears the temple." Although Bede testifies that in his time it stood in the middle of the church. Gregory of Tours also mentions this column, and the miracles wrought through it. This is scourging at home, and at the column. But what of scourging along the way? It was done under the yoke (furca), of which I will speak in its proper place.

units.la: 1 Epist. ad Eustoch. 2 Ibidem. 3 De Glor. Mart. cap. 11.
units.tr: 1 Letter to Eustochium. 2 Ibid. 3 On the Glory of the Martyrs, chap. 11.
CHAP. V.

units.la: Crucem suam tulisse, aut totam, aut ejus partem.
units.tr: That he carried his cross, either the whole of it or a part of it.

units.la: AD Deductionem venio, in quâ duo observo, Ludibrium & Tormentum. Ludibrium, quòd ipsi coacti crucem suam ferre, aut certè ejus partem: ut verè esset illud quod dicitur, Suo sibi jumento malum. Artemidorus 1: Βασάζειν τινὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων χθονίων κακούργων μὲν ἰδίᾳ Σταυρὸν ἑαυτῷ σημαίνει, οἷον ἐκ ἡ καὶ ὁ Σταυρὸς Βασάτω, καὶ ὁ μίαν σταυρὸς λεῖς, πρότερον αὐτὸν Βασάζει: Ferre aliquem Deorum inferorum, malefico quidem id videnti Crucem prodicit. Similis enim & Crux morti; & qui in eâ figendus, prius eam portat. Plutarchus 2 etiam comparatione quadam utili: Καὶ τῇ μὲν
units.tr: I come now to the Deduction, in which I note two things: Mockery and Torment. The mockery lies in their being forced to carry their own cross, or at least part of it, so that the saying a burden to himself on his own donkey is literally true. Artemidorus, book 1: To carry something belonging to the underworld gods, for an evildoer, signifies a cross for him in a dream; for the cross is like death, and the one who is to be fixed to it carries it first. Plutarch also makes a useful comparison: [Καὶ τῇ μὲν σώματι τῷ κολαζομένων ἕκαστος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ Σταυρόν, ἡ δὲ κακία τῇ κολασιγένῳ ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν ἕκαστος ἐξ αὐτῆς τίκτεται]

units.la: 1 Lib. II. cap. XLI. 2 De tarda Dei vindicta. μὲν σώματι τῷ κολαζομένων ἕκαστος [?] τὸν ἑαυτῆς Σταυρόν, ἡ δὲ κακία τῆ κολασιγένῳ ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν ἕκαστος ἐξ αὐτῆς τίκτεται : Et corpore quidem quisque maleficorum suam effert Crucem : malitia autem cruciatuum quemque in se, ex se, gignit & fabricatur. Bene hoc & salubriter Plutarchus : & Dii Deaque (ait quispiam 1) quàm male est extra legem viventibus? quidquid meruerunt, semper exspectant. Sed repono me in gradum. Ferebant Crucem. atque ita Iohannes 2 de Christo : Βαστά-ζων τὸν Σταυρὸν αὑτῆς ἐξῆλθεν εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον κρανίου τόπον : Bajulans suam Crucem, exivit in locum Calvariæ dictum. Quâ sola caussâ vetera quædam vaticinia aut imagines Doctores nostri ad Christum trahunt. Vt Tertullianus 3 hoc de Isaaco. D 3 Cùm,
units.tr: 1 Book 2, chap. 41. 2 On the Delayed Vengeance of God. In the body, indeed, each of the wrongdoers bears his own cross; but in the soul, each one is born from vice itself, and begets his own torments from himself. Plutarch says this well and wholesomely: And how bad is it, gods and goddesses (someone says), for those who live outside the law! Whatever they have deserved, they always await. But I return to my point. They did carry the cross. So John says of Christ: [Βαστάζων τὸν Σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ ἐξῆλθεν εἰς τὸν λεγόμενον κρανίου τόπον]: Bearing his own cross, he went out to the place called Calvary. It is for this sole reason that our teachers draw certain ancient prophecies or images over to Christ, as Tertullian does with Isaac. 3 When
1 Petronius, Satyricon.
2 Chap. xix.

units.la: ³ Adversus Iudaeos cap. x. Cum, inquit, Isaac à patre hostia duceretur, & lignum ipse sibi portaret, Christi exitum jam tunc denotabat, in victimam concessi à Patre, lignum passionis sua bajulantis. Idem in Isaiæ verbis istis : Cujus imperium factum est super humerum ipsius. Solus, ait, novus rex Christus novæ gloriæ potestatem & sublimitatem in humero extulit, id est, Crucem. Et Christus sanè totam plenamque Crucem tulit. Ni fecisset, quid opus erat auxiliatore & subsequâ, qui adlevasset? Alii non semper totam : atque ideò cautè prædixi, ejus partem. Nam qui ritu veteri sub furcâ cæsi ducebantur, * ferebant non nisi istam. Imò interdum nec istam. Nam fac in arbore aliquâ crucifixum, & subitò : profectò, præter se, nihil tulit.
units.tr: 3 Against the Jews, chap. x. "When," he says, "Isaac was led by his father as a victim, and carried the wood himself, he already then foreshadowed Christ's going out, given up as a victim by the Father, carrying the wood of his passion." The same writer, on those words of Isaiah, whose rule was upon his shoulder, says: "The new king Christ alone bore on his shoulder the power and sublimity of a new glory, that is, the Cross." And Christ indeed carried the whole and complete cross. If he had not, why was there need of a helper and follower to lift it? Others did not always carry the whole; so I predicted cautiously, a part of it. For those who were led out to die under the old rite, struck beneath the yoke, carried only that, and sometimes not even that. Suppose someone was fastened to some tree and killed on the spot: surely he carried nothing but himself.
1 Same book.
CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Deductos cum vexatione, Sti- mulis etiam actos.
units.tr: Led away with harassment, and also driven with goads.

units.la: TOrmentum etiam in Deductione: quia trahere, divexare, & stimulis agere per viam solent. Dionysius 1 de tractione: δι ἀγεῦς ἀνθρώπους μαστιγοωθέντας εἴλκειν ἰλκειν: pen forum flagellatum ipsum, trahere eos jussit. Nec dubium est quin impulerint, dejecerint, crexerint, per saevitiam aut per lusum. De Stimulis etiam non temere addo. & aperte auctor adfirmandi Plautus 2, apud quem confervo servus: O carnificinum cribrum! quod credo fore, Ita te forabunt patibulatum per vias Stimulis, si nostler huc revenerit senex.
units.tr: There is also torment in the leading away itself, since people were usually dragged along the road and harassed and driven with goads. Dionysius, in book VII of his Antiquities, speaks of the dragging: he ordered men who had been flogged through the forum to be dragged along [δι ἀγορᾶς ἀνθρώπους μαστιγωθέντας εἵλκειν]. There is no doubt that they were also pushed, thrown down and dragged, either in savagery or in sport. I do not add the point about goads lightly, and Plautus clearly confirms it, where a fellow slave says: "O sieve of a torturer! I believe it will come to pass: they will pierce you through, hung on the gibbet, along the roads with goads, if our old man comes back here."
1 Book VII, Antiquities. 2 Mostellaria.

units.la: Habes Stimulos, idque in Patibulato (ad furcam astricto) & per vias. Jungit iterum cum Cruce Plautus 1: Stimulos, Laminas, Crucesque. & alias meminit, sed sic ut seorsim eos fuisse sciamus inter cruciatus & tormenta, sicut laminas & ignes. Pictores nostri aflerculum sive tabellam imae Christi vesti appingunt, quae clavis praeacutis consita pedibus calcibusque euntis illidatur: numquid alludentes ad hanc Destimulationem? quae tamen stimulis aliis facta. quos oblongos, sive e sudibus praeacutis, sive & ferro praefixis, gestabant ad hunc usum. Sumptum a bubus, quos sic exstimulabant. Sed nisi ea Pictorum mens, ipsi vidento: ego inventiunculae ejus nec auctor sim, nec interpres.
units.tr: You have goads here, and that for one fastened to a gibbet (a fork-shaped stake) and "along the roads." Plautus again links goads with the cross: "goads, plates, and crosses." He mentions them elsewhere too, but in such a way that we know they were, apart from the other torments, among the instruments of torture themselves, just as plates and fires were. Our painters attach to the lower part of Christ's garment a small board or tablet, which is studded with sharp nails and struck against the feet and heels of one who walks. Are they perhaps alluding to this goading? That, however, was done with other goads, long ones made either of sharpened stakes or also tipped with iron, which they carried for this purpose. The name is taken from oxen, which they goaded in this way. But whether that was the painters' intention, let them see for themselves: I am neither the author nor the interpreter of this little invention of theirs.
1 Asinaria.
CHAP. VII.

units.la: In ipsâ Fixione nudi in crucem dati: an altam, an in terrâ depositam? id quæsitum, & utrumque firmatum.
units.tr: At the Fixing itself, were the naked men put on the cross laid flat or upright? The question is raised, and both positions are supported.

units.la: ISta sunt quæ ante fixionem: nunc quæ in ipsâ. Tria considero, Suspensionem, Astrictionem, Inscriptionem. Suspensio præit, & ante illam etiam Nudatio. quia simul ad crucem ventum, spoliabant hominem, & sic in eam dabant. Receptum hoc in plerisque suppliciis, velut Naturæ suasu, quæ nudos induxit in vitam, & educit: etiam in isto. Artemidorus 1: Σταυρούσ ἀγαθὸν πῶ πίπτει· ἡ γὰρ ὑψηλὸς ὁ σταυρωθεὶς τὰς δὲ πλαστὰς βλάπτει· γυμνοὶ γὰρ σταυρῶνται. Crucifigi bonum pauperi, quia sublimis est crucifixus: noxium vero diviti, quia nudi D 5 cru-
units.tr: These are the things that come before the fixing; now I consider what happens in it itself. I consider three things: the hanging up, the binding, and the inscription. The hanging up comes first, and before it the stripping. For as soon as they reached the cross, they stripped the man and so put him on it. This was customary in most punishments, as if nature itself suggested it, since nature brought us into life naked and brings us out of it so too. Artemidorus, book 1: "To be crucified is good for the poor man, since the one crucified is raised high; but it harms the rich man, since men are crucified naked." To be crucified is good for a poor man, because the crucified man is raised high; but it is harmful for a rich man, because men are crucified naked. [Σταυροῦσθαι ἀγαθὸν πένητι πίπτει· ἡ γὰρ ὕψωσις ὁ σταυρωθεὶς τὰς δὲ πλουσίους βλάπτει· γυμνοὶ γὰρ σταυροῦνται] Crucifiers.

units.la: 1 Lib. II. cap. LVIII. crucifiguntur. In Christo factum hoc observes: quem Euangelistæ narrant recepisse vestes post flagellationem jam deducendum, & posuisse iterum deductum. Ergo nudi dati in crucem: sed Jacentem an Erectam? Pro Jacente, Acta vetera de Pionio Martyre: Ultro se vestimentis spoliavit, & in calum suspiciens ac Deo gratias agens, super lignum seipsum extendit, militiqué tradidit ut clavis configeretur. Satis clare: atque etiam mox clarius: Eumigitur ligno fixum erexerunt. Dici nihil potest, quin fixio hic in Jacente facta fuerit, quæ post erecta. Et ratio etiam aliqua suadet. Nonne enim facilius hominem sic affigere supinum & inclinatum: quàm tollere in erectam, pendulum, labentem, fortasse & reluctantem? videtur. Tamen quod in Erectam, plusculi adfirmant testes. Cicero ro {1} in Gaviană cruce describendâ : Quid attinuit, cùm Mamertini more atque instituto suo Crucem fixissent post urbem in viâ Pompeiâ, te jubere figere in viâ qua Rhegium spectat? Et verba & rei seriem vide, observabis fixam primò crucem, & tum in eam datum. Idem in Rabiriană: In campo Martio Crucem ad civium supplicium defigi & constitui jubes. Stabat jam defixa, dum causa diceretur, & cruciarium suum exspectabat. Galba apud Suetonium {2}, cuidam inclamanti se civem Romanum esse, multò praeter ceteras altiorem & dealbatam crucem statui jussit. Statui, ac tum suffigi. Josephus {3} de Judaeo quodam à Romanis capto : o' δὲ Βάσσῳ ἀσσεῖτως ἀλλαπηγόραν Σταυρὸν, ὡς ἀυλίκῳ χεισῶν τ' Ἑλλεσφρες : Bassus jussit defigi crucem, tamD 6 quam
units.tr: (1) Book 2, chapter 58. They are crucified. You may notice this in Christ, whom the Evangelists tell us was stripped of his garments after the scourging, and was stripped and laid bare again before he was led out. So they were given naked to the cross; but were they put on it lying down or standing up? For lying down, there is the old Acts of the martyr Pionius: He stripped himself of his garments of his own accord, and looking up to heaven and giving thanks to God, he stretched himself out upon the wood and gave himself to the soldiers to be fixed with nails. That is quite clear, and what follows is clearer still: They then raised him up, fixed to the wood. Nothing can be said more plainly than that the fixing here was done with him lying down, and that he was raised up afterwards. Reason, too, seems to support this: is it not easier to fasten a man lying on his back and bent than to lift him upright, hanging, slipping, and perhaps resisting? Yet several witnesses affirm that it was done with him upright. Cicero, in describing the cross in Gavia's case: Why was it necessary, when the Mamertines had, after their custom and practice, fixed a cross outside the city on the Pompeian road, for you to order one to be fixed on the road that faces Rhegium? Look at both the words and the order of the matter, and you will observe that the cross was first fixed, and only then was the man put on it. The same in the speech for Rabirius: In the Campus Martius you order a cross to be fastened and set up for the punishment of citizens. It was already standing, fixed, while the case was being pleaded, and it was waiting for its victim. Galba, in Suetonius, when a man cried out that he was a Roman citizen, ordered a cross far higher than the others and whitewashed to be set up. It was set up, and only then fastened in place. Josephus, of a Jew captured by the Romans: Bassus ordered the cross to be fixed, as if he were about to hang Eleazar on it immediately. [ὁ δὲ Βάσσος ἐκέλευσεν ... σταυρὸν ... ὡς αὐτίκα κρεμάσων ἐν αὐτῷ Ἐλεάζαρον] Lastly, in the book of Ezra, chapter 1: Whoever shall change this decree, let a beam be taken from his house, and let him be raised up and fixed upon it. In both places the raising up comes before the fixing. I do not see what can be put against this, except the weak point that the cross was set up but then lowered again when the criminal arrived. Who would believe that? Or what would be the reason for such pointless labour? The old phrases also contradict it, which we know usually match the things themselves. For they say to lift, to drive, to carry, to give to the cross; all these words denote raising or effort. Likewise in the sources themselves, to run out, to climb, to leap onto the cross; these seem to fit only an upright cross. Examples of the earlier phrases are well known and common; of the later, these are rare. Plautus, Bacchides:
(1) In chapter 6.

units.la: {3} Lib. vii. Excid. Iud. quam statim suspensurus in ea Eleazarum. Denique & libro Esdrae 1: Ut omnis homo qui hanc mutaverit jussionem, tollatur lignum de domo ipsius, & erigatur, & configatur in eo. Utrobique hic erectio, fixionem antecedit. Nec video quid obduci possit: nisi istud infirmum, statutas quidem, sed sub adventum noxii iterum demissas. Quis credat? aut irriti laboris quae ratio? Abnuunt etiam phrases veteres, quae scimus plerumque adsimiles rebus ipsis. Dicunt enim Tollere, Agere, Ferre, Dare in crucem: quae omnia elationis sunt aut molitionis. Item in ipsis fontibus, Excurrere, Ascendere, Salire, in crucem: quae mihi videntur convenire non nisi in Erectam. Priorum phrasium exempla nota atque obvia sunt: posteriorum capae ista. Plautus 2:
units.tr: {3} Lib. vii. of the Destruction of Jerusalem: which he was about to use at once to hang Eleazar on. Finally, in the first book of Esdras: Whoever shall alter this decree, let a beam be taken from his house, and let him be raised up and fastened to it. In both places the raising comes before the fixing. I cannot see what can be objected, except that this is weak: the beam was indeed set up, but was afterwards lowered again when the guilty man came. Who would believe that? Or what would be the point of such useless labour? Ancient phrases also oppose this, and we know they are for the most part closely matched to the things themselves. They say to lift, to drive, to bear, to give to the cross, all of which denote raising or effort. Likewise in the very sources: to run out, to ascend, to leap to the cross, which seem to fit only the upright cross. Examples of the former kind of phrase are familiar and common; examples of the latter are rare. Plautus:

units.la: Quorum versuum (haud sanè * optimorum, liberè dicam) hæc sententia. Duƈtum & subduƈtum in altam crucem ad ultimum ejus finem : rectum ita statutum : tum ad transversarium lignum manus fixas : denique & pedes ad stipitem desixum. Atque ista pro Erectâ. In dissensu autem nos quid definimus ? consensum, quâ licet. Dicimus utrumque usurpatum, sæpiùs tamen hoc postremum. Imò interim necessariò hoc postremum. Pone enim in arbore suspensos (sæpe factum :) quomodo demitti ea potuit, & tunc attolli?
units.tr: The sense of these verses (not the best, I will say freely) is this: the body was drawn up and pulled to the top of the high cross, the upright beam being set so; then the hands were fixed to the crossbeam, and finally the feet to the upright stake. And these verses speak for the upright cross. But in the disagreement, what do we decide? We grant agreement where we can. We say that both forms were used, but the latter more often. Indeed, at times the latter is necessary. For suppose men hanging on a tree (as often happened): how could they be let down and then lifted up again?

units.la: CAP. VIII. Clavis figi solitos, interdum funibus adstringi.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. That they were commonly fixed with nails, and sometimes bound with cords.

units.la: SEd jam ad Astrictionem transeo; quæ facta clavis, aut sunibus, sed plurimùm illis. Seneca : Cùm refigere se crucibus conentur, in quas unusquisque vestrum clavos suos ipse adigit. Ita legendum, non adjicit. Illi, inquit, conantur tollere se de crucibus suis: vos contrà, magis magisque affigitis, & clavos adigitis in lignum. Meminit & Apollo in oraculo quopiam, de Christo: Γὶμφοις κ̣ͅ σκολόωτσι ωιχῆν ἀντλησι τιλευτὴν:
units.tr: But now I pass to binding (astrictio), which was done with nails or with cords, though mostly with cords. Seneca: When they try to get themselves down from the crosses, on which each of you drives in his own nails. So it should be read, "non adjicit" (he does not add). They, he says, try to take themselves down from their crosses; but you, on the contrary, fix yourselves more and more and drive your nails into the wood. Apollo also mentions Christ in some oracle: [γόμφοις καὶ σκολόπεσσι βίαιον ἀνταλῆσαι τελευτήν]
He endured a bitter death with nails and stakes.

units.la: 1 De vita beata cap.xix. 2 Apud Lactant. lib. iv. cap. xiii. crucem : quia, ut ¹ Artemidorus ait, ἐκ ξύλων ἢ ἥλων γίσονται ὁ σταυρὸς : ex lignis & clavis crux confecta est. Atque ab hac re Græcis passim ipsa crucifixio, σταυρίλωσις dicta : quasi dicas clavi-fixio. Ulpianus in Demosthenem ² explicat σταυρηλῶσαι, Σταυρῷ σταυρηλῶσαι ὑπὸ ἥλοις : cruci affigi clavis. Et fortasse eò respexit Strabo ³ cùm de Cantabris dixit, ἀνασταυρωμένους ἐπὶ τῶν Σταυρῶν : suffixos in crucibus. Ergo de clavis certum : an etiam de sunibus ? sunt exempla. Ausonius suum Cupidinem facit. Devinctum post terga manus, substrictaque plantis Vincula mærentem.
units.tr: 1 On the Blessed Life, chap. xix. 2 Quoted in Lactantius, bk. iv, chap. xiii. (cross): because, as Artemidorus says, [σταυρὸς ἐκ ξύλων ἢ ἥλων γίνεται], the cross is made of wood and nails. For this reason the Greeks commonly called crucifixion itself stauriloseis [σταυρίλωσις], as if you said "nail-fixing." Ulpian, in his commentary on Demosthenes, explains staurēlōsai [σταυρηλῶσαι] as to be fixed to a cross with nails. Perhaps Strabo had this in mind when he said of the Cantabrians that they were hung up on crosses [ἀνασταυρωμένους ἐπὶ τῶν σταυρῶν]. So much for nails, which is certain. But what of cords? There are examples. Ausonius makes his Cupid with hands bound behind his back and cords drawn tight on his feet, grieving.

units.la: ¹ Lib.ii. cap.lviii. ² Contra Mid. ³ Lib.iii. ⁴ Lib.ii. cap. lviii. ꝛasoχιύ, διὰ τὴν διʹσιν: Crucifigi (in somnis) viro caelibi nuptias defignat, ob ligaturam, quia scilicet ligno jungitur copulaturque.Plinius 1 inter magicas ineptias Spartum etiam è cruce numerat, id est sparteos funes. Quid, quòd D. Andreas ita alligatus? Abdias 2 aperte, & caussam etiam addit: Proconsul mandat quaestionariis, ut ligatis manibus & pedibus, non clavis affixus suspenderetur, quo diutino cruciatu deficeret. Ex quo colligas, habitum id magis saevum. Etsi prima fortasse crucifixio talis, & in Livii 3 prisicis scriptisque libris legas: Arbori infelici recte suspendito. Recte, inquam, additur: quod tamen heri ac nuper ejecerunt correctores. An sic quoque appensi latrones bini, qui cum Christo? Vulgò sentiunt,
units.tr: 1 Bk. ii, chap. lviii. 2 Against Midias. 3 Bk. iii. 4 Bk. ii, chap. lviii. that is, because he is joined and coupled to the wood." Pliny, among magical absurdities, also counts spartum taken from a cross, that is, ropes of esparto. And what of St Andrew, who was bound in this way? Abdias states it plainly and even gives the reason: "The proconsul orders the torturers that he be hung up, with hands and feet bound and not fixed with nails, so that he would die of a long-drawn torment." From this you may gather that this was regarded as the crueler form. Yet perhaps the first crucifixion was of this kind, and in the older and manuscript copies of Livy you may read: Hang him on the unlucky tree. "Rightly" is added, I say; yet the recent correctors removed it. Were the two thieves who were hung with Christ likewise bound? Commonly they think so, and paint them no differently.

units.la: Et magis Historia prisca, quæ est de Helenâ Constantini matre. Ea cùm venisseт sacra & Deohomini trita loca, cupidine visendi & venerandi : de Cruce etiam inquisivit nostrâ illâ servatrice. Fodit, tres reperit, ac diu animi anceps hæsit quæ esset illa vera. Nam Titulus, quo dignosci potuisset, jacebat seorsim disjectus. Denique miraculo & divinâ indicatione opus fuit ad discernendum. Quid autem opus, si vestigia clavorum modò in unâ? Argumentum certum est, & res ipsa per Ecclesiæ annales.
units.tr: The older story is even more to the point, the one about Helena, Constantine's mother. When she came to the sacred places, trodden by the divine man, eager to see and venerate them, she also made inquiry about the Cross of that Saviour of ours. She dug, found three, and for a long time was torn in mind as to which was the true one; for the Title, by which it could have been recognized, lay apart, disjointed. In the end a miracle and a divine indication were needed to tell them apart. But what need would there be, if the traces of nails were on one alone? The argument is sound, and the matter is recorded in the annals of the Church.

units.tr: That these nails, or even ropes, were on the hands and feet is well enough known. Nonnus, on the Saviour:

units.la: Tertullianus de veteri vaticinio: Foderunt manus meas & pedes] quæ propria atrocitas crucis. Habent atrocia libri scripti: & rectè, ut amat loqui ille scriptor. At quàm multi isti clavi? enimvero dissident. Alii de ternis asserunt, ut Nonnus, qui Christum depingit:
units.tr: Tertullian, on the old prophecy: "They pierced my hands and my feet," which is the peculiar atrocity of the cross. The written books have atrocia, and rightly so, as that writer likes to speak. But how many nails were there? They certainly disagree. Some assert three, as Nonnus does, who depicts Christ:

units.la: Facit ecce magno & singulari clavo pedis utriusque pectusculum transfigi, & quidem uno ictu, idque pedibus mutuò impositis & complicatis. Clarum est etiam illud Nazianzeni, 1 pariter de Christo, ubi cruce deponitur:
units.tr: Behold, this makes the little breast of both feet pierced through by one large and single nail, and indeed by one blow, the feet placed one upon the other and folded together. The saying of Nazianzen is also clear, likewise concerning Christ, where he is taken down from the cross:
Γυμνὸν τρίκλαρον κάμψον ξύλῳ λαβών [Taking the naked one, bent down from the wood]
Taking down the naked one, laid back from the wood, pierced with three nails.

units.la: At contrà tamen tendunt alii, & suggerunt quaternos. De eodem Christo Gregorius Turonus : 2 Clavorum dominicorum, quod quatuor fuerint, hæc est ratio. Duo sunt affixi in palmis, & duo in plantis. Sed & Cyprianus 3 melior lior
units.tr: On the other hand, however, others stretch the number and propose four. Gregory of Tours, on the same Christ: "As to the Lord's nails, that there were four, this is the reason: two are fixed in the palms and two in the soles." But also Cyprian, the better and greater author, wrote in his passionate style: "Nails piercing the sacred feet."

units.la: 1 In Christo patiente. 2 De Glor. cap. vi. 3 Serm. de Passione. lior majorque auctor πλανθυτικὼς scripsit : Clavis sacros pedes terebrantibus. Quid, quòd ' Plautus ex more astruere videtur tantos? Ego dabo ei talentum, primus. qui in crucem excucurrerit, Sed ea lege, ut offigantur bis pedes, bis brachia.
units.tr: ¹ In Christo patiente. ² De Gloria, ch. vi. ³ Sermon on the Passion. What of the fact that Plautus seems to assume, in the usual way, so many? "I will give him a talent, the first who runs to the cross. But on this condition: that the feet be fastened twice, and the arms twice."

units.la: Nisi is tamen ibi sensus. ut servulus ad majorem quasi cautionem, & ne facile se refrigeret, voluerit non semel manus pedesque, sed bis singula figi: ita inquam, ut bini in quoque membro essent clavi. Quàm magis confidero, tam magis hoc dictum censeo: cùm id quoque reperiam, per sævitiam multiplicatos alibi clavos. Ut in Martyrologio : Agricolam plurimis clavis Cruci affigentes interemerunt. Interdum & in aliâ corporis parte.
units.tr: Unless, however, the meaning there is this: that the little slave, for greater security and so as not to cool off easily, wished the hands and feet to be fixed not once but twice each; so that each limb had two nails. The more I consider it, the more I think this saying is meant so, since I find elsewhere that nails were multiplied through cruelty. As in the Martyrology: "They killed the farmer by fixing him to the cross with very many nails." Sometimes also in another part of the body.
