units.la: In eodem Martyrologio: Philomenus manibus pedibusque, ac demum capite clavis confixo, martyrium consummavit. Itaque si morem veterem vides; arbitrarium fuit de clavis, & frustra litigemus. Si de Christo tamen quaeritur; nescio, & in dissensu Patrum non est meum arbitrari.
units.tr: In the same Martyrology: "Philomenus, having been fixed with nails through the hands and feet and at last through the head, completed his martyrdom." So if you see the old custom, the question about the nails is a matter of opinion, and we would quarrel in vain. If we ask about Christ, however, I do not know, and in the disagreement of the Fathers it is not for me to judge.

units.la: CAP. X. Ordo & Modus affigendi. An lignum aliquod in Cruce suppe- daneum?
units.tr: CHAPTER X. The order and manner of fixing. Was there some support in the cross, a kind of footrest?

units.la: ADdo magis de figendi modo. Is fuit, ut manus primum figerent, inde pedes. Graphicè Lucianus in Dialogo ubi Prometheus figitur, Vulcanus Mercurio loquitur: Ἀνιστάω ... Crucifigatur, extensus ambas manus ab hac parte in ad-
units.tr: I add more on the manner of fixing. It was this: they first fixed the hands, then the feet. Lucian graphically, in the Dialogue where Prometheus is fastened, has Vulcan speak to Mercury: "Let him be crucified, stretched with both hands on this side and on that." And the beginning is made from the right hand.

units.la: ¹ XXIX. Novemb. adversum. Atque initium à manu dextrâ. Ibidem Mercurius Prometheo : Ἀ'ϰ' ὀ͏ϱιγι τὴν διξιὰν, σὺ δ' ὦ Ἡφαιστε, καλάχλεις, καὶ σεσηλὰς, καὶ τὴν σφύραν ἐμπαμένας καταδήσει· ὃς καὶ τὴν ἐτέραν, καταλιφθὼ ἰὸ μάλα καὶ αὐτή : Sed prœbe dexteram. tu autem Vulcane, astringe, & confige, & malleum fortiter demitte. Da & alteram, quò illa etiam rectè astringatur. Tum itum ad pedes. Sed ambigas, Manúsne fuerint toti moli ferendæ ? Apparet enim corpus omne (præsertim si quis pedes inflecteret) pependisse manibus solis. Ego ita arbitror. Quidni? Duræ & nervosæ illæ partes, & lentè frangi. Fortasse nec in media semper manus vola clavi fixi, sed superius paullo quà cum brachio coit, id est circa carpum. Plautus facit suspicari, qui diserte scribit brachia offigi, non manus. Sed puto equidem amplius. si corpus gravius,
units.tr: ¹ XXIX. Novemb. adversum. And the beginning is made with the right hand. In the same dialogue Mercury says to Prometheus: [Ἀ'ϰ' ὀ͏ϱιγι τὴν διξιὰν, σὺ δ' ὦ Ἡφαιστε, καλάχλεις, καὶ σεσηλὰς, καὶ τὴν σφύραν ἐμπαμένας καταδήσει· ὃς καὶ τὴν ἐτέραν, καταλιφθὼ ἰὸ μάλα καὶ αὐτή] But offer your right hand. And you, Vulcan, bind it, fasten it, and drive the hammer down hard. Give the other one too, so that it may be bound securely as well. Then they went on to the feet. But you may wonder whether the hands were enough to bear the whole weight. For it appears that the whole body (especially if someone bent the feet) hung by the hands alone. I think so. Why not? Those parts are hard and sinewy, and they are slow to tear. Perhaps the nail was not always driven through the middle of the palm, but a little higher up, where the hand joins the arm, that is, around the wrist. Plautus leads us to suspect this, since he writes plainly that the arms were fastened, not the hands. But I think more: if the body were heavier, or the hands more slender, ropes were often the support. These too were added, and fastened about the shoulders or the middle of the chest, to the cross. I would prefer this to introducing, with others, a small board or tablet on which the feet rested and were fixed together. That construction is too precise, indeed too dainty. Yet Gregory of Tours recognises such a board in Christ's cross. Whether because it was so, or because he imagined it devoutly, I cannot say. He himself writes: In the upright post a hole is clearly visible. A small tablet was also inserted into this hole, and the holy feet were fixed upon this tablet, as if on a standing man. Nor do I know whether the words of Innocent belong here: In the Lord's cross there were four pieces of wood: an upright post, a crossbeam, a trunk placed beneath, and a title above

units.la: Anser- : ἀνφερ- (Gloss-Vermerk „anferre" zu corpus omne) vius, aut manus tenuior; adminiculum sæpe fuisse funes. Illos quoque additos, & circa humeros aut pectus medium, ad crucem adstrictos. Hoc malim, quàm cum aliis asserculum sive tabellam inducere, in quâ innixi & fixi-simul pedes. Nimis accurata ea fabrica, imò delicata. Tamen in Christi cruce Gregorius Turonicus 1 agnoscit; quiâne fuit, an quia piè imaginatus est? Ipse quidem sic: In stipite erecto foramen factum manifestum est. pes quoque parva tabula in hoc foramen insertus est: super hanc verò tabulam, tamquam stantis hominis, sacra affixa sunt planta. Nec scio an illuc Innocentii 2 hæc referenda: fuerunt in cruce dominicâ ligna quatuor, stipes erectus, & lignum transversum, truncus suppositus, & titulus super-
units.tr: Anser- (a marginal gloss, "anferre" ("to carry"), on "corpus omne") [ἀνφερ-] vius, or the hand thinner. Ropes were often a support, and these were also added and fastened to the cross around the shoulders or the middle of the chest. I would prefer this to introducing, with others, a small plank or tablet on which the feet rest and are fixed at the same time. That construction is too precise, indeed too delicate. Yet Gregory of Tours¹ recognises it in Christ's cross. Was it because it really was so, or because he imagined it devoutly? He himself writes thus: In the upright post a hole is plainly visible. A small tablet was also inserted into this hole for the foot; and upon this tablet the sacred feet were fixed, as of a standing man. Nor do I know whether the words of Innocent² should be referred there: In the Lord's cross there were four pieces of wood: an upright post, and a transverse beam, a trunk placed beneath, and a title placed above

units.la: ¹ De Glor. Martyr. cap. vi. ² Serm. 1. de uno Martyr. superpositus. Nam vidi qui de Trunco sic acciperent: etsi vox videtur abnuere: quæ parùm apta ad minutam illam tabellam. Verba etiam plura & sequentia Innocentii cùm examino, sentire eum dixerim non de hac impositâ, sed verè (ut loquitur) suppositotrunco, è quo ipsa crux surgat. Ita enim sensisse videtur: truncum aliquem fuisse, sive fulciendæ cruci in imo appositum (ἀντερείδια Græci id genus obliqui sustentaculi vocant;) sive sub ipso recto stipite in terrâ, cui ille immissus, ut firmior staret. Neque ego affero id factitatum: sed mentem scriptoris pono. Trahunt etiam Irenæum istuc, qui crucem sic deformat: Ipse habitus crucis fines & summitates habet quinque: duos in longitudinem, & duos in latitudinem, & unum in medio ubi requiescit E qui
units.tr: ¹ De Glor. Martyr. cap. vi. ² Serm. 1. de uno Martyr. superpositus. For I have seen people who took trunk in that sense, though the word seems to resist it, since it is hardly suited to that little tablet. I also weigh the longer and following words of Innocent, and I would say that he means not this placed-on piece, but truly (as he puts it) a trunk placed beneath, from which the cross itself rises. For he seems to have meant this: there was some trunk, set at the foot to prop up the cross (the Greeks call this kind of oblique support [ἀντερείδια]), or placed in the ground beneath the upright post itself, into which the post was sunk so that it would stand firmer. I do not claim that this was a common practice; I am setting out the writer's meaning. They also drag Irenaeus into this, who describes the cross in this way: The very form of the cross has five ends and summits: two in length, two in breadth, and one in the middle, where it rests. And he who is fixed with nails. Behold, they say, that middle end is the tablet on which the body rests. I admit the words seem to point that way, and I would not rashly contend about another man's mind. Yet Justin Martyr, from whom these words seem to be taken, speaks thus about this matter

units.la: 1 Lib. II, cap. XLII. qui clavis configitur. En, inquiunt, medius ille finis tabella est, in quâ corpus requiescit. Fateor verba huc ire, nec temerè contenderim de alienâ mente. Tamen Iustinus martyr, è quo sumpta hæc videntur, sic de isto fine: Καὶ τὸ ἐν τᾷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ξύλον ὡς κέρας ἡσὶ ἀνὰ ἐξίχον ἐστὶν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐποχῆσι ἐσταυρωμένοι: Et illud in medio defixum lignum, ut cornu ipsum etiam eminet, in quo feruntur & quasi inveniuntur qui crucifiguntur. Cornu id appellat, & notare vult: quomodo aptè in planâ hac tabellâ? Videndum ne uterque ille scriptor aliud intelligat à jam dicto sensu. Dividunt crucem in quinque fines (Apices Tertullianus scitè appellat:) quattuor illos, qui noti sunt & incurrunt: quintum, quem in medià cruce collocant, ubi lignum transversum scin-
units.tr: ¹ Book II, ch. XLII. "...who is fixed with nails." Look, they say, that middle end is the tablet on which the body rests. I admit the words point that way, nor would I rashly contend about another's mind. Yet Justin Martyr, from whom these words seem to be taken, says of that end: "And the wood fixed in the middle, which projects like a horn, on which they are carried and, as it were, found, those who are crucified." [καὶ τὸ ἐν τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ξύλον ὡς κέρας ἠσὶν ἀνὰ ἐξέχον ἐστίν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐποχῇσι ἐσταυρωμένοι] He calls it a horn, and wants to note this. How does that fit well on this flat tablet? We should consider whether both writers mean something other than the sense just given. They divide the cross into five ends (Tertullian neatly calls them apices): the four which are well known and project, and the fifth, which they place in the middle of the cross, where the transverse wood cuts across and passes over the fixed upright.

units.la: ¹ Adverf. Triph. Iud. ² Lib. III. adverf. Marc. cap. XIX. scindit transitque stipitem defixum. Hac consideratione, quinque sunt fines: & unus ille stipes (sed sectus) facit ternos. Quod autem ajunt invehi & requiescere: verum est. corpus acclinatur ei & quasi innititur a tergo. Augustinus hoc sensu scripsit, Longitudinem crucis a terra surgentem, cui corpus erat infixum. An totum corpus? imo pedes tantum quod liquet: sed adfixum innixumque intelligit, nec scio an innixum scripsit. Tamen in picturis sculpturisque etiam priscis vestigium tabellae hujus extare audio: non ergo temere [?]preverim. non certe a Christi cruce: de aliis, audacius. Quod enim vestigium in scriptoribus antiquis?
units.tr: ¹ Against Trypho the Jew. ² Book III against Marcion, ch. XIX. By this reckoning there are five ends, and that one upright (though divided) makes three. As for their saying that the body is "carried and rests," that is true: the body leans on it and, as it were, rests against it from behind. Augustine wrote in this sense: "the length of the cross rising from the earth, to which the body was fixed." The whole body? Rather the feet only, as is clear; but he means fixed and leaning, and I do not know whether he wrote "leaning." Yet even in ancient paintings and sculptures, I hear, a trace of this tablet survives, so I would not rashly reject it. Certainly not for Christ's cross; about other crosses I would be bolder. For what trace of it is there in the ancient writers?
CHAP. XI.

units.la: De Titulo, quid is Latinis? quomo- do assriptus, aut prælatus.
units.tr: On the Title: what it is called in Latin, and how it was fixed or carried before.

units.la: POst Astrictionem Inscriptio. Quid ea est? Caussa supplicii, & ipsum crimen, & Romana voce Titulus: quâ & Iohannes est usus. Atque item Nonnus1: Γεάμμα , τόπος κφλίσσι Λατινίδι Τίτλος ἰωὴ.
units.tr: After the fastening comes the inscription. What is it? It is the cause of the punishment, the crime itself, and in Roman speech titulus, which John also used. Nonnus likewise: a letter, a place, in Latin a title [Γράμμα, τόπος ... Λατινίδι Τίτλος ἰωὴ].

units.la: Matthæus Αἰτία benè & signanter dixit. Glossæ Græcanicæ veteres: Αἰτία, caussa, materia, titulus. Eædem Latinè, Titulus, ἐπίγραμμα. Latini etiam passim pro caussâ. Ut poëta:
units.tr: Matthew said aitia [Αἰτία] well and pointedly. The old Greek glosses have: aitia, cause, matter, title. The same glosses in Latin give titulus for epigramma [ἐπίγραμμα]. The Latins also often use it for cause. As the poet has it:
And will you be able to have a title for my death?

units.la: Valerius2: Fine vitæ nostræ variis & occultis caussis expositio, interdum
units.tr: Valerius says: the end of our life, set forth by various and hidden causes, sometimes, while certain undeserved things take up the title of the final fate.

units.la: 1 In cap. xix. 2 Lib. ix. cap. xii. dum quædam immerentia supremi fati titulum occupant. Atque hic Titulus præferri aut apponi solet damnatis. Præferri, ut in Suetonii Caligulâ: Præcedente titulo qui causam pœna indicaret, per cætus epulantium circumducitur. Epistola Lugdunensium, de Attalo Martyre: Πεμφθεὶς κύκλῳ περιφερόμενος, πίναξ ἀνὰ ἀπὸ προάγοντος, ἐν ᾗ ἐγέγραπτο ῥωμαϊστὶ, οὗτός ἐστιν Ἄτταλος ὁ Χριστιανός: Circumactus per amphitheatrum, tabella ipsum præeunte, in quâ Latinè scriptum, Hic est Attalus Christianus. Sed & appendi, aut apponi damnatis solet. Suetonius Domitiano: Patrem familias detractum è spectaculis in arenam canibus objecit cum hoc titulo, Impiè locutus parmularius. Quintilianus ostendit Gladiatores quoque sic productos: Quidam ut patrem sepelirêt,
units.tr: 1 On chap. xix. 2 Book ix, chap. xii. And here the title is usually carried before the condemned or attached to them. It was carried before, as in Suetonius's Caligula: "With the title going before, which stated the cause of the punishment, he was led around through the groups of diners." The letter of the Lyonnese on the martyr Attalus: "Led around the circus, carried about, a tablet going before him, on which was written in Roman letters, 'This is Attalus the Christian'" [Πεμφθεὶς κύκλῳ περιφερόμενος, πίναξ ἀνὰ ἀπὸ προάγοντος, ἐν ᾗ ἐγέγραπτο ῥωμαϊστὶ, οὗτός ἐστιν Ἄτταλος ὁ Χριστιανός]: "He was driven round the amphitheatre, with a tablet going before him, on which was written in Latin, 'This is Attalus the Christian.'" But it was also customary to hang or attach it to the condemned. Suetonius, on Domitian: "He threw a head of a family, dragged from the shows, to the dogs in the arena, with this title: 'Spoke impiously, the small-shield fighter.'" Quintilian shows that gladiators too were presented in this way: "Some man, to bury his father, hired himself out. Brought forth on the day of the show under the title of his case, he received the wooden sword at the people's demand."

units.la: ¹ Cap. xxxviii. ² Apud Eusebium lib. v. cap. 1.
units.tr: ¹ Chap. xxxviii. ² In Eusebius, book v, chap. 1.

units.la: ³ Cap. x. ⁴ Declam. cccii. ret, auctoravit se. Die muneris productus sub titulo causæ, rudem populo postulante accepit. Sed facit proprie ad Crucem Dionis locus, de servo, quem dominus agi in crucem, idque per forum jussit: Μετὰ γεγραμμένην τὴν αἰτίαν ᾧ θανατώσεως ἐπλήρωσαν: Cum litteris (sive Titulo) quæ causam mortis aperirent. Sæpè etiam neglecto aut spreto titulo contenti Superdictione fuerunt, id est ut Præconis præeuntis voce populo id nuntiaretur: de quo more alii, & ego alias.
units.tr: ³ Chap. x. ⁴ Declamation cccii. But the passage of Dio pertains properly to the Cross: about a slave whom his master ordered to be led to the cross, and through the forum: "With the written accusation for which they fulfilled the sentence of death" [Μετὰ γεγραμμένην τὴν αἰτίαν ᾧ θανατώσεως ἐπλήρωσαν]: "with the letters (or title) that made known the cause of death." Often, too, when the title was neglected or disregarded, they were content with the superdictio, that is, with having this announced to the people by the voice of a herald going before. Others have written about this custom, and I have elsewhere.
CHAPTER XII.

units.la: Post fixionem, quomodo mortui in cruce? languore, aut fame. Vitalitas quorumdam.
units.tr: After fixing: how do the crucified die on the cross? Of weakness or of hunger. The vitality of some.

units.la: BENE jam & fideliter fiximus: quid post fixionem? hæc tria, Mors, Corruptio, Custodia.
units.tr: We have now fixed them well and faithfully. What follows fixing? These three things: death, corruption, guarding.
¹ Book LIV.

units.la: dia. Mors, lenta, molesta, & vel à stillante paulatim sanguine, vel à fame. Quid si etiam ab avium ferarum quel aniatu? videbimus, & singillatim diducemus. De sanguine quem demittebant fixi, clarum est, nec testimonii eget: & tum ea causa, tum ex verberatione quæ præiverat, credo invalidiores multos obiisse. At de fame, Eusebius 1 ubi Martyres narrat crucifixos in Ægypto: Τηξούμβοι τι ζῶντες, ὅτι ... ; & servati sunt vivi, donec in ipsis patibulis fame morerentur.
units.tr: Death is slow and painful, coming either from blood dripping away little by little or from hunger. What if it also comes from the attacks of birds and wild beasts? We shall see, and take each in turn. That the blood which the fixed men lost was a cause is clear and needs no witness. I believe that many died weaker, both from that cause and from the scourging that had gone before. As for hunger, Eusebius, where he tells of the martyrs crucified in Egypt, says: "wasting away while still alive, because ..." [Τηξούμβοι τι ζῶντες, ὅτι ...]; they were kept alive, until they died of hunger on the very gibbets.

units.la: Itaque legas quosdam diu in cruciabus vixisse, ut ingenitum scilicet robur erat, aut vires. Beatus Andreas in cruce suspensus, in ea populum docens 2, (ô athletam Deo dignum!) biduo super vixit. Victorinus sub Nerva, jussus suspendi capite deorsum, ita
units.tr: So one may read of some who lived a long time in their torments, presumably because they had innate strength or stamina. Blessed Andrew, hanging on the cross, taught the people from it (O athlete worthy of God!) and lived on for two days. Victorinus under Nerva, ordered to be hanged head downwards, so

units.la: 1. Lib. VIII. cap. VIII. 2 Martyr. xxx. Novemb. ita per triduum vixit1. Quod fanè miror in schemate illo minimè apto ad longam vitam. Magis etiam istud: quòd Timotheus & Maura in Cruce novem diebus vivi pendentes, ac se ipsos in fide corroborantes, martyrium consumpserunt2.
units.tr: ¹ Book VIII, chap. VIII. ² Martyr., 30 November. lived on for three days¹. I wonder at this indeed, since that posture is in no way suited to a long life. Even more remarkable is this: Timotheus and Maura, hanging alive on the cross for nine days, strengthening themselves in the faith, finished their martyrdom².

units.la: Vnde hæc vis aut vitalitas, nisi à vitæ ipso fonte? Quamquam & alii quidam animosè egisse in extremissimis istis rebus legantur. velut Bomilcar ille apud Iustinum3: qui patibulo suffixus in foro medio, magno animo crudelitatem civium tulit: adeò ut de summâ Cruce, veluti de tribunali, in Pœnorum scelera concionaretur. Quidam etiam petulanter: ut protervuli apud Senecam4, qui ex patibulo spectatores suos conspuunt. Atque etiam adnotavi, quosdam miseratione Principis, aut Magistratuum è Cruce E 5 ab-
units.tr: Where does such strength or vitality come from, unless from the very source of life? Yet we also read that some men, in their last extremities, bore themselves bravely. Such is that Bomilcar in Justin³, who, fixed to a gibbet in the middle of the forum, bore the cruelty of his fellow citizens with great courage, so much so that from the top of the cross, as from a tribunal, he preached against the crimes of the Carthaginians. Some even behaved insolently, like the wanton ones in Seneca⁴, who spat from the gibbet upon their spectators. I have also noted that some, through the pity of a prince or of the magistrates, were taken down from the cross and lived afterwards.

units.la: ¹ Martyr. v. Septemb. ² Martyr. iii. Maii. ³ Lib. xxii. ⁴ De vit. bea. cap. xix. ablatos, post vixisse. Iosephus in vita sua recitat: Redibam, inquit, e vico quodam, & vidi multos ex hostibus (Iudaeis) crucifixos: & tres ex iis adagnoscens, cum quibus ante mihi consuetudo, valde in animo dolui, & cum lacrimis progressus, dixi Tito. Ille autem statim depositos eos mandat diligentissime curari, atque ex iis duo inter ipsam curam obierunt, tertius supervixit.
units.tr: ¹ Martyr., 5 September. ² Martyr., 3 May. ³ Book XXII. ⁴ De vita beata, chap. XIX. Josephus relates in his own life: "I was returning," he says, "from a certain village, and I saw many of the enemy (the Jews) crucified; and recognising three of them, men with whom I had once been friendly, I was greatly grieved in mind, and going forward with tears I said to Titus." He at once ordered them taken down and most carefully cared for, and of these two died during the very care, the third survived.
CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: Quosdam a volucribus, aut feris etiam vivos laceratos, & plerosque omnes mortuos. interdum & lanceis interfectos.
units.tr: Some were torn apart by birds, or even by wild beasts while still alive, and most were dead. Sometimes they were also killed with lances.

units.la: {a}AT de laniatu etiam addidi, & caussam illam quoque feci mortis. Haud temerè, quia sic ligati, & cùm se non {b}commoverent, dati revera * ιλάσ- γίας, ut cum poëta dicam, κύνεσσιν Οἰω-
units.tr: I have also added the mangling, and made that the cause of death as well. Not without reason, because, bound in this way and unable to move, they were given, in truth, as [ιλάσγίας] to be the prey of dogs and birds, as the poet says: [κύνεσσιν Οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι], "to dogs and to all birds."

units.la: O'ιαναῖοι τι πᾶσι. Atque id etiam vivi. Prudentius1: —— Crux illum tollat in auras, Viventesque oculos offerat alitibus.
units.tr: And this was done even to the living. Prudentius: "Let the cross lift him into the air, and offer his living eyes to the birds."

units.la: Horatius 2 aspexit: Non hominem occidi, non pasces in cruce corvos.
units.tr: Horace looked at it: "I have not killed a man; you will not feed the crows on a cross."

units.la: quia sicarii scilicet & homicidae dari solent in crucem. Item Iuvenalis: Vultur jumento, & canibus, crucibusque relictis Ad fœtus properat, partemque cadaveris affert.
units.tr: Since assassins and murderers are customarily given over to the cross. Likewise Juvenal: "The vulture, leaving the beast of burden, the dogs and the crosses, hastens to its young and brings them a piece of carrion."

units.la: Quin reperio in sententiâ judiciali quoque id aliquando expressum. Actis Martyrum: Claudius, Asterius, Neon, cruci affigantur, & corpora eorum avibus laceranda relinquantur. Itaque Apu-
units.tr: Indeed I find this also sometimes expressed in a judicial sentence. In the Acts of the Martyrs: "Claudius, Asterius and Neon are to be fastened to the cross, and their bodies left to be torn by the birds." So Apu-

units.la: 1 Περὶ στέφ. Hymn. xi. 2 Lib. I. epist. xvi.
units.tr: 1 On the Crowns [Περὶ στεφάνων], Hymn 11. 2 Book 1, letter 16.

units.la: Apuleius proprium hunc refert Patibuli cruciatum, cum canes & vultures intima protrahunt viscera. Addit autem & Canes: & discas licet cruces non semper fuisse peraltas. Quomodo enim, si canes attingerent atque etiam lupi? Nam & hos Catullus addit in Epigrammatio, quod mihi quidem non nisi circumlocutio videtur cruciariæ hujus mortis.
units.tr: Apuleius reports this as the particular torment of the gibbet, when dogs and vultures drag out the entrails. But he also adds dogs; and you may learn that the crosses were not always so high. For how could dogs, or even wolves, reach them? Catullus adds these as well, in an epigram, which seems to me nothing but a roundabout description of this kind of death by crucifixion: "If by the judgment of the people of Comum your grey window, defiled by impure habits, should perish,

units.la: Si Comini arbitrio populi, tua cana fenestus Spurcata impuris moribus, intereat:
units.tr: "I certainly do not doubt that first your tongue, the enemy of good men, will be cut out and given to the greedy vulture,

units.la: Non equidem dubito, quin primum inimica bonorum Lingua exsecta avido sit data vulturio:
units.tr: "the crow will devour your eyes dug out with its black throat,
The raven devours the gouged-out eyes with its black throat,
the dogs the entrails, and the wolves the remaining limbs.
These

units.la: ¹ Lib. vi. De Afin. in fine. Istæ mortes. nisi quòd interdum lanceis etiam transverberatos legongo, an ad accelerandum fatum, an explorandum ? Illud fuit in Marcelliano & Marco : quibus ad stipitem ligatis in pedibus eorum affixi sunt clavi ? cumque transisset unus dies & nox, jussit ambos (Fabianus judex) lanceis per latera verberari. At istud in nostro Domino ; cui miles jam mortuo lancea latus aperuit, scilicet periculum an bonâ fide obiisset,
units.tr: ¹ Lib. vi. De Afin. in fine. These deaths, except that sometimes they were also pierced through with lances, we read, either to hasten the end or to make sure of it. The former happened in the case of Marcellianus and Marcus: "they were bound to a stake, and nails were driven through their feet; and when one day and a night had passed, the judge Fabianus ordered both to be pierced through the sides with lances." But in the case of our Lord it was otherwise, for when he was already dead, a soldier opened his side with a lance, namely to test whether he had really died.
CAP. XIV.

units.la: Crurifragium à Cruce remotum. Quid fuerit, in quos receptum, & quomodo?
units.tr: Breaking of the legs, which was far from the Cross. What it was, among whom it was practised, and how?

units.la: NOn autem & crura iis fracta, inquies, atque ita interempti ? Vulgò invaluit hæc opinio, sed vulgò. Qui penetrant & exa-fracta.
units.tr: But, you will say, were their legs broken too, and so they were killed? This view has become common, but it is only a common view. Those who look more closely and examine the evidence fractured.

units.la: 1 Martyr. XVIII. Iunii. & examinant, vident disparata hæc supplicia & seorsim fuisse. Induxit vulgum, quòd in sacrâ historiâ latronibus duobus crura fracta leguntur. Atque sciant pro moribus Iudæorum id fuisse: atque illic fortasse tantùm. Lactantius monuit: Suffixus itaque Christus cùm spiritum depositset, necessarium carnifices non putaverunt ossa ejus suffringere, sicut eorum mos ferebat. Ait cautè eorum mos: nempe Iudæorum. Et cur hoc Iudæi? ne fraus legi fieret, quæ jusserat ad Solem occasum suspendiosos deponi. At deponi nisi mortui non debebant: diutiùs autem plerique vivebant: ergo hac aut aliâ viâ mors festinanda. Aliâ etiam dicò viâ: nec crediderim fuisse hanc solam. Lex quam tango, est in Deuteronomio, & vertit sic doctor Afer : Si autem fuerit in aliquo de-
units.tr: 1 Martyr. XVIII. Iunii. See that these punishments were different and carried out separately. What led the common people astray is that in sacred history the legs of the two robbers are said to have been broken. Let them know that this was done according to the customs of the Jews, and perhaps only there. Lactantius warned: So when Christ had been hanged and had given up his spirit, the executioners did not think it necessary to break his bones, as their custom required. He says cautiously "their custom," meaning the Jews'. And why did the Jews do this? So that the law would not be evaded, the law which had ordered hanged men to be taken down at sunset. But they were not to be taken down unless they were dead, and many lived for a long time. So death had to be hastened by this way or another. I say "another way" too, and I would not believe this was the only one. The law I am touching on is in Deuteronomy, and the teacher Aquila renders it thus: But if there is in someone a sin

units.la: ¹ Lib. IV. c. XXVI. ² Tertull. Adverf. Iud. cap. x. delicto, ita ut judicium mortis sit, & morietur, & suspendetis eum in ligno, sed & sepultura sepelietis eum ipsa die. Ergo crurifragium proprie nihil ad Crucem : tamen quia se ingerit, & vile, atque item sævum est juxta crucem, breviter de eo dicam. Vox ipsa proba & vetus. Glossæ priscæ : Crurifragium, σκελοκοπία atque alibi Crurifrangium recte etiam scribunt. Nam Tago & Tango, & Frago & Frango, dixerunt : sed prior scilicet scriptio magis pro archaismo. Divisit elegantiæ gratia Apuleius 1 : Uxor diras in eum devotiones deprecata, & crurum ejus fragium abominata, ubi adominata pro vero magis & pro sensu. Ipsa res antiqua, & jam Plauti 2, & ante ævo, passim Crurifragium minati servis. In ejus Asinaria :-
units.tr: ¹ Lib. IV. c. XXVI. ² Tertull. Adverf. Iud. cap. x. so that the sentence is of death, and he dies, and you hang him on a tree, yet on the same day you shall bury him in a grave. So breaking the legs has nothing to do with the Cross as such. Still, since it forces itself upon us, and is both base and cruel in the neighbourhood of the cross, I will say briefly something about it. The word itself is sound and old. The old glosses have: Crurifragium, σκελοκοπία [skelokopia, leg-cutting], and elsewhere they also rightly write Crurifrangium. For they said Tago and Tango, and Frago and Frango, but the former spelling is more an archaism. Apuleius, for the sake of elegance, distinguished them: His wife, begging the gods to curse him with dreadful curses, and abhorring the breaking of his legs, where adominata is more correct and suits the sense. The practice itself is ancient: already in Plautus, and even earlier, slaves were often threatened with breaking of the legs. In his Asinaria:

units.la: ¹ Lib. ix. de Asin. ² Asinar. Crura hercle offringentur, Age impudice, nisi istum percies.
units.tr: ¹ Lib. ix. de Asin. ² Asinar. By Hercules, their legs will be broken! Come on, shameless one, unless you beat him.

units.la: Et credam, ut crucem ipsam, peculiare fuisse servis. Seneca: Magnam rem sine dubio fecerimus, si servulum infelicem in ergastulum miserimus. Quid properamus verberare statim, crura protinus frangere? Suetonius Augusto: Thallo a manu, quod pro epistola prodita denarios quinquenos accepisset, crura effregit. Idem in Tiberio: Utrique mox (ministro cuipiam, & tibicini) quod mutuo flagitium exprobrassent, crura fregisse. Ergo in servis: sed ita, ut liberi non immunes, sive in crimine, sive potius per saevitiam vindicantis. Ita M. Mario Gratidiano Cornelius Sulla perfringi crura, erui oculos, amputari manus jussit. Et Spen-
units.tr: And I believe, like the cross itself, it was peculiar to slaves. Seneca: We would certainly be making a great fuss if we sent an unhappy little slave to the workhouse. Why do we hurry to beat him at once and break his legs straight away? Suetonius, on Augustus: Because Thallus, from his office of secretary, had taken five denarii for betraying a letter, he broke his legs. The same author, on Tiberius: Soon afterwards both of them, a certain attendant and a flute-player, had their legs broken because they had reproached each other with a disgrace. So it was used on slaves, but not in such a way that free men were exempt, whether for a crime or rather out of the cruelty of the avenger. Thus Cornelius Sulla ordered that the legs of Marius Gratidianus be broken, his eyes gouged out, and his hands cut off. And the

units.la: diani rebelles in Africa, cùm Poenorum optimates cepissent, κολοβώσαντες, ὑφ' αὐτῶν ἱππεῖς τὰ σκέλη, ἔτι ζῶντας ἐμβιψαν εἰς τινα τάφον: admutilantes, & crura conterentes, adhuc vivos projecerunt in foveam aliquam. Et in Martyres nostros plurifariam sic saevitum. Eusebius de his quae in Arabia aut Cappadocia: Τὰς Μαρτύρων τοτὲ πέλυξιν ἀπαγχθέντων, τοτὲ δὲ τὰ σκέλη κατασφυγέντων: Martyribus aliàs securibus interfectis, aliàs Crurifragio punitis. Martyrologium memorat Hadrianum Nicomediae, cum aliis viginti tribus, omnes sub Diocletiano martyrium crurifragio consummasse. Idem de pluribus, atque innominatis: Commemoratio SS. Martyrum, qui in persecutione Maximini fractis cruribus necati sunt. Et saepius. Modus hujus supplicii ut incus cum malleo,
units.tr: rebel Spendius in Africa, when he had captured the leading men of the Carthaginians, mutilating them, and having the cavalry hack their legs, threw them still alive into some pit [kolobosantes, hyph' auton hippeis ta skelē, eti zōntas embiphan eis tina taphon]. They maimed them and crushed their legs, and threw them alive into a pit. And our martyrs were treated cruelly in this way in many places. Eusebius, speaking of those in Arabia or Cappadocia: Of the martyrs, some were at one time beheaded with axes, at another time had their legs cut through [Tas Martyrōn totè pelyxin apangchthentōn, totè de ta skelē kataphygentōn]. Some martyrs were killed with axes, others were punished by breaking of the legs. The Martyrology records that Hadrian at Nicomedia, together with twenty-three others, all completed their martyrdom under Diocletian by breaking of the legs. The same work says of several more, and of unnamed ones: Commemoration of the holy martyrs who were put to death with their legs broken in the persecution of Maximinus. And often. The manner of this punishment was that an anvil with a hammer,

units.la: 1 Polyb 1. 2 Lib. VIII. cap. XII. 3 IV. Martii. 4 xxxiii. Maii. malleo, vel veâte ferreo inferretur, ac tibias incudi imponerent, validis ictibus sic frangendas. Colliges ex Actis Martyrum priscis, quæ Surius vulgavit. Sublatum hoc supplicium à Constantino Victor asseverat, de quo
units.tr: 1 Polyb 1. 2 Lib. VIII. cap. XII. 3 IV. Martii. 4 xxxiii. Maii. or an iron mallet, was applied, and they set the shins on the anvil, to be broken by heavy blows. You will gather this from the old Acts of the Martyrs, which Surius published. Victor asserts that this punishment was abolished by Constantine, concerning which
CAP. XV.

units.la: Corrumpi in cruce passi sunt, & ne- fas sepelire.
units.tr: They were left to rot on the cross, and it was unlawful to bury them.

units.la: Corruptio jam post Mortem. Quam sic intelligo, quòd nec mortuos deponerent, sed tabo illic passi sunt diffluere, & à Sole ac pluviâ corrumpi. Valerius non impressè hoc narrat de Polycrate, qui ab Oroete cruci affixus: E quâ, inquit, putres ejus artus, & tabido cruore manantia membra, atque illam lævam, cui Neptunus annulum manu piscatoris
units.tr: Corruption already after death. I understand this to mean that they did not take the dead down, but let them dissolve there, rotting away and being decayed by sun and rain. Valerius does not explicitly narrate this of Polycrates, who was fixed to the cross by Oroites: From which, he says, his rotting limbs, and the members dripping with putrid blood, and that left hand on which Neptune had restored the ring to the fisherman's hand, now withered with decay, Samos looked upon with wide eyes.

units.la: 1 Tom. V. die VIII. Sept. 2 Lib. VI. cap. IX. ris restituerat, situ marcidam, Samos latis oculis aspexit. De quo ipso Afer noster, ut solet, succincte: Polycrati Samio filia Crucem prospicit de Solis unguine & lavacro Jovis. Tangit historiam, & somnium quod in Herodoto 1, & tu abeo pete. Sed hæc mens somnii, sublimem in cruce madidandum à Jove cùm plueret, à Sole ungendum cùm is calidus ē nudo corpore saniem eliceret adipemque. Hanc in cruce putrefactionem intellexit Theodorus Cyrenæus, cùm Tyranno minanti eam respondit: Suâ nihil interesse, humi, an sublimi putresceret 3. Neque aliam Artemidorus 4, cùm malum divitibus ominatur à somniatâ cruce: Τὰς σάρκας ... οἱ ἐπὶ σταυροῦ ... Carnes enim amittunt qui in cruce sixi. Ita inquam, amittunt: sive tempore 1 Tertull. de Anim. 2 Lib. iii. 3 Apud Cic. & Valer. 4 Lib. ii. cap. lviii. pore & defluxu : sive & laniena volucrum ferarumque, de quâ dixi.
units.tr: 1 Tom. V. die VIII. Sept. 2 Lib. VI. cap. IX. ...restored it, withered with decay, and Samos looked upon it with wide eyes. Our African says of this same Polycrates, as is his way, in brief: Polycrates' daughter of Samos looks out upon the cross, from the Sun's ointment and Jupiter's bath. He touches on the story, and you may seek the dream itself in Herodotus. But the meaning of the dream is this: that she, hung aloft on the cross, was to be drenched by Jupiter when it rained, and anointed by the Sun when he, being hot, drew out the ichor and fat from her naked body. Theodorus of Cyrene understood this putrefaction on the cross, when he answered the threatening tyrant that it made no difference to him whether he rotted on the ground or aloft. Artemidorus understands it no otherwise, when he foretells harm for the rich from a dreamed cross: τὰς σάρκας ... "for those who are fixed upon a cross lose their flesh" [τὰς σάρκας ... οἱ ἐπὶ σταυροῦ ...] Carnes enim amittunt qui in cruce sixi. Yes, I say, they lose it: either through time and wasting away, or also through the mangling of birds and beasts, of which I have spoken. 1 Tertull. de Anim. 2 Lib. iii. 3 Apud Cic. & Valer. 4 Lib. ii. cap. lviii.

units.la: CAP. XVI. Custodia & miles ad Crucem, ne quis detraheret.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. A guard and a soldier at the Cross, so that no one would take the body down.

units.la: ITaque hoc fine asservati in Cruce, & deponi rarum omnino fuit. Nisi quod Philo1 tamen notat, receptum moribus fuisse in Natali Imperatoris, aut simili die festo quosdam e crucibus deponi, & permitti ad sepulturam : at Flaccum contrà, novos etiam tum iis affixisse.
units.tr: So, once they were fastened to the Cross, the bodies were almost never taken down. Philo does note, however, that it was the custom, on the Emperor's birthday or some similar festival day, for some to be taken down from the crosses and allowed burial; but Flaccus, on the contrary, even then nailed up new ones.

units.la: Ne quis autem deponeret, miles & custodia asedit. Petronius2: Miles cruces asservabat, nequis corpora ad sepulturam detraheret. Plutarchus in Cleomene : o'λί- γαις δὲ ὑπὸ ὑσέρων ἡμέρας οἱ τὸ σῶμα τῶ Κλεομένης ἀνεσταυρωμένου φυλάττοντες, εἶδον ἐμφανισθὲν δράκοντα τῆ κεφαλῆ ἐπεπλησ-
units.tr: To prevent anyone from taking them down, a soldier and a guard were posted. Petronius: The soldier guarded the crosses, so that no one would take the bodies down for burial. Plutarch, in the Life of Cleomenes: A few days later, those who were guarding the body of Cleomenes, which was hung on the cross, saw a dragon appear, wrapped around its head, and wiping its face, so that no bird of prey might settle on it.
1 Against Flaccus. 2 In the Satires.

units.la: {Greek text}, ἡ ἀπουξύσωντα τὸ πρό- σωπον, ὥστε μηδὲν ὀφιν ἐφιπλα πάρε- φαλον : Paucis post diebus, ii qui Cleomenis cruci affixum corpus custodiebant, viderunt magnum serpentem capiti ejus circumplexum, & faciem velantem tegentemque, ne qua carnivora avis attingeret. Ubi utrumque habes, & custodiri solitos mortuos ; & aves faciem in primis involasse. Possis ad hanc custodiam illud Euangelistæ ¹ re- ferre : Ἐ'χετε φυλακὴν, ἀπάγετε : Habetis custodiam, abite. Quæ Pilati vox fuit ad Judæos petentes asservari monumentum. Videtur autem intelligere custodiam, quæ paullò ante ad crucem. nisi quis malit, Habete custodiam ; quasi ab imperante, & indignanter dante. Vox enim Græca in utrumvis valet.
units.tr: "A few days later," those who were guarding the body of Cleomenes fastened to the cross saw a great serpent coiled around its head, and it veiled and covered its face, so that no flesh-eating bird might touch it. Here you have both points: that the dead were customarily guarded, and that birds in particular swooped down on the face. To this guard you may also refer that saying of the Evangelist: [Ἔχετε φυλακήν, ἀπάγετε]: You have a guard; go away. These were Pilate's words to the Jews who asked that the tomb be guarded. He seems to mean the guard that had been set shortly before at the cross. Unless someone prefers to read Habete custodiam, as though spoken by a commander, and given in anger. For the Greek word can carry either sense.
Matth. 27.

units.la: IVSTI LIPSII DE CRVCE LIBER III.
units.tr: JUSTUS LIPSIUS, ON THE CROSS, BOOK III.
CHAPTER I.

units.la: Transitiò ad Rarum figendi Mo- dum. Furca divisa, & hîc de Ignominiosâ dictum.
units.tr: Transition to the Rare Mode of Fixing. The Divided Fork; and here the Ignominious Kind Is Discussed.

units.la: ABunde, quæ ad Vulgarem crucifigendi modum, diximus : Rarus superest, quem ipsum pari curâ imus expunctum. Eum suprà descripsimus (& vox præfert) sepositum, & minùs in assiduo usu. Sepositum ævo, Inusitatum vel Schemate vel Fine. De his tribus ordine & partitè dicam (juvat in his talibus) & in lucem fortasse protraham, quæ usque adhuc parum claro oculo conspecta. Ævo seposita Furca est: olim quidem in creberrimo usu, sed quæ paulatim desiit atque abolevit. Mentio crebra non in historiis solùm, sed Comœdiis prisicis : mentio tamen magis, quàm explicatio. ego hîc faciam, & pro copiâ ingenii dabo in splendorem. Ut possim, duplicem illam facio, Veterem & Novam. Priorem, quæ priscis Romanis (non enim apud alias gentes legi) usitata: atque hanc iterùm duplicem. Ignominiosam & Pœnalem. Illa est, quâ collo impositâ servi circumduci solent ob culpam aliquam, ostentui & ad irrisum. Isidorus: Furcifer dicebatur olim, qui ob leve delictum cogebatur à dominis, ignominiæ magis quàm supplicii causâ, furcam circa urbem ferre, prædicans peccatum suum, & monens ceteros ne quid simile peccarent. Plutarchus in Coriolano, Humane habitos servos à prisciis dominis notat, & addit : Ἡ δὲ μισ- γάλη
units.tr: We have said enough about the common manner of crucifixion. The rare one remains, and we shall go through it with equal care. Above, as its very name indicates, I described it as set aside, and less in constant use. It is set aside by age, unusual either in its form or in its end. I shall treat these three in order and in parts, since such matters please me, and perhaps bring into the light what has so far been viewed with too dim an eye. The Furca is set aside by age. Once it was in very frequent use, but it gradually fell into disuse and disappeared. It is often mentioned, not only in histories but in early comedies; yet the mention is more frequent than any explanation. I shall supply one here, and give it what brightness my ability allows. So that I may do so, I divide it into two kinds, Old and New. The former, which was in use among the early Romans (for I have not read of it among other peoples), is again twofold: Ignominious and Penal. The former is that in which a slave, with a fork put on his neck, is customarily led about for some fault, for display and for ridicule. Isidore: The furcifer was formerly the name given to one who, for a slight offence, was compelled by his masters to carry a fork about the city, for the sake of disgrace rather than punishment, proclaiming his sin and warning others not to commit the like. Plutarch, in the Life of Coriolanus, notes that slaves were treated humanely by their early masters, and adds: The great punishment of a slave who had done wrong was to be made to take the axle of a cart, or the pole, and go round the neighbourhood carrying it. One who had suffered this, and been seen so, no longer had credit, and was called a furcifer. [Ἡ δὲ μεγάλη κόλασις οἰκέτου πλημμελήσαντος ἦν ἐξ ὅλης ἁμάξης ἢ τὸν ῥῦμον ὑπερθέντα ἀράμενον διεξελθεῖν παρὰ τὴν γειτνίαν.]
1 Book 10, Origen.

units.la: γάλη κόλασις οἰκίτυ πλημμελήσαντ(ος) ἐξ ὕλου ἀμάξης ὢ τὸν ῥύμον ὑπιςέιδεςιν ἀςάμβω, διεξέλθοι παςὰ τῆς γῆτνίας-σιν. ὁ γὰς τέτο παθὼν ἢ ὀφθεὶς, ἐκίτι πίςιν ἄχιν, ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ Φυςκίφιςς:
units.tr: The greater punishment for a household slave who has done wrong is to take up the whole wooden beam of a wagon, the one that supports the pole, and carry it around the neighbourhood. The one who suffered this, or was seen so, no longer had credit and was called Furcifer. [ἡ δὲ μεγάλη κόλασις οἰκέτου πλημμελήσαντος ἐξ ὅλου ξύλου ἁμάξης ὃ τὸν ῥῦμον ὑποστηρίζει ἀράμενον διεξελθεῖν παρὰ τὴν γειτνίαν· ὁ γὰρ τοῦτο παθὼν ἢ ὀφθεὶς οὐκέτι πίστιν ἄγων ἐκαλεῖτο δὲ Φουρκίφερος]

units.la: Erat autem magna castigatio serv delinquentis, si lignum currus, quo temonem sustentant, tollens & ferens exiret circa viciniam. Id enim passus, & sic conspectus, non ultrà fidem habebat, & vocabatur Furcifer. Talia idem in Quæstionibus Romanis. Et Glossæ veteres: Furcifer, σαμξοκίμις, διχαυοφόρος. οἱ πλείοντις ἀντὶ τιμωρίας δίκαυον ἐν τοῖς τραχήλοις ἔχοντες ἀξιεκόμιζον, διὰ τ πολέως πειγόμενοι: qui patibulum fert, qui furcam. Qui peccaverant, pro pœnâ furcam in collo habentes circumbant, per urbem undique ducti. Atque hæc illa prima est, ab ipsâ re & fine Ignominiosa à me dicta: quæ origo aut exemplar tamen Pœnalis.
units.tr: There was a great punishment for a slave who had offended, if he took up and carried the wooden beam of a wagon, which holds up the pole, and went out round the neighbourhood. For one who had suffered this and was so seen no longer kept his credit, and he was called Furcifer. The same author says such things in his Roman Questions. And the old glosses: Furcifer: [σκαμβοκοπίς], [διχαυοφόρος]: one who carries a gallows-beam, one who carries a fork. Those who had sinned, as punishment, carried a fork on their necks and were led around, driven through the city on every side. And this is that first kind, which I have called "ignominious" from the thing itself and its purpose; yet it is the origin or model of the "penal" kind.
CHAPTER II.

units.la: De Furcâ Pœnali, & cæsos sub eâ ad mortem.
units.tr: On the Penal Fork, and those beaten to death under it.

units.la: EA est, quâ item collo impositâ circumductì, sed cum verberibus & pœnæ caussâ. Atque adeò mors, plerumque huic consequa: sive sub ipsâ Furcâ ad neccm cæsis, sive cum eâ in crucem latis. Seorsim utrumque explicabo, & firmabo. Sub eâ ad mortem cæsi: ex Suetonio , qui pœnam more majorum interpretatur, nudi hominis cervicem inseri furcæ, corpus virgis ad necem cædi. Atque idem etiam Victor: Senatus sententiâ constitutum, ut, more minorum, collo in furcam conjecto, virgis ad necem caderetur. Ac reperio exempla etiam in historiâ, etsi haud crebra. Livius * incestum cum Vestale F sic
units.tr: It is that to which, the neck being placed in it in the same way, men are led about, but with blows and for the sake of punishment. Death for the most part follows this, either by being beaten to death under the fork itself or by being carried with it to the cross. I shall explain and confirm each separately. For those beaten to death under it, there is Suetonius, who explains the punishment after the custom of the ancestors: the neck of a naked man is put into the fork, and the body is beaten to death with rods. And the same is found in Victor: By decree of the Senate it was established that, after the manner of the ancestors, with the neck thrown into the fork, he should be beaten with rods to death. I also find examples in history, though not very frequent. Livy shows that an incest with the Vestal F. was punished in this way:

units.la: 1 Neron. cap. xlix. 2 In Nerone. sic punitum ostendit1: L. Cantilius scriba Pontificum, quos nunc minores Pontifices appellant, qui cum Floronia stuprum fecerat, à Pontifice Max. eousque virgis in Comitio cæsus, ut inter verbera exspiraret. Dionysius2 in culpâ simili, & de iis qui Urbiniam stuprarant: Τῶν δὲ διαπεξαμένων τὴν ἀνοσίαν φθορὰν, ἐμὲν ἕτερος ἑαυτὸν διεχείρισαλο, τ δὲ ἕτερον οἱ τ ἱερῶν Ἐπίσκοποι συλλαβόντες, ἐν ἀγορᾷ μάστιξιν ἀνισάμενοι, καθάπερ ἀνδραπόδον, ἀπέκτειναν: Ex iis autem qui illicitam corruptionem patraverant, alter seipsum interemit, alterum ii qui sacris præerant (ii sunt Pontifices) comprehendentes, in flagris secantes, tamquam mancipium, interemerunt. Nam etsi neuter furcæ hic mentionem faciat, tamen cum verberibus ad necem datos denarrent, probabile id ita ritu prisco factum: hoc magis, quòd Dionysius quasi 1 Lib. xxii. 2 Lib. ix. Antiq. quasi indicans addidit, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρ-χεδέλπο̈ν, servilem in modum. Quod autem liberi etiam sub furcâ interdum cæsi, exemplum in Epitomâ Livii 1 clarum, de C. Matieno: qui accusatus apud Tribunos quòd exercitum in Hispaniâ deseruisset, damnatusque, sub furcâ diu virgis cæsus, & sestertio nummo venüit. Nam etsi ille non ad veram mortem cæsus, tamen ad civilem, & libertatem civitatemque pariter amisit. Atque ideò dixi plerumque mortem consequam: cùm & in Plauto 2 legam:
units.tr: 1 Nero, chap. 49. 2 In Nero. Lucius Cantilius, a clerk of the Pontiffs, whom they now call the lesser Pontiffs, who had committed fornication with Floronia, was beaten with rods in the Comitium by the Pontifex Maximus, to the point that he died amid the blows. Dionysius, describing a similar offence and those who had defiled Urbinia, says: Of those who had committed the unholy defilement, one killed himself; the other was seized by those who presided over the sacred rites (these are the Pontiffs), and, flogged in the marketplace, was killed like a slave. [Τῶν δὲ διαπεξαμένων τὴν ἀνοσίαν φθορὰν, ἐμὲν ἕτερος ἑαυτὸν διεχείρισαλο, τ δὲ ἕτερον οἱ τ ἱερῶν Ἐπίσκοποι συλλαβόντες, ἐν ἀγορᾷ μάστιξιν ἀνισάμενοι, καθάπερ ἀνδραπόδον, ἀπέκτειναν.] For although neither of them mentions the fork here, yet since they relate that these men were given over to death with blows, it is probable that this was done according to the ancient rite. This is all the more likely because Dionysius, as if pointing it out, added and from the beginning, in the servile manner. [καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχεδέλπον, servilem in modum.] 1 Book 22. 2 Book 9 of the Antiquities. That free men too were sometimes beaten under the fork is shown clearly by an example in the Epitome of Livy, concerning Gaius Matienus, who was accused before the tribunes of deserting the army in Spain, was condemned, was beaten with rods under the fork for a long time, and was sold for a sestertius. For although he was not beaten to true death, yet he was beaten to civil death, and he lost his liberty and citizenship alike. And so I said that death for the most part follows, since I also read in Plautus:

units.la: Et ob eam rem in carcerem te desse compastum scio, Et postquam es emissus, cæsum virgis sub furcâ scio.
units.tr: And for that reason I know you were put in prison in chains, and after you were let out, I know you were beaten with rods under the fork.

units.la: Quæ objiciutur seni vivo etiam & videnti.
units.tr: These words are addressed to an old man who is still alive and also sees.
1 Book 55. 2 Menaechmi.
CHAPTER III.

units.la: Ligatos ad Furcam in Crucem solere tolli, Furcam & patibulum videri eadem, aut haud longè dissita.
units.tr: That those bound to the fork are usually raised onto the cross, and that the fork and the patibulum are seen as the same, or not far apart.

units.la: SEd cum Furcâ in crucem latos etiam dixi : quod rei nostræ facit, atque id tale fuit. Ligati ad Furcam, & sub eâ cæsi, per viam ducebantur ; fixi deinde ad eam, tollebantur in crucem. Firmamus veterum scriptis. Arnobius : Servum pessime meritum per Circi aream mediam traduxisse cæsum virgis, & ex more, multasse post patibuli poenam. Ita legimus, non poenam. Et quod ait, ex more, huic rei seligimus : quasi receptum videlicet & tralaticium post cæsionem hanc, suspendi. Nam etsi Arnobius non expressit sub Furcâ cæsum:
units.tr: But I have also said that those carried to the cross were carried with a fork, and that this suits our point and was indeed the practice. Those bound to a fork, and beaten under it, were led through the street; then they were fixed to it and raised onto the cross. Let the writings of the ancients confirm this. Arnobius: That a slave who had deserved very badly was led across the middle of the Circus, beaten with rods, and, as was the custom, punished after the penalty of the patibulum. So we read it, not poenam. And when he says as was the custom, we choose this case for it: as if, clearly, being hanged after this beating was an established and traditional practice. For although Arnobius does not state that he was beaten under the fork,

units.la: ¹ Lib. VII. adverf. Gent. cæsum: tamen ita fuit, & in ipsâ hac narratiunculâ alii omnes consensu produnt. Livius : Servum quidam paterfamilias nondum commissso spectaculo, sub Furcâ cæsum, medio egerat Circo. Cicero : Servus per Circum, cum virgis caderetur, Furcam ferens ductus est. Valerius : Cùm servum suum verberibus multatum sub Furcâ, ad supplicium egisset. Denique Lactantius, qui & Patrisfamiliæ nomen expressit: Antonius Maximus (potius Autronius, ex Macrobio) diverberatum servum sub Furcâ, medio Circo ad supplicium egerat. Ergo sub Furcâ ad supplicium acti: sed numquid in eâ appensi? Ita. quia hæc Furca non aliud quàm Patibulum fuit. Certa auctoritas Macrobii : qui de illo ipso facto.
units.tr: ¹ Lib. VII. adv. Gent. he nevertheless was, and all the others agree in this very little story. Livy: A certain master, before the show had begun, had led his slave, beaten under the fork, through the middle of the Circus. Cicero: A slave was led through the Circus, carrying a fork, while he was being beaten with rods. Valerius: When he had taken his slave, punished with blows, under the fork, to execution. Finally Lactantius, who also names the master: Antonius Maximus (or rather Autronius, according to Macrobius) had led his slave, flogged to pieces, under the fork, through the middle of the Circus, to execution. So they were led under the fork to execution; but were they not also hung on it? Yes, because this fork was nothing other than the patibulum. Macrobius is a reliable authority, and he speaks of that very deed.

units.la: 1 Lib. II. 2 De Divinat. I. 3 Lib. I. cap. VII. 4 Lib. II. cap. VIII. 5 Lib. I. Saturn. cap. X. Autronius, inquit, Maximus quidam servum suum verberatum, patibuloque constrictum, per Circum egit. Quid hoc est, patibulo constrictum, nisi quod alii omnes Furcam dixerunt, & Livius de Horatio, sub Furca vinctum? Nam ita res fuit. Alligari brachia manusque ad hanc furcam solent: atque ita circumduci, mox in ea attolli. In Plauto legis, Dispessis manibus patibulum habere. item: ire patibulatum per vias. Et quod Nonius ex eo citat: Patibulum ferre per urbem, deinde affigi cruci. Nota verba & seriem: Ferre, deinde Affigi. Quae ipsa in Licinii historici fragmento apud eumdem Nonium: Ad patibulos (ita mutato genere, pro patibula) deligantur, & circumferuntur, cruci defiguntur. Clare omnia. Habes, ut in Macrobio, ligari constringique ad
units.tr: 1 Lib. II. 2 De Divinat. I. 3 Lib. I. cap. VII. 4 Lib. II. cap. VIII. 5 Lib. I. Saturn. cap. X. Autronius, he says, Maximus, a certain man, led his slave, beaten and bound to a patibulum, through the Circus. What is this, bound to a patibulum, except that all the others said fork, and Livy said of Horatius bound under the fork? For this is how it was. The arms and hands were usually tied to this fork, and in that state the man was led around, and soon afterwards raised up on it. In Plautus you read to carry the patibulum with outstretched hands; likewise to go through the streets patibulated. And what Nonius cites from him: to carry the patibulum through the city, then to be fixed to the cross. Note the words and the sequence: to carry, then to be fixed. The same appears in the fragment of the historian Licinius, in the same Nonius: They are bound to the patibula (the gender changed, for patibula) and are carried around, and are fixed to the cross. Everything is clear. You have, as in Macrobius, being bound and tied to the patibulum;
¹ Mostell.

units.la: ad patibulum ; habes , circumferre ; habes defigi. Circumferre inquam. nam quod vulgò est circumferuntur, vereor ut rectum fit. quia non profecto circumlati , sed ipsi pedibus suis ibant : nisi tamen capias quasi circumductos. Sed ego malim , circumferunt reponi. ut sit ligatos ad patibula, ea ipsa circumtulisse. Ita Plautus 1 : Tu quidem hodie canem & furcam feras. Nam ibi Furcam, quod patibulum alias, dixit. sicut & hic : Cum furcâ inurbem , tamquam Carbonarium. Atqui docendum etiam est, inquies , in eâ appensos : Nónne res clamat ? Si enim Furca idem quod patibulum : quid ambigas ? Constat certè in patibulo suspensos. Sed firmo & testibus. Festus : Furcilla sive Furcilla, quibus homines suspendebant. Cedò de quibus aliis hoc acci{1} Cafina. pies? Plinius: Supplicia annua canes pendunt, inter ædem Iuventutis & Summani, furcâ sambucea, arbore fixi. Vix est ut aliter intelligas, quàm in furcâ ad arborem fixos. At clarissimè jam Firmicus: Severâ animadvertentis sententiâ patibulo suffixus, in crucem crudeliter erigetur. En, primò patibulo suffigitur, deinde tollitur in crucem. Atque hinc illa phrasis, Patibulo crucis affigi: quia patibulum scilicet, hoc sensu, pars crucis. Distinguit & Tacitus: Patibula, ignes, cruces. & quod patens hæc transversaque pars sic dicta, Seneca indicat: Alii brachia patibulo explicuerunt. sicut inferior defixusque stipes, Crux proprie dictus.
units.tr: you have being carried around; you have being fixed. I say being carried around, for what is commonly printed as circumferuntur I fear is not right, since they were certainly not carried around, but walked on their own feet, unless you take it as "led around". But I would prefer that circumferunt be restored, so that the sense is that they carried those same patibula around. So Plautus: You, today, will carry the dog and the fork. For there he called the patibulum a fork, which elsewhere is called patibulum; so too here: with a fork through the city, like a charcoal-seller. But you may object that one must also show that they were hung on it. Does the thing not cry out for itself? For if the fork is the same as the patibulum, why do you hesitate? It is certain that they were hung on the patibulum. But I confirm this with witnesses too. Festus: Furcilla, or furcilla, the things on which men were hanged. Tell me, of what others do you take this? Pliny: Every year dogs hang as punishment, between the temple of Youth and of Summanus, on a fork of elder, fixed to a tree. It is hardly possible to understand it otherwise than as men fixed to a tree on a fork. But Firmicus is already quite clear: Fixed to the patibulum by the sentence of a severe punisher, he will be cruelly raised onto the cross. See, first he is fastened to the patibulum, then he is raised onto the cross. And hence that phrase, to be fastened to the patibulum of the cross, since the patibulum, in this sense, is part of the cross. Tacitus also distinguishes: patibula, fires, crosses; and that this transverse part, spreading out, is so called, Seneca shows: Others stretched their arms out on the patibulum. Just as the lower upright stake, fixed in the ground, is properly called the cross.

CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Quæ forma Furcæ fuerit, obscurè traditum in veterum scriptis.
units.tr: What shape the fork had is obscurely handed down in the writings of the ancients.

units.la: SEd qualis hæc suspensio, & qua vera germanaque facie ipsa Furca; ut ingenuè dicam, hæreo, & velut inter Solem & Orcum erro. Video, non video; probo, improbo; & planè quod Græci dicunt, τὴν γράμμα τηλαυγίαν. Suidas Furcam sic describit : Φῦρξ πεζὸν Ῥωμαίοις ξύλον διπλοῦν: Furca Romanis est lignum duplex sive geminum. Plutarchus paullò magis videtur aperire : διπλᾶ ξύλον ἃ τοῖς ἁμάξαις ὑφίστανται: duplex lignum quod curribus subjicunt. Tamen hoc ipsum satis Ἀθηναῖος & ἀσφαλῶς. itaque distinctius alibi : ξύλον ἁμάξης ὃ τ' ῥυμὸν ὑπεχέ-ὄντι : lignum currus, quo temonem sustentant. Atque addit: ὁ δὲ Ἐὐριπίδης ὑπο-
units.tr: But what this suspension was, and what the true and genuine shape of the fork itself was, I will frankly confess I am stuck. I wander, as it were, between the sun and Orcus. I see, I do not see; I approve, I disapprove; and altogether it is what the Greeks call the far-shining clarity of letters [τὴν γραμμάτων τηλαυγίαν]. Suidas describes the fork thus: "For the Romans the fork is a double piece of wood" [Φῦρξ πεζὸν Ῥωμαίοις ξύλον διπλοῦν: Furca Romanis est lignum duplex sive geminum]. Plutarch seems to explain it a little more fully: "a double piece of wood that they set under the carts" [διπλᾶ ξύλον ἃ τοῖς ἁμάξαις ὑφίστανται: duplex lignum quod curribus subjiciunt]. Yet even this is said only in a general way, and not with full certainty. So elsewhere he is more precise: "a piece of wood of the wagon, which they hold under the pole" [ξύλον ἁμάξης ὃ τ' ῥυμὸν ὑπεχέ-ὄντι: lignum currus, quo temonem sustentant]. And he adds: "Euripides..."
