units.la: ὑποστᾶτην ἐ σύστγμα, τῷ Ῥωμαῖοι Φέρεγαν ὀνομάζεσι: quod enim Graeci Hypostaten & Sterigma (suffulcimentum & sustentaculum) id Romani appellant Furcam. Benè & clarè pro suis Græcis: nos anscitiores? In Hesychio hoc saltem reperio: σὺεγγ[ας (idem quod σύγγραφα) dici à quibusdam, τὸ διςγοῦν, ὅπερ ὑποδιδόασι τῷ ἐ ἁμάξης ζυγῷ: illud biceps aut furcatum, quod subjiciunt currus jugo. Juvat, an moratur? istud potiùs, quoniam Zυγὸν scribit sive jugum, quod Plutarchus Temonem & ζυγὸν. Vtri accedimus Plutarcho magis, nec video quid Jugo fulciendo subjeceris, quod dependet & fertur collo boum. Ergo, me quidem arbitro, Hesychius, in vicinis voculis, sic corrigatur. Atque ex istis rem factam habeamus, si nota veterum curruum membra. Opinamur tamen similia nostris suisse, & Dionysium etiam audiamus.
units.tr: ... "what the Greeks call a hypostasis and a sterigma (a support and a prop), that the Romans call a fork" [ὑποστάτην ... σύστγμα, τῷ Ῥωμαῖοι Φέρεγαν ὀνομάζεσι: quod enim Graeci Hypostaten & Sterigma (suffulcimentum & sustentaculum) id Romani appellant Furcam]. Well and clearly said for their own Greeks; are we more ignorant? In Hesychius I find this much at least: that some call the sygga (the same as syngrapha) "that which is two-pronged, or forked, which they put under the yoke of the wagon" [illud biceps aut furcatum, quod subjiciunt currus jugo]. Does it help, or does it delay? I would rather read it the other way, since he writes "yoke" [ζυγόν], which Plutarch calls the pole [temo] and the yoke [ζυγόν]. Which of the two readings do we follow more? Nor do I see what you would put under a yoke to support it, since it hangs down and is carried on the necks of the oxen. So, in my judgement, Hesychius should be corrected by the neighbouring words. From these we may have the matter settled, if we know the parts of ancient carts. I suppose, however, that they were similar to ours, and let us also hear Dionysius.

units.la: ¹ Lib. VII. Antiq. mus. In eo, ubi poenam describit servi illius Autronii Maximi (de quo plusçula supra) haec lego: A'νὴς Ρ'ωμαῖ@ ἐκ ἀφανῆς Διονυσίου πολλὰ ἰδίον ἐπὶ τιμωρίᾳ θανάτῳ παρέδωκε τοῖς ὁμοδούλοις ἄγειν, ἵνα δὴ περιφανὴς εἶ. ἡ τιμωρία τ ἀνθρώπῳ γίνῃ, δὲ ἀγοράς αὐτὸν μαστιγούμενον σκέλευσιν ἔλκειν, ἢ ἄ τις ἄλλ@ ἐν τ πόλεως τόπῳ ἐπιφανῆς. οἱ δὲ ἄγοντες τ Διονύσιον ἐπὶ τὴν τιμωρίαν, τὰς χεῖρας ἀποτείναντες ἀμφοτέρας, καὶ ξύλῳ ἀπορθ.
units.tr: 1 Book VII of the Roman Antiquities. In it, where he describes the punishment of that slave of Autronius Maximus (about whom more above), I read these words: "A certain Roman, of no obscure name, handed over his slave Dionysius to his fellow slaves to be led to death as punishment, so that the punishment might be conspicuous and public. They were to drag him whipped through the market place, or through any other conspicuous place in the city. Those who led Dionysius to the punishment stretched out both his hands and bound them to a piece of wood" [Ἀνὴρ Ῥωμαῖος ... ξύλῳ ἀπορθ.: the Greek is corrupt in the transcription].

units.la: Vir Romanus haud ignobilis, servum suum ad mortis supplicium tradens conservis alios ducendum, ut conspicua & illustris poena hominis ejus fieret, per forum verberibus affectum trahere ipsos jussit, & si quis alius in urbe locus celebris. Qui autem ducebant eum ad poenam, manus ejus ambas extendentes, & ad lignum alligantes, quod circa pectus & humeros
units.tr: A Roman man of no little standing, handing his slave over to his fellow slaves to be led to execution, ordered that, so that the punishment of that man should be conspicuous and notable, he be dragged through the forum, struck with whips, and also through any other famous place in the city. Those who led him to the punishment stretched out both his hands and tied them to a piece of wood which reached around his chest and shoulders down to the palms of his hands, and they followed, beating the naked man with whips.

units.la: Dionysii verba de Furio. meros ad manuum volam pertingeret, sequebantur flagris cædentes sic nudum. Jam Plautus 1 imagine etiam videtur voluisse expressam : ——— ego remittam ad te virum Cum furca in urbem, tanquam carbonarium.
units.tr: The words of Dionysius about Furius. Down to the palm of the hand, they followed, beating the naked man with whips. Plautus also seems to have wanted to express the same image: "I will send your man back to you into the city with a fork, like a charcoal-seller."
1 Casina.
CHAPTER V.

units.la: Ex iis tres sententiæ eruta, & singulæ explicatæ. Tertiam πιθανω-τάτλω videri.
units.tr: Three opinions are drawn from these and each is explained. The third seems the most plausible.

units.la: HÆc sunt quæ apud veteres quidem legerim rei huic illustrandæ. Nos ex iis sententias, an somnia nostra? proponemus: impetrabili tamen veniâ, sicubi in antiquitatis illis tenebris subsistemus, aut labemur. Sententias, dixi. nam tria sunt quæ ex descriptiunculis elicio jam dictis. Primùm, Furcam potuisse tuisse esse facie quâ nostrum hodie Patibulum : atque idipsum reliquias & exemplar esse à pœnâ priscâ. Ait Plutarchus, currus aut temoni subjectum fuisse. quid olim, nescio : tale aliquid in nostris curribus supra ipsum axem. Ait Dionysius, per humeros, per pectus iisse : hoc in isto, si collo imponas. Obstat tamen huic, quod diserté ajunt ζύλον διπλοῦν, διxḗν, διϑυμον. lignum duplex, biceps, geminum. Nam certè hoc triplex lignum est: etsi ista quoque forma Furca olim dicta. Sententia altera, Lignum fuisse geminum, quod à tergo per humeros, & ante per pectus, hominem medium includeret ; atque ita rectum ad expansas utrasque manus iret. Forma, quam Dionysius ingerere videtur & suadere. Quid tamen hîc simile Furcæ? quomodo in utroqᵱisto ligno homo suspensus? Nam anterius illud incommodaverit, imò ad guttur strangulárit. Sed nec in curribus quid simile, scio. Sententia tertia. Furcam, veram esse furcam: quam * hodieque dicimus, & quam Varro ᵗ indicat, ubi Vallum ἱτυμολογὴ: quòd singula ibi extrema bacilla furcillata figuram habeant litterae V. Pro hac sententiâ multa sunt. Primum quòd Furca διχέαρ, in bonis priscisque Glossis. Item Furcifer, διχεαφόρος. Atqui διχέαρος Hesychius describit τὰς ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς ἐπὶ δύο ἐκτάσεις, οἷον δύο τέλη ἔχούσας: eas quae ab uno initio & capite in duo desinunt, tamquam duos fines habentes. Est plane figura Varroniana, & litterae jam dictae. Quid, quòd in curribus hodie, quâ Temo cum axe coit, Furca est sustentando illi aut fulciendo? Quâ mente in Sidonio, de Baccho:
units.tr: These are the things I have read among the ancients that illustrate this matter. From them we will set out opinions, or are they our own dreams? We ask for the indulgence we can hope for, if we stumble or slip somewhere in the shadows of antiquity. Opinions, I said, for from the short descriptions just cited I draw three points. First, the fork could have had the shape of what we today call a patibulum (the cross-beam), and this same thing is a relic and copy of the ancient punishment. Plutarch says it was placed under the chariot or the pole. What it was in those days I do not know; something like it exists in our carts above the axle itself. Dionysius says it went through the shoulders and across the chest, as this one would if you put it on the neck. Yet this is opposed by the fact that they expressly call it ξύλον διπλοῦν, διχηρόν, δίθυμον, "a double wood, two-pronged, twin" [ξύλον διπλοῦν, διχηρόν, δίθυμον]. For this is certainly a three-part wood, although that form too was once called a fork. The second opinion: the wood was double, which would enclose the man in the middle, passing across the back over the shoulders and in front over the chest, and so would reach out to both outstretched hands. This is the form Dionysius seems to suggest and to favour. But what here is like a fork? How could a man be hanged on a wood of this kind? The front piece would have got in the way, or rather would have throttled him by the throat. Nor do I know of anything similar in the chariots. The third opinion: the fork was truly a fork, which we still call by that name today, and which Varro points to, where he gives the etymology of the word vallum: "because the single ends there, each forked stick, have the figure of the letter V." Many things support this opinion. First, that in good old glosses furca is διχέαρ. Likewise furcifer is διχεαφόρος. Hesychius describes διχέαρος as "those that from one beginning and head end in two extensions, like having two ends" [τὰς ἀπὸ μιᾶς ἀρχῆς ἐπὶ δύο ἐκτάσεις, οἷον δύο τέλη ἔχούσας]. This is plainly the Varronian figure and the letter already mentioned. And what of the fact that today in carts, where the pole joins the axle, there is a fork to support and prop it? In that sense Sidonius speaks of Bacchus:
With the vine
* IV. On the Cross, Book II

units.la: Vite capistratas cogebat ad esseda tigres, Intrabat duplicem quà temo racemiser arcum.
units.tr: With vine-shoots he would bridle the tigers and drive them to the war-chariots; where the vine-bearing pole entered the double arch.

units.la: Denique cum descriptione Dionysii mihi convenire videtur examussim. Da Furcam istam paulatim divaricantem; ab humeris per pectus, & inde manus veniat; est illud ipsum lignum quod descripsit. Jam Plauti Carbonarium, quò nisi huc referas? Ecce qui lignarios fasces aut carbonum faccellos hodieque ferunt, furcam jungunt. cujus caput cum exstantiâ aliquâ bacillorum à tergo est; longiores duo fines diversi per pectus descendunt, & manu utrâque ( quasi ad contranixum ) sustentantur. Atqui inquies, manus hîc non in alto expansæ. Fateor non in alto, expansæ tamen : & cùm funibus traherentur, ligatis ad extre-mas
units.tr: Finally, it seems to me to agree exactly with the description of Dionysius. Imagine that fork gradually spreading apart: from the shoulders, through the chest, and then the hands come. That is the very wood he described. Now, Plautus's carbonarius (the charcoal-bearer): how else would you refer it here? Look at those who even today carry bundles of wood or little bundles of charcoal: they join a fork. Its top, with some projection of sticks at the back, has two longer, separate ends that run down across the chest, and they are held with each hand, as it were pressing against resistance. But, you will object, the hands here are not stretched out high. I grant they are not high, yet they are stretched out; and when they were dragged along with ropes tied to the extreme hands, they were also stretched forward and lifted up.

units.la: Injessi remota. mas manus, etiam protendebantur tollebanturque. Quin alius locus Plauti est, qui videatur ab hac modestâ expansione, si attendis. Nam in Milite, servus quispiam in ostio stabat, mulierculam redituram exspectans, & nequa elaberetur. Ad eum servus alter:
units.tr: Restraints removed. Indeed there is another passage in Plautus which, if you consider it, seems to refer to this moderate stretching. In the Miles, some slave was standing at the door, waiting for the little woman to return and making sure she did not slip away. Another slave says to him:

units.la: Credo ego istoc tibi exemplo eundum esse actutum extra portam, Dispessis manibus, patibulum cum habebis.
units.tr: "I think you will have to go out of the gate at once, by that example, with your hands spread, when you have a patibulum."

units.la: Bene est, inquit, forma & statur in te, qui mox erit; cum herus alligatum te patibulo per urbem ducet. Atquin stetisse ego eum opinor, manibus ante se projectis & leviter didu&tis, habitu quo solent captantes & apprehensuri.
units.tr: "Good," he says, "the shape and stance are in you, who soon will be such, when your master leads you through the city tied to the patibulum." And yet I think he stood thus, with his hands thrust forward before him and slightly spread, in the posture people adopt when grabbing and about to seize.
CAP. VI.

units.la: Ratio suspendendi per singulas illas formas exposita, atque etiam ocu- lis proposita.
units.tr: The method of hanging, explained for each of those forms and also set before the eyes.

units.la: TRes sententias super Furcæ formâ habes : tu elige : etsi nos ad ultimam vides proclinatos. Quomodo autem nunc Suspensio? Pro formis distinguenda est. Si prima placet, res facilis. in trunco absciso, in paxillo infixo, imò in sissurâ superne factâ, potuit firmiter appendi. Imaginem (oculorum enim magis res quàm verborum est) infrà habes. Si altera, tùm sic censeo, ductos quidem cum duplici ligno ad Crucem, sed non cum utroque in eam actos. Quod ante pectus, depositum putem: manus fixas in altero, atque id ipsum in trunco, paxillo, sissurâ (ut priùs) firmatum. Imaginem vide. Nec absurda aut vero nimis extranea sententia est: cùm & Patibulum reperiam singularem ejusmodi rectumque stipitem dictum. Nonius ex Titinio citat: — si quisquam hodie * praeter hanc Posticum nostrum pepulerit, patibulo hoc Ei caput defringam.
units.tr: You have three opinions about the shape of the Furca; choose whichever you like, though you see that I lean toward the last. How then is the hanging to be done? It must be distinguished according to the forms. If the first pleases you, the matter is easy: on a trunk cut off and fixed in a stake, or indeed in a cleft made at the top, the man could be hung firmly. You have a picture below, since this matter is better grasped by the eyes than by words. If the second, then I think this: they were indeed led to the Cross with a double piece of wood, but were not fastened to it with both. I would think the piece that was in front of the breast was set down, the hands fixed to the other, and that piece itself secured on the trunk, the stake, or the cleft, as before. See the picture. Nor is the opinion absurd or too far-fetched, since I find that the patibulum was also called a single upright stake of this kind. Nonius cites Titinius: if anyone today, apart from this man, has knocked at our back door, I will break his head with this patibulum.

units.la: Et interpretatur Seram, quâ ostia occluduntur, quò hac remotâ valva pateant. Credo eum ex ipso argumento fabulæ sic proferre, & quòd janitor aliquis atque ostii custos hæc dicat. Certè quidem Sera est lignum transversum quod ostiis opponi solet, in postem utrimque immissum. Hodie quoque usus. Itaque Glossæ: Sera, μοχλὸς θύρας. Et Poëta aliquis — excute poste seram. Atque
units.tr: And he explains Sera as that by which doors are shut, so that when this is removed the leaves may open. I believe he says this from the very plot of the play, and that some doorkeeper and guardian of the door says it. Certainly the sera is a transverse bar that is usually set against doors, fitted into the doorposts on either side, and it is still in use today. Hence the Glosses: Sera, bar of the door [μοχλὸς θύρας]. And the poet: someone ... shake the bar from the doorpost. And
¹ Ovid, Amores.

units.la: Atque ego ampliùs arbitror. et- iamsi olim Furca aliâ facie fuerit : tamen commodi causâ, & quia pronior faciliorque hæc appensio, succeßiße singulare hoc rectumque lignum, & id tuliße in humeris, manibus inibi revinctis, in eoque mox figendis. At si tertia sententia sedcat, facilis suspensio. sive in ipsâ Furcâ defixâ in terram simpliciter ; sive cum eâ in altiorem arborem aut lignum sint sublati. Figuræ videantur.
units.tr: And I think further that, even if the Furca once had another shape, nevertheless, for convenience and because this hanging is more natural and easier, this single straight piece of wood succeeded it, and they carried it on their shoulders, with the hands bound to it there, to be fixed on it soon after. But if the third opinion holds, the hanging is easy: either on the Furca itself simply fixed in the ground, or with it raised onto a taller tree or beam. Let the figures be looked at.

units.la: CAP. VII. De novâ Furcâ, quæ nostrum Patibulum. Tribonianum substit- uisse passim in Legum libris.
units.tr: CAP. VII. On the new Furca, which is our patibulum, and how Tribonian substituted it throughout the books of the Laws.

units.la: DE veteri Furcâ, sic censemus, cum lege resipiendi & resiliendi, si quis meliora. Mutare in his talibus non mihi probrum. Nova sequitur quam dixi, quia inferioris ævi inventum. Ea est instrumentum e ligno triplici, forma fugi veteris, cui appensos homines laqueo strangulamus. Hodie quoque usum & speciem hanc habet in plerâque Europâ. Non & prisci s cognita? non arbitramur. Poena quidem laquei Homero expressa, qui facit impudicas ancillas ab Vlysse sic puniri. atque idem infamem ης μὴ καὶαχεών δάταλον (ita loquitur) & impuram mortem ostendit: uti & Plinius, qui prapositeram dixit. quia spiritus intercluditur, cui exitus quaerebatur. Sed à Græcis usurpatam vix reperias: nec à Romanis quidem in publico. etsi ii, in carcere, damnatis gulam laqueo frangebant. Credo coepisse, cùm crux desiit; & vicariam illi factam. Isidori quidem ævo nomen hoc & usum habuit. Patibulum vulgò, inquit, Furca dicitur (ita nunc quoque in Hi-
units.tr: Of the old Furca we think as follows, with the law of repentance and withdrawal, if anyone proposes something better. To change such things is no disgrace to me. The new one follows, which I mentioned, because it is an invention of a later age. It is an instrument of triple wood, in the shape of the old fork, on which we strangle men hung by a noose. Today too it has this use and this appearance in most of Europe. Were they not known to the ancients? We think they were. The punishment of the noose is expressed by Homer, who has shameless maidservants punished so by Ulysses; and the same poet shows an infamous ... (so he speaks) and impure death, as Pliny also does, who called it prapositera, because the breath is shut off, for which an exit is sought. But you would scarcely find it used by the Greeks, nor even by the Romans in public, though they, in prison, broke the throats of the condemned with a noose. I think it began when the cross ceased, and was made its substitute. In the age of Isidore indeed the name and the usage had it. The patibulum, he says, is commonly called Furca (so it is even now in Hi-

units.la: {1} Lib. v. Orig. Hispaniâ, ubi ille scripsit) quasi Quanferens caput. Suspensum enim & strangulatum hæc examinat. In libris legum, quas Tribonianus atque ejus adjuvæ collegerunt, satis frequens hoc nomen: &, ut opinor, significatione novitiâ: quia sublato Crucis supplicio, quidni etiam Furca vetus? Itaque ipsos Iurisconsultos usurpasse, non habet fidem apud juris & moris antiqui peritos. qui verè nominant, substitutum id pro Cruce: caussâ apertâ & liquidâ, quia Constantinus lege latâ sustulerat Crucem. Ergo ipsi quoque, qui leges collectum ibant in ævi illius & sequentis usum. Exempla plura sunt, & notata aliis: quædam etiam ubi inconspectio. ut in isto Calliistrati , de Pœnis: Famosos latrones furcâ figendos placuit. Inconspectè, inquam imò ineptè. Quid? ad Furcam novam
units.tr: {1} Book v of the Origines, in Spain, where he wrote) as if it were "carrier of the head." For it examines the hanged and strangled. In the books of laws, which Tribonian and his helpers collected, this name is quite frequent, and, as I think, in a new sense, because when the cross punishment was abolished, why not the old Furca too? So the claim that the jurists themselves used it is not credible to those skilled in ancient law and custom, who rightly name it as a substitute for the Cross. The cause is open and clear: Constantine had abolished the cross by a law. So those who gathered the laws also went along with the usage of that age and the following one. There are many examples, noted by others, and some where the wording is careless, as in Callistratus's book On Punishments: It has been decided that notorious robbers are to be fixed to a furca. Carelessly, I say, or rather foolishly. What? To the new Furca

units.la: ¹ Lib. xxix. novam homines figuntur? certum est astringi. Sed fuerat Cruci figendos: moverunt alterum, altero retento, quod non debebant. Simile in Ulpiani ′ de Poenis: quod exscriptor etiam fortasse corrupit. Decuriones in metallum dari non possunt, nec furca subjici. Cruci in Ulpiano fuerat: sed quis dixerit, Cruci subjici? Itaque subfigi, vel suffigi, verum censeam; & eandem ἀπεξεσλυφίαν hîc agnoscam.
units.tr: ¹ Book xxix. Are men fixed to it? It is certain they are bound to it. But the text had been to be fixed to a cross; they changed one word and kept the other, which they should not have done. A similar case is in Ulpian's On Punishments, which the copyist perhaps also corrupted: "Decurions cannot be sent to the mines, nor be placed under a furca." In Ulpian it had been "cruci," but who would say "to be placed under a cross"? So I think subfigi or suffigi is the true reading, and I would recognise here the same slip [ἀπεξεσλυφίαν].

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Raro modo in Schemate. & pri- mum de Inversâ suspensione.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. Of the Other Mode of Crucifixion in Form, and first of Hanging Upside Down.

units.la: ADfatim de Furcâ, quæ inter Raros figendi primus Modus fuit. Alter, qui Schemate à vulgari diversus. Intelligo, cùm alio atque alio habitu hominem affigebant. Id quoque factitatum, ut ingeniosa cru-
units.tr: I have said enough about the fork, which was the first mode of fixing among the Romans. The second, which differed from the common form in shape, I understand as this: they fixed the man to the cross in one posture or another. This too was practised, so that cruelty was inventive in punishments.

units.la: ¹ L. IX. crudelitas est in poenas. Josephus 1, ubi narrat Judæos jussu Titi crucifixos: Προσηλωσαν ἡ οἱ στρατιῶται διὰ ὀργὴν ἐ μίας τῆς ἀλότητας, ἄλλον ἄλλῳ σχήματι, πρὸς χλεύην: Affigebant milites, ab ira & odio, eos quos ceperant alium alio schemate, ad ludibrium. Hæc schemata varia fuêre; quæ in lectione vidi, tangam. Est illud, quod Inversum dixeris, cùm hominem in caput suspendunt, pedibus sublatis. Seneca 2: Alii capite conversò in terram suspendêre. Eusebius 3 ostendit Martyribus in Ægypto id factum. Καὶ ἄλλοι πάλιν μὲν ἀναπολωσι&ἱντες, οἱ μὲν ἐν τῷ σύνδεσι ἐν καὶ ἐμβρῖος χαλεπός, οἱ δ' ἐ χειρώτας ἀνάπαλιν κατωκάεψ ἀπολωθηντες: Atque alii iterum crucifixi quidam more in maleficis recepto; quidam etiam deterius, inversa figura, & in caput pendentes. Quod ipsum in D. Petro, sed eo rogante, ne assimularetur Magistro. Abdias: Et accedens ad
units.tr: Josephus, where he relates that the Jews were crucified at the command of Titus, says: "The soldiers, from anger and hatred, nailed those whom they had taken, one in one posture and another in another, for mockery" [Προσηλωσαν ... ἄλλον ἄλλῳ σχήματι, πρὸς χλεύην]. These postures were various; I will touch on those I have seen in my reading. One is what you might call the inverted posture, when they hang a man head downwards with his feet raised. Seneca: "Others hung with their heads turned down toward the ground." Eusebius shows that this was done to martyrs in Egypt: "And others again, nailed up, some in the common manner, bitterly; others, worse, hanged head downwards in an inverted figure, and were burned" [ἄλλοι ... ἀνάπαλιν κατωκάεψ]. The same was done to St Peter, though at his own request, that he might not be made like his Master.

units.la: ¹ Lib.v. Excid. cap.xxviii. ² Consolat. ad Marc. cap xx. ³ Lib.viii. cap.vii. ad Crucem, rogavit ut inverfis vestigiis figeretur. Chrysostomus : Χαίροις Πέτρε, ὁ τῆ ξύλᾳ τῆ σαγρῷ λῃ-λαύτας, τῇ καθ' ὁμοιότητα τῆς Διδασκάλου σαγραθήναι ὁ θελήσας ἐν ἐρᾲᾳ κρέμασθαι, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν, ὡς εἰς ἔφυον τὴν ποτάμων ἐπὶ γῆς ποιήμων: Gaudeas ô Petre, crucis lignum degustans, & ad instar Magistri crucifixi recusans in recto schemate, sed magis in caput obversus, tamquam in cælum viam a terra faciens. Et Petrum quidem etiam clavis inibi fixum, idem Chrysostomus testatur: Ω᾽ ἰυλογημένοι ἡλοι, οἵτινες τὰ ἅγια σώματα μέλη διήλθον: O benedicti Clavi, qui sacra illa membra penetrarunt! Sicut & Calliopius martyr , post tormenta, verso in terram capite Cruci affixus est. Affixus, non devinctus. Tamen & funibus adstricti: ut Simeon Metaphrastes de Philippo Apostolo: Flagris cadunt & verberant, deinde
units.tr: ¹ Lib. v. Excid. cap. xxviii. ² Consolat. ad Marc. cap. xx. ³ Lib. viii. cap. vii. At the cross he asked that he be fixed with his feet turned the other way. Chrysostom: Χαίροις, Πέτρε, ὁ τῷ ξύλῳ τοῦ σταυροῦ γευσάμενος, ὁ παραιτησάμενος σταυρωθῆναι κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα τοῦ Διδασκάλου ἐν ὀρθῷ σχήματι, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ κεφαλήν, ὡς εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀπὸ γῆς ὁδὸν ποιούμενος [Rejoice, Peter, who tasted the wood of the cross, who refused to be crucified in the upright posture like your Master, but rather head downward, as though making a road from earth to heaven]. Rejoice, O Peter, you who tasted the wood of the cross, and who refused to be crucified in an upright posture, like your Master, but rather turned head downward, as if making a way from earth to heaven. And that Peter was also fastened there with nails, the same Chrysostom bears witness: Ὦ ηὐλογημένοι ἧλοι, οἵτινες τὰ ἅγια ἐκεῖνα σώματα μέλη διῆλθον [O blessed nails, who pierced those holy members]. O blessed nails, who pierced those holy limbs! So too Calliopius the martyr: after torments, with his head turned toward the earth, he was fixed to the cross. Fixed, not bound. Yet they were also bound with cords, as Simeon Metaphrastes says of the Apostle Philip: They beat him with whips and scourges, then
¹ Oration on Peter and Paul.

units.la: 2 Martyrol. vii. April. deinde cum funibus a talo vinxissent, sublimem suspendunt praci- pitem. In cruce enim aut stipite sic suspensum accipio. Nec aliter Ammianum : Dracontius & Diodotus, injectis per crura funibus, exanimati sunt.
units.tr: ² Martyrology, 7th of April. then, having bound him with cords from the ankle, they hang him up headlong. For I understand him to have been hung in this way on a cross or stake. Nor otherwise Ammianus: Dracontius and Diodotus, with ropes thrown about their legs, were put to death.
Book 22.
CHAP. IX.

units.la: De obliquâ suspensione, de varican- te, & inter arbores scissione.
units.tr: Of the oblique suspension, of the varicose [crux], and of splitting between trees.

units.la: REperio & obliquos super crucem crucesve positos: ut in Plutarchi Artaxerxe : Is narrat Parysatidem regis matrem infensam Eunucho cuipiam, arte eum redegisse in suam potestatem. tum jussisse ἐκδεῖςαι ζῶντα, ἡ̣ τὸ μὲν σῶμα πλάγιον διὰ τριῶν σταυρῶν ἀναπήξαι, τὸ δὲ δέρμα χωρὶς διαπαττάλευσαι : cutem vivo detrahi, & corpus quidem obliquum jacensque tribus stipitibus sive G crucrucibus infigi, pellem feorsim in palo poni. Video & inter duos palos dispeffis manibus pedibusque alligatos, ut in Martyrologio, de Anastasiâ: Manibus & pedibus extensis ligata est ad palos. Video & inter arbores appensos, &, reductis iis, scissos. De Coronâ 1 martyre: Ipsa inter arbores scissa, Victor autem decollatus est. Quod ipsum Schema ad Cruces referendum Propertio facilè accredam, qui sic appellat:
units.tr: I find also those placed obliquely upon a cross or crosses, as in Plutarch's Artaxerxes. He relates that Parysatis, the king's mother, hostile to a certain eunuch, had by a trick brought him into her power. Then she ordered that he be flayed alive, and that his body, lying obliquely, be fixed to three stakes or crosses, while the skin be hung separately on a pole. [Greek: ἐκδεῖςαι ζῶντα, ἡ̣ τὸ μὲν σῶμα πλάγιον διὰ τριῶν σταυρῶν ἀναπήξαι, τὸ δὲ δέρμα χωρὶς διαπαττάλευσαι]. I also see men fastened between two posts, with hands and feet spread apart, as in the Martyrology, concerning Anastasia: With hands and feet stretched out, she was bound to the posts. I also see men hung between trees and, when the trees were drawn apart, torn in two. Concerning the martyr Coronas: She herself was torn between trees, but Victor was beheaded. I readily agree that this manner of execution should also be referred to crosses, as Propertius, who calls them so:

units.la: Arboreasque cruces Sinis, & non hospita Graiis Saxa, & curvatas in sua fata trabes.
units.tr: The Sinis made crosses of trees, and rocks not hospitable to the Greeks, and beams bent to their doom.

units.la: Senecam 2 etiam huc traham, si fidem libris priscis habeo; qui inter genera Crucium recenset, distracta in diversum actis cruribus membra. Ita libri inquam, quos ego vidi. Est tamen vulgò curri-bus,
units.tr: I would also draw Seneca into this, if I may trust the older books, who among the kinds of crosses lists limbs pulled apart with the legs stretched in opposite directions. So the books I have seen read, I say. Commonly, however, it is printed curribus [chariots].

units.la: 1 Martyr. xiv. Maii. 2 Epist. xiv. bus,bono & suo sensu. ad Metium enim respiciat: etsi vetus desitumque id supplicium, nec inter usitata fortasse ibi referendum.
units.tr: 1 Martyrology, 14 May. 2 Letter 14. -bus, with a good and suitable sense; for it refers to Metius. Yet that punishment is old and obsolete, and perhaps should not be counted among the usual ones here.

units.la: CAP. X. De modo qui Fine diversus, pri- mum de his qui in Cruce ustulati.
units.tr: CHAP. X. On a method differing in its end, and first on those who were burned on the cross.

units.la: TErtius figendi modus Rarior, qui Fine divertit à vulgato. Quem intelligo, cùm cruces alio spectant, & hominem capiunt moriturum in ipsis, non per ipsas. In exemplis discès. Tale, cùm appensi flamâ aut fumo necati. Olim factum ex Cicerone discas: qui fratrem objurgans, Quid opus fuit, inquit, ejusmodi litteris, quas ad ipsum misisti? Illum crucem sibi constituere, ex quâ tu eum antè detraxisses. te curaturum fumo ut comburatur, totâ plaudente provinciâ. Verba
units.tr: A third mode of fixing, rarer, differs from the common one in its end. I understand it as when the crosses face elsewhere and hold a man who is to die in them, not by them. You will learn this from examples. Such is the case when men hung up are killed by flame or smoke. You may learn that it was once done from Cicero, who, rebuking his brother, says: What need was there for such a letter, which you sent to him himself? He would have set up a cross for himself, from which you had earlier taken him down. You would have taken care that he be burned with smoke, while the whole province applauded. The words

units.la: ¹ Lib. 1. ad Q. Frat epist. 11.
units.tr: ¹ Book 1, to Quintus his brother, letter 11.

units.la: Quinĉti & minæ eò spectant, ut homo in cruce fixus ustulctur fumo. Alexander etiam Imperator quempiam qui fumum vendiderat, quasi compari pœnâ afsecturus, ad stipitem ligari præcepit, & fumo apposito quem ex stipulis & humidis lignis fieri jusserat, necavit, præcone dicente, Fumo punitur qui vendidit fumum. Atque in Martyribus nostris hoc genus crebrum. Acta vetera de Pionio: Confixus clavis in cruce, aggestis lignis, flamâ combustus est. Nec aliter Polycarpus mortuus, antistes Smyrnæorum, ipsi in epistolâ: Μιχαὴλ δ' ἀυτὸν ἠμὶ προαπολιπὼν, ἀπιὼν... ἐρπὶ τὸν πῦρ ...
units.tr: Threats of this kind also aim at a man fixed to a cross being smoked to death. The Emperor Alexander too, intending to exact a like punishment from a certain man who had sold smoke, ordered him to be tied to a stake, and, with smoke applied, which he had ordered made from straw and damp wood, to be killed, a herald calling out: "He is punished with smoke who sold smoke." And among our martyrs this kind is frequent. The old Acts concerning Pionius: Fixed with nails to a cross, with wood heaped round, he was burned with flame. Nor did Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, die otherwise; in his letter he writes: [Greek: Μιχαὴλ δ' αὐτὸν ἠμὶ προαπολιπὼν, ἀπιὼν... ἐρπὶ τὸν πῦρ ...]

units.la: 1 Lampr. in Alex. 2 Apud Eusch. lib. IV. c. XV. dabit & fine vestra clavorum firmitate, folutum manere in rogo. Illi autem non confixerunt eum, fed ligarunt. Quin uno etiam tempore plures, appenfi pedibus in fublime ¹ (nota hic & Schema inverfum) capite verfo deorfum, fuffocati fumo, & lento igne confumpti funt.Non ergo injuria Tertullianus ² fcripfit: Licet nunc Sarmentitios & Semaxios appelletis, quod ad ftipitem dimidii axis revincti, farmentorum ambitu exurimur. fignificat enim adeo crebrum in majores illos noftros & in religione proceres fupplicium hoc fuiffe; ut in illudium convitiumque venerit; & Chriftiani vulgò Semaxii,à ftipite cui aftringebantur, & Sarmentitii, à farmentis quibus urebantur, fint dicti. Atque hoc eft quod Axem vocat alibi ³ incendio confiriftum, id
units.tr: ¹ Lampridius, in Alexander. ² In Eusebius, book 4, chapter 15: He will grant that, your firmness of nails notwithstanding, he remain unloosed in the pyre. But they did not nail him, they bound him. Indeed, at one time several were hung up by the feet on high ¹ (note here also the inverted figure), with the head turned downward, suffocated with smoke, and consumed by a slow fire. Not without reason, then, did Tertullian write: ² Although you now call us Sarmentitii and Semaxii, because we are bound to a stake of half an axle, we are burned with a ring of brushwood. For this indicates that this punishment was so frequent among those our elders and leaders in religion, that it passed into mockery and insult; and Christians were commonly called Semaxii from the stake to which they were bound, and Sarmentitii from the brushwood with which they were burned. And this is what he elsewhere calls an axis fixed to the fire ³, that is, to a fire already tied to the man.

units.la: ¹ Martyrol. xxiii. Iunii. ² Apolog. cap. ult. ³ Lib. de pudicit. cap. ult. id est, ad incendium jam cum homine ligatum.
units.tr: ¹ Martyrology, 23 June. ² Apology, last chapter. ³ Book on Modesty, last chapter.
CHAPTER XI.

units.la: De his qui bestiis in Cruce objecti.
units.tr: On those who were thrown to beasts while fixed to the cross.

units.la: CRux & ista Fine alia, cùm homines in eâ fixos bestiis objiciebant. In publicis spectaculis id sæpe factum. Epistola Lugdunensium , de Blandinâ Martyre : Βλανδίνα ἐπὶ ξύλῳ κρε- μασθεῖσα πρὸς κυνῶν ... Blandina in ligno suspensa prostituta est esca & laniena incurrentium ferarum. Quæ & quòd in specie Crucis videbatur, & ob continuam orationem, multam alacritatem injiciebat certantibus. Sed factum & non Christianis. ut illi apud Martialem Laureolo :
units.tr: This cross, too, was different in form from the other kind, when men were fixed to it and thrown to the beasts. This was often done in public spectacles. In the letter of the Lugdunese on the martyr Blandina: [Βλανδίνα ἐπὶ ξύλῳ κρεμασθεῖσα πρὸς κυνῶν...] Blandina, hung upon a stake, was given up as food and prey to the wild beasts that rushed upon her. Because she seemed to be in the shape of a cross, and because of her continual prayer, she put great eagerness into those who were contending. But this was also done to non-Christians, as in Martial's lines on Laureolus:

units.la: 1. Apud Eufeb. lib. v. cap. 1. 2 Lib. 1.
units.tr: 1. In Eusebius, book 5, chapter 1. 2. Book 1.

units.la: Qualiter in Scythica religatus rupe Prometheus / Assiduam nimio pectore pa- vit avem, / Nuda Caledonio sic pectora praebuit urso / Non falsa pendens in cruce Laureolus.
units.tr: How Prometheus, bound to a Scythian rock, fed the bird that gnawed his breast without end, so Laureolus, hanging on a cross, not in pretence, offered his bare breast to a Caledonian bear.

units.la: Nec satis capiunt, certè non revelant, interpretes. Vult quempiam sustinuisse velut in fabula personam Laureoli: & cum is pro argumento crucifigendus esset, sed in speciem & moris causa: rem ex fabula Titus fecit, & noxium quempiam ita fixit, & fixum bestiis etiam objecit. Dico objecit, atque ita proprie: aliud est, dare ad bestias. Vopiscus in Aureliano: Sane Mnestheus postea surrectus ad stipitem, bestiis objectus est. Surrectus, valet rectus ligatus. Hic est stipes, quem Tertullianus appellat lat Leoni concessum. Ita lego, non Leone, libello de Pudicitiâ extremo. Atque ad hunc ipsum motem infamis & infanda illa turpitudo Neronis : quâ viros feminasque ad stipitem deligatos, ipse fera pelle contectus, emissus e cavea, medios invadebat. Xiphilinus 2 è Dione : Μεγάλια ἡμῖν κόρας γαμεῖς γυμνὰς ἀξιοδίων, Ὀνείς τε τιν@ δοξὰν ἀντιλάμβανει ἐς ἀσπίδα τῶν σφισὶν ἱπιλ-γαινεν, ὥστε τι ἐξίαν.
units.tr: The commentators do not grasp this fully, and certainly do not explain it. He means that someone took the part of Laureolus, as in a play; and although he was to be crucified as the plot required, it was only for show and out of custom. Titus took the scene from the play: he fixed some condemned man in this way and then threw him to the beasts while he was still fixed. I say threw to (objecit), and properly so: it is different from giving to the beasts. Vopiscus in the life of Aurelian: Indeed Mnestheus, afterwards raised upright at the stake, was thrown to the beasts. "Surrectus" means "set upright", that is, bound. This is the stake which Tertullian calls given to the lion. So I read it, not "to the lion", in the last chapter of the book On Modesty. And to this very custom belongs that infamous and unspeakable outrage of Nero, in which, covered in a wild beast's skin and let out of a cage, he attacked the men and women tied to stakes. Xiphilinus, from Dio: At the Megalia he married naked girls, and taking up a shield... [Μεγάλια ἡμῖν κόρας γαμεῖς γυμνὰς ἀξιοδίων] ...and one who took up a certain opinion against the shield of those who were set against them... [Ὀνείς τε τιν@ δοξὰν ἀντιλάμβανει ἐς ἀσπίδα τῶν σφισὶν ἱπιλ-γαινεν]
CAP. XII.
On the hanging of the dead on the cross.

units.la: A Ç postremò Crux Fine alia, cùm non vivi sed mortui in eâ appensi. Notabis. & quod nobis solenne in rotâ exponere supplicio jam affectos, ad notam sceleris & infamiam, id olim in Cruce, & Orientalibus præsertim. De Romanis nondum legi. nisi
units.tr: Lastly, at last, there is another kind of cross, where the dead, not the living, were hung on it. Note this too: just as we are accustomed to display on the wheel those already condemned to punishment, as a mark of crime and infamy, so formerly this was done on the cross, especially among the Orientals. I have not yet read of this among the Romans, except that

units.la: 1 Sueton. cap. XLIX: 2 In Neron. nisi quòd Cæsar {1} piratas, à quibus captus esset, cùm in deditionem redegisset, quoniam suffixurum se cruci juraverat, jugulari prius jussit, atque ita suffigi. Sed id per clementiam, & ut subtraheret diurnæ pœnæ. Alii per sævitiam & ad infamiam, ut dixi. Ita Carthaginenses {2} in Hannone. qui captus virgisque cæsus, effossis oculis, & manibus cruribusque fractis, velut à singulis membris pœna exigerentur, in conspectu populi occiditur: corpus verberibus lacerum in cruce figitur. Idem Paryfatis in Eunucho, de quo *supra. Item Ptolomæus Ægypti rex, in Cleomene. qui etsi manu suâ animo-sè cecidisset, tamen [illegible, ~8 letters] τὸ σῶμα κρεμάσαι κελεύσας [?]: jussit corpus crucifigi, cùm cutem prius detraxissent. Ubi observo obiter, antiquum hunc morem excoriandi in suppliciis, Ægyptiis Per-
units.tr: 1 Suetonius, ch. XLIX. 2 In Nero, except that Caesar, when he had forced the pirates who had captured him to surrender, ordered them first to be strangled and then fixed to the cross, because he had sworn that he would fasten them to it. But he did this out of mercy, to spare them a long punishment. Others did it out of cruelty and for infamy, as I have said. So the Carthaginians did to Hanno, who, when captured and beaten with rods, had his eyes gouged out, his hands and legs broken, as if punishment were being exacted limb by limb, and was killed in the sight of the people; his body, mangled by blows, was fixed to a cross. Likewise Parysatis did to the eunuch, about whom I spoke above. Likewise Ptolemy, king of Egypt, did to Cleomenes, who, though he had killed himself with his own hand, nevertheless [illegible], ordering the body to be hanged [τὸ σῶμα κρεμάσαι κελεύσας]: he ordered the corpse to be crucified, after first stripping off the skin. Here I observe in passing that this ancient custom of flaying in punishments was practised by the Egyptians and Persians, and the Egyptians still keep it today. For they punish highwaymen and assassins in this way: they keep them alive for a long time, until the executioner reaches the navel. John Leo reports this, a man who wrote about the affairs of Africa and Egypt with reliable knowledge and judgment. Not only the corpse but also images were raised on the cross, as in the example of Celsus, whose body was consumed by dogs, and an image of him was raised on the cross, a new kind of insult. The author is Pollio, in the Thirty Tyrants.
{1} Suetonius, ch. LXXIV.
{2} Justin, book XXI.

units.la: Persisque fuisse, quem & hodie Ægyptii tenent. nam grassatores sicariosque ita puniunt, diu vivos, donec ad umbilicum carnisex perveniat : quod narrat Johannes Leo, qui cum fide fatis & judicio res Africæ & Ægypti scripsit. Nec cadaver solùm, sed imagines sublatæ in crucem. exemplo in Celso : cujus corpus a canibus consumptum est, & novo injuria genere imago in crucem sublata. Auctor Pollio in xxx. tyrannis.
units.tr: Persians as well, which the Egyptians hold to this day. For they punish highwaymen and assassins in this way: they keep them alive for a long time, until the executioner reaches the navel. John Leo, who wrote about the affairs of Africa and Egypt with reliable knowledge and judgment, reports this. Nor was it only the corpse but also images that were raised on the cross, as in the example of Celsus, whose body was consumed by dogs, and an image of him was raised on the cross, a new kind of insult. The author is Pollio, in the Thirty Tyrants.
CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: E quo ligno Crux fuerit? Item in monte plerumque defixam, ipsam sæpe altiusculam.
units.tr: From what wood was the cross made? Likewise, it was usually fixed on a hill, and the cross itself was often rather high.

units.la: PEregimus, de Formâ & Modo : duo velut succisiva & extra divisionem relicta ; nunc adjungo Materiam & Locum. E quâ materie Crux? ex obvio & & prompto aliquo ligno.. E quâ nostri Servatoris ? censemus è quercu. Primùm quia viri fide digni asserunt, frusta sacratissimi hujus ligni quæ hodie exstant, speciem hanc referre. Tum, quia crebra & frequens in Judæâ olim & nunc quoque illa arbor. Tertiò, quia robustum lignum & fixioni laturæque aptum. Itaque Silius in eo etiam crucifigit.
units.tr: We have dealt with the form and the manner. These two are, as it were, leftover scraps set aside outside the main division. Now I add the material and the place. Of what material was the cross made? Of some common and readily available wood. Of what wood was our Saviour's made? We think of oak. First, because trustworthy men assert that the pieces of this most sacred wood which still exist today show this kind. Second, because that tree was and still is common and abundant in Judaea. Third, because it is a sturdy wood, fit for fixing and for bearing weight. Thus Silius also has him crucified on oak:
When he saw him hanging from the dreadful oak.
Again:

units.la: Ereẞo suffixum robore mastis Ostentabat ovans populis.
units.tr: Fixed to the mast of a tall oak, he exultantly displayed him to the peoples.

units.la: Nam quod superioris aliquot ævi scriptores tria aut * quatuor genera ligni in Cruce dominicâ agnoscunt, curiosè magis dictum arbitramur quàm verè. At
units.tr: For what some writers of a few earlier ages recognise, three or four kinds of wood in the Lord's Cross, we judge to be said more curiously than truly. But

units.la: At quis Locus cruci? Incertus, & pro arbitrio: tamen plerumque conspectus aliquis, & juxta vias. Exempla enim exempla esse definunt; nisi aliorum animum oculosque in se vertant. Quinctilianus1: Quoties noxios crucifigimus, celeberrimae eliguntur viae, ubi plurimi intueri, plurimi commoveri hoc metu possint. Ita Alexander Imperator Eunuchum in crucem tulli jussit per eam viam, quae erat servis suis ad suburbana Imperatoria iter frequentissimum. Quin-etiam opida, certa loca habuisse videntur, huic rei adtributa. Sic Mamertini, more atque instituto, crucem fixerunt in via Pompeia2. Sic Romae juxta Urbem Tacitus3 agnoscit Locum servilibus poenis sepositum: quod de Cruce & Crucifragio interpretamur. Hac ipsa de causa posita ea saepe in monte.
units.tr: But what place was assigned to the cross? It was uncertain and at the discretion of the executioners; yet usually some conspicuous spot, and beside the roads. For they hold that examples are meant to be examples, unless they turn the minds and eyes of others towards themselves. Quintilian¹: Whenever we crucify the guilty, the most crowded roads are chosen, where many can see and many can be moved by this fear. So the Emperor Alexander ordered a eunuch to be carried to the cross along the road which was the most frequented route for his servants to the imperial estates in the suburbs. Indeed, towns seem to have had certain places assigned to this purpose. Thus the Mamertines, by custom and practice, fixed a cross on the Via Pompeia². Thus at Rome, near the City, Tacitus³ recognises a place set apart for servile punishments, which we interpret as referring to the Cross and to crucifracture. For this very reason it was often placed on a hill.

Irrisio Galbæ? huc pertinuit. qui cuidam implorantı leges, & civem Romanum se testificanti, quasi solatio & honore aliquo pœnam levaturus, mutari, multoque prater ceteras altiorem, & dealbatam, statui crucem jussit. Altiorem, ut digniori; albatam, * ut civi, * qui in veste alba. Tale in Justino3, de Carthalone: quem pater, cum gis no-ornatu suo, in altissimam crucem, in conspectu urbis suffigi jussit. Et Pœni factitarunt in Regulo. Apud Silium: vide cum robore pendens Italiam cruce sublimis spectaret ab alta.
units.tr: As with our Saviour's, on Calvary; as with Polycrates, on the highest peak of Mount Mycale¹. Indeed the cross itself was often high, especially for some notable criminal. Galba's mockery belongs here: to a man who implored the laws and declared himself a Roman citizen, he ordered, as if to lighten the punishment with some consolation and honour, that a cross be changed and set up, much higher than the rest and whitewashed. Higher, as for a more worthy man; whitewashed, as for a citizen, who wore white clothing. Such a case is in Justin³ concerning Carthalo, whom his father ordered to be fixed, with his finery, on a very high cross in full view of the city. And the Carthaginians did the same to Regulus. In Silius: see how, hanging from the oak on the cross on high, he gazed at Italy from the height.

units.la: Jam illa Amanis 4 præalta: qui ipsa Mardochæo crucem quinquaginta cubi-ta.
units.tr: Now that of Haman is very high: he ordered a cross fifty cubits high for Mordecai.

units.la: 1 Valer. lib. vi. cap. ult. 2 Sueton. cap. ix. 3 Lib xviii. 4 In Esthere cap. vi. & vii. cubitorum posuit 1, sed ipsi ascendendam. Sanè pleræque omnes altiusculæ, atque ideò communiter Tertullianus 1: Timebit forsitan caro gladium gravem, aut crucem excelsam. Quam ipsam rationem Lactantius 2 in Dominica assignat. Nam quoniam, inquit, is qui patibulo suspenditur, & confixus est omnibus, & ceteris altior: crux potius electa est, qua significaret illum tam conspicuum tamque sublimem futurum, ut ad eum cognoscendum pariter & colendum cunctæ nationes ex omni orbe concurrerent. O inopinatam, sed veram dictionem! cui fides maximè nostro ævo facta: cùm, virtute & gloriâ magnâ Hispanicæ gentis, Novus etiam orbis venit in Christianas leges.
units.tr: ¹ He set it up, but he himself was to climb it.⁴ Certainly nearly all of them are rather high, and so Tertullian¹ commonly says: The flesh will perhaps fear a heavy sword, or a lofty cross. Lactantius² gives this very reason in his Divine Institutes: For since he who is hung on the gibbet and fixed to it is seen by all and is higher than the rest, the cross was rather chosen, so that it would signify that he would be so conspicuous and so exalted that all nations from every part of the world would come together to know him and worship him. O unexpected but true saying! It was made especially credible in our own age, when, through the virtue and great glory of the Spanish nation, the New World too has come under Christian laws.

CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Crux sublata, atque etiam Crurifragium fortasse. Quando id factum, quaesitum.
units.tr: The cross abolished, and perhaps the breaking of legs too. When this was done, inquired into.

units.la: NUnc pedem in ultimo velut spatio pono, quod est Quatenus Crux usurpata. Postquam enim Vitam ipsam interfecit, non diu illi vita: & sustulit ex humanis, aut certè Romanis rebus, Constantinus. Serió jam ille Christianus, noluit salutare signum subservire ad perniciem; & colendum illud atque eximium, poenis vilescere damnatorum. Ergo sustulit. Victor: Vetus veterrimumque supplicium patibulorum, & cruribus suffringendis, primus removit1. Cassiodorus2: Supplicium Crucis, quod primitus apud Romanos erat in usu, lege prohibuit. Atque efficaciter etiam
units.tr: Now I set my foot, as it were, on the last stretch, which is how far the Cross was in use. For after Constantine had put Christ himself to death, the Cross did not live long, and he removed it from human affairs, or at least from Roman ones. He was a Christian late in the day, and he did not want the saving sign to serve destruction, or that which ought to be revered and held in honour to be made cheap by the punishments of condemned men. So he abolished it. Victor: "He first removed the ancient and very old punishment of gibbets and of breaking legs." Cassiodorus: "He prohibited by law the punishment of the Cross, which was first in use among the Romans." And indeed effectively

units.la: 1 In Constant. 2 Histor. Tripar. I. cap. IX. etiam sustulit: nec postea reperies reductam. Augustinus i: Ante homines cruci figebantur; quod postea edicto prohibitum, manet. Scholiastes Juvenalis ad illud Partemque cadaveris adfert, notat: Hominum. nam antiqui crucibus figebant. Non ergo ejus ævo. atque ex eo discas non nimis antiquum ipsum, etsi antiqua doctum. Quando autem sustulit? sero, nec nisi sub imperii extrema. Colligo, quia illo jam imperante mentio etiam crucium: quid, quòd apud ipsum? Lex in ejus nomine exstat Theodosii 2 Codice: quà servi ac liberti, qui dominos aut patronos accusare aut deferre tentaverint, denegatâ audientiâ, patibulo adfiguntur. Jam Julius Firmicus3, qui ejus regno scripsit, non semel Crucis meminit ut recepti supplicii atque usitati. Supra exempla reperies,
units.tr: 1 In Constant. 2 Histor. Tripar. I. cap. IX. also abolished it, nor will you afterwards find it restored. Augustine i: "Before, men were fixed to crosses; which, afterwards forbidden by edict, remains." The scholiast on Juvenal, at the words "and brings a part of the corpse," notes: "Of men; for the ancients fixed them to crosses." So it was not in use in his age, and from this you may learn that the thing itself was not very ancient, though it was known to the ancients. But when did he abolish it? Late, and only towards the end of his reign. I infer this because even under his rule there is mention of crosses. What about under his own rule? A law in his name is extant in the Theodosian Code, by which slaves and freedmen who have tried to accuse or inform against their masters or patrons, having been denied a hearing, are fastened to the gibbet. Now Julius Firmicus, who wrote in his reign, mentions the Cross more than once as an accepted and customary punishment. You will find examples above,

units.la: 1 Quæst. in Vet. Test. 2 Lib. ix. Tit. v. 3 Lib. viii. cap. xx. ries, atque adde istud de latronibus: Hi, inquit, in crucem tollentur, aut publica animadversione damnati crudelissimâ nece peribunt. Atquin illa ipsa Firmicus scripsit, sub finem ejus imperii, & liberis jam adultis. Disces ex fine libri primi. Ergo sero, ut dixi, & sub vitæ finem. Indicat clare Sozomenus , qui inter omnes ab eo leges hanc recenset postremam. Α'μιλετοι ιεροριστ-μινλω Ῥωμαίοις τὴν τῆ ςαωξῆ τιμω-ρίαν νέμη ἀντὶ τ χρῆσιως τ δικα-ςηρίων: Denique priùs usitatam Romanis crucis pœnam, lege sustulit ex usu tribunalium ac judiciorum. Ait, δικαςηρίων: an hoc indicans, quòd nondum sublata ex usu omni privato? & quòd dominis etiam in servos vetus suum jus? cogitandum sit. Sicut & illud, satisne Victor ex vero de Crurifragio pariter sublato scripserit, s suna su-ver-blatum.
units.tr: 1 Quæst. in Vet. Test. 2 Lib. ix. Tit. v. 3 Lib. viii. cap. xx. you will find them, and add this about robbers: "These, he says, are raised on the cross, or condemned to public punishment and perish by the most cruel death." Yet that same Firmicus wrote this near the end of that reign, when his sons were already grown. You will learn it from the end of the first book. So it was late, as I said, and at the end of his life. Sozomen clearly indicates this, who lists this as the last of all the laws of his. [τὴν τοῦ σταυροῦ τιμωρίαν νέμειν ἀντὶ τῆς χρήσεως τῶν δικαστηρίων] Lastly, he abolished by law the punishment of the cross, long customary among the Romans, from the use of the courts and of judgements. He says "of the courts." Is this to indicate that it had not yet been abolished from all private use, and that masters still kept their old right over their slaves? That should be considered. So too should this: whether Victor wrote truly in saying that the breaking of legs was abolished at the same time, sublatum.

units.la: 1 Lib. I. cap. VIII. verbis quæ jam ante dedi. Ratio vix esse videtur. Quid enim Cruci aut Christo etiam cum Crurifragio? nisi quia latrones fortasse juxta Christum. Ridiculum videatur. & si fuit; illud magis sit, quòd martyres multi eo tætro supplicio sint interfecti. Sed prosectò sub Constantio ejus filio vivum id reperio. Apollinares ambo, ait Ammianus 1 pater & filius, ut mandatum est, fractis cruribus occiduntur. Firmicus 2 etiam agnoscit: Hi tales aut in crucem tolluntur, aut illis crura publica judicum animadversione franguntur. Ubi notabis, palàm, ut diversum, à cruce sejungi: quod suprà monui.
units.tr: 1 Lib. I. cap. VIII. in the words I have already given. The reason hardly seems sound. For what has the Cross to do with Christ, or with breaking of legs? Unless perhaps because robbers were crucified beside Christ. That may seem ridiculous; and if it was so, it is more ridiculous that many martyrs were killed by that foul punishment. But certainly under Constantius, his son, I find it still alive. "Both Apollinares," says Ammianus, "father and son, as ordered, are killed with their legs broken." Firmicus also acknowledges it: "Such men are either lifted onto the cross, or their legs are broken by the public punishment of judges." Here you will note that the breaking of legs is plainly set apart from the cross as a different thing, as I noted above.

CHAP. XV.

units.la: Honores quos Constantinus Cruci habitum ivit. Signis ea & vexillis impositta, aut inserta.
units.tr: The honours which Constantine paid to the Cross. It was placed on standards and banners, or inserted into them.

units.la: HIc exitus Pœnalis Crucis fuit : & jam à Constantini primordiis Salutaris nostra cœpta honorari. Caussa & origo à victoria contra Tyrannum . Nam cùm Maxentium aggressurus esset,ἀγω-νισῶλι διὰ τῦτα, τύπῳ ἀντῷ σωτῆρ-ος μυστήρης ἡμέρας δὲ ἐςίφων ἐφάνη κατ' ἐξυνὸν, καὶ γραφῇ περὶ τ σωτῆρ Ρωμαϊκοῖς σοιχείοις, Ἐν τύτῳ νίκα. Ἐκ χρυσῶ τοίνυν ἀντίκα σχιδιάσας σωτῆρ τ φανέντα τύπον αὐτῶ, καὶ τῷ κελέυσας σεχλιᾶς ἀυτῷ ἀπομοφίυ-εσθαι, τοῖς τῆ Μαξιντίῳ συμμαχ[ῶν] καὶ ὑπεξλησεῖ: ambigenti & animo anxio ob ista, figura ei crucis media die, stellis effecta, apparuit in calo, & scriptura circa eam Romanis litte-
units.tr: Here was the end of the cross as a means of punishment, and from the beginnings of Constantine our Saviour's cross began to be honoured. The cause and origin lay in his victory over the tyrant. For when he was about to attack Maxentius, [Eusebius says that he prayed to God and was given a sign: "They fight for this reason ... in this conquer" (ἀγωνίζεσθαι διὰ τοῦτο ... ἐν τούτῳ νίκα)]. Being perplexed and anxious in mind about these things, he saw at midday, in the sky, the figure of a cross made of stars, with a writing about it in Roman letters, In hoc vince, that is, "In this conquer." Therefore he at once had a cross made of gold, in the shape of the figure that had appeared to him, and ordered it to be carried before the army. When he joined battle with the followers of Maxentius, he defeated them.

units.la: Zonar. in Constantino. litteris, In hoc vince. Igitur ex auro statim subitario opere efformans crucem, juxta speciem quae apparuisset, & hanc jubens praegredi exercitum, cum Maxentianis proelium committfit, & superavit. Itaque statim victrix illud signum militaribus signis inseruit, & maximè Labaro, quod inter ea primum. Prudentius ad ipsam Romam:
units.tr: Zonaras, in his life of Constantine. "In this conquer." Therefore, making a cross of gold at once, according to the appearance that had been seen, and ordering it to go before the army, he engaged the Maxentians in battle and conquered them. And so the victorious emperor straightaway inserted that sign among the military standards, and especially the labarum, which was the first of them. Prudentius, addressing Rome herself:

units.la: Agnoscas Regina lubens mea signa necesse est, In quibus effigies crucis aut gemmata refulget, Aut longis solido ex auro praefertur in hastis.
units.tr: Queen, you must gladly acknowledge my standards, on which the image of the cross shines, set with jewels, or is carried aloft on long spears of solid gold.

units.la: Duplicitèr Poëta notat Crucem insitam signis, semel in vexillorum purpurâ, gemmis intextam & expressam: iterum in hastarum vertice superstantem, solido auro formatam. Sed, ut dixi, in Labaro maximè ea conspicua. de quo Prudentius:
units.tr: The poet notes the cross in two ways: once as set into the purple of the banners, woven and embossed with jewels, and again as standing on the tops of spears, formed of solid gold. But, as I have said, it is most conspicuous on the labarum. Of this Prudentius says:

units.la: Quomodo Christus? quia & nomen ejus in ipso velo expressum, & crux nihilominus in hastâ. Eusebius diffusè: Ὑψηλὸν δόρυ χρυσῷ χεύ-σῳ καλυμμένον, κέρας ἔχον ἐγκάρσιον, σαυρὸς ἄχρι τῆς πάντης, σίφων δὲ ἐν λίθων πολυτελῶν κατεσκευασμένον [?] καθ' ὃ τῆς σωτηρίας ἐπηγορίας τὸ σύμβολον δύο γράμματα, τῷ Χριστῷ παραδηλῶντα ὄνομα, διὰ τῶν πρώτων ὑπεσημασμένον χαρακτῆρων, χιάζομένῳ Ρ Χ τὸ μυστήριον: Sublimis hasta auro circumvéstita, cornu transversum habebat effigiem in formâ crucis. Supra vero, in ipso culmine omnium, corona è lapidibus pretiosis & auro contexta infigebatur: juxta quam salutaris appellationis symbolum, duæ litteræ Christi nomen exprimentes, per
units.tr: Why Christ? Because his name was also written on the cloth itself, & and the cross nonetheless on the spear. Eusebius goes into more detail: [a high spear covered with gold, having a crosspiece like a horn, reaching to the top in the form of a cross; and at the summit a crown of precious stones, set in place, on which was the symbol of the saving name, two letters showing the name of Christ, through the first characters of it, the mystery being marked by the Greek letters P and X crossed]: A lofty spear clothed in gold had a crossbar in the form of a cross. Above, at the very top of all, a crown woven of precious stones and gold was fixed; beside it was the symbol of the saving name, two letters expressing the name of Christ, through

Neque cruces modò signis inseri voluit ; sed hoc amplius, solas: καὶ Τ χευσᾶν ἀγαλμάτων, ὁποῖα προ-τεθεν ἀυλοῖς ἐθ᾽ ἦν, τὸ μηδὲν: & aurearum imaginum cujusmodi antea solebant, nullas. Intelligit aureas imagines vultusque Imperatorum. Forma ecce in Nummis.
units.tr: the first letters only, namely the Greek P crossed and cut through the middle by the X. Nor did he wish only crosses to be inserted in the standards, but furthermore, only them: [no golden images of the kind formerly placed on the standards]: and no golden images of the kind that used to be customary before. The author means golden images and likenesses of the emperors. The shape can be seen on the coins here.
CAP. XVI.

units.la: Crux in Militum armis : in Impe- ratorum capite & manibus ; & pro insigni.
units.tr: The cross on the soldiers' arms, on the emperors' heads and hands, and as an emblem.

units.tr: Nor was the cross displayed only on standards, but also on the soldiers' own arms. Eusebius says: "He also caused the symbol of the cross to be marked on the weapons themselves" [Ἡ ἴδη ὁ καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀυλῶν Τ ὅπλων τὸ τῶ σταυρῷ τὸ σύμβολον καὶ ἀσημαίνεσθαι ἐποίει]:

units.la: 2 Ibidem. ꝰ : Iam vero in armis ipsorum militum salutaris tropæi signum jußit exstare. Quibus armis? duplicibus, Clypeis & Galeis: sed ita, ut Christi quidem ipsum nomen (litteris & notis, quibus in Labaro) clypeis inscriberetur, Galeis autem imponeretur superne Crux ipsa. Prudentius sic discriminat:
units.tr: 2 Ibid. He ordered the sign of the saving trophy to be displayed on the arms of the soldiers themselves. What arms? Double ones, shields and helmets. But the name of Christ itself (in letters and symbols, as on the standard) was inscribed on the shields, while the cross itself was placed on top of the helmets. Prudentius distinguishes them thus:
Christ on the emblems of the shields
"Christ had written on the shields, and the cross, added to the crests on top, blazed."

units.la: Et merito Christus in clypeis, eo ritu quo solent nomina Imperatorum. Atque etiam hodie Constantinopoli sunt columnæ, à Constantino, ut putatur: in quarum basibus clypei cum his notis [monogram].
units.tr: And rightly so, Christ was on the shields, in the manner in which the names of emperors are usually inscribed. Even today at Constantinople there are columns, said to be from Constantine's time, and on their bases are shields bearing these letters [monogram].

units.la: Sed & crucem in suum caput & ad Diadema Imperator tran-stulit,
units.tr: But the emperor also transferred the cross to his own head and to the diadem,

Et credo ab ipso esse Constantino: qui, & in figurationibus solidorum & imaginibus propriis signum crucis jussit inscribi Id Sozomenus ³ quoque asserit: Πλαττομένω τι ἐν νομίσμασι, καὶ εἰκόσι γεγραμμένω, ἐκίλλουσιν ἀει συγγεάφεσθαι καὶ σωτυπουδα τοῦτο τὸ θεῖον σύμβολον· καὶ μαρτυροῦσιν εἰς ἔτι νῦν εἰκόνες αὐτὰ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ὅσαι ἡ χρίμαλον: Impresso autem sibi in nummis, aut pictão in imaginibus, jussit semper adprimi & adpingi istud divinum symbolum: & testantur etiamnunc imagines que in eo schemate exstant. Statuam etiam sibi erigi fecit Romæ in urbe mediâ, quæ manu hoc salutare signum teneret, cum inscriptione quam apud Eusebium,
units.tr: 1 Against Symmachus. Was it transferred to this one or another? In Jerome I indeed read: "The purple robes of kings and the glowing gems of their diadems are adorned with a painting of the Saviour's gibbet." And I believe this is from Constantine himself, who "ordered the sign of the cross to be inscribed both on the stamping of coins and on his own images." Sozomen also asserts this: "Impressed on coins, or painted on images, he always ordered this divine symbol to be stamped and painted; and the images that still exist in this form bear witness to it" [Πλαττομένω τι ἐν νομίσμασι, καὶ εἰκόσι γεγραμμένω, ἐκίλλουσιν ἀει συγγεάφεσθαι καὶ σωτυπουδα τοῦτο τὸ θεῖον σύμβολον· καὶ μαρτυροῦσιν εἰς ἔτι νῦν εἰκόνες αὐτὰ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ὅσαι ἡ χρίμαλον]. He also had a statue of himself erected in the middle of the city of Rome, which held this saving sign in its hand, with an inscription that anyone who wishes may read in Eusebius.

Alias victoriae sunt quae manu eas levent; alias ipsi, idque dupliciter. aut enim solam eam gestant, aut globulum cui ea infixa. De globulo Suidas etiam tangit, & caussam aperuit, in Justiniano. Qui, inquit, ἐσῆσι μυλο τὴν ἰαῖλῆ ἀχόγα ἐπὶ χίον ἐφ' ἵππε. τῇ μὲν ἀεἰστιξᾷ χειρὶ φίρει σφαῖραν, ἐμπεπηγότα τὸ σαυροῦ ἐν αὐτῇ, ὑποσημαίνοντα ὡς διὰ τῆς εἰς τὸν σαυρὸν πίστεως, τῆς γῆς ἐγκρατὴς γέγονε, σφαῖρα fixa. μὲν γὰρ ἡ γῆ, διὰ τὸ σφαιροειδὲς τῆς αὐτῆς ἡμέρας. πίστις δὲ ὁ σαυρὸς, διὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ σαυρὶ ἀναστηλωθέντα θεόν: Justinianus imaginem suam posuit super columnam in equo. Ea sinistra manu fert globum, cruce in eo infixa: significante quod per fidem in crucem, terrae dominus sit factus. Globus enim terra est, ob hanc ejus H 2 rotun- 1 De vita Const. 1. c. xxxiii. & alibi. rotundam formam : fides autem crux, ob Deum qui carne in eâ affixus. Nec tamen Justinianus inventi ejus auctor; exstant Theodosii aliorumque nummi sic insigniti diu ante illum. Quin observo Principes Byzantinos in progressibus publicis crucem hanc praetulisse suapte manu. Johannes Curopalates 1: Ἀ'πὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν τοιούτων Φοῤῥημάτων φορεῖ ὁ βασιλεὺς διὰ ἂν βάλοιτο, τ δὲ γε σαυρὸν ἐν δεξιᾷ φέρει αἰεί. E reliquis gestaminibus gestat Imperator quae voluerit cunque : Crucem autem dextera semper gestat. Atque infrà: Καὶ τῇ μὲν δεξιᾷ χειρὶ καθέχει τ σαυρὸν, ὡς σύνηθές ἐστι κρατεῖν τ βασιλέα ὅταν κῇ τὸ σίμμα φορεῖ : Et dextrâ quidem manu tenet crucem, sicut solenne est teneri ab Imperatore, quoties & Stemma fert, id est diadema. Ab hoc ritu etiamnunc crucifer ille globus inter Sacri illius Imperii infi-
units.tr: Epist. ad Lætam, Historia Tripart. Lib. ap. ix.[?] Whoever wishes may read it. Following this example, other emperors, on whose coins we still see crosses in various forms today. Some crosses are carried in the hand and others are shown on the coins in another way, either alone or on a globe in which the cross is fixed. Suidas also touches on the globe and gives the reason, in the entry on Justinian: He set up his own statue on a column, on horseback. In his left hand he bears a globe, with a cross fixed in it, signifying that through faith in the cross he became master of the earth. The globe is the earth, because of its roundness; the faith is the cross, because of God who was fixed to the cross [ἐσῆσι μυλο τὴν ἰαῖλῆ ἀχόγα ἐπὶ χίον ἐφ' ἵππου. τῇ μὲν ἀριστερᾷ χειρὶ φέρει σφαῖραν, ἐμπεπηγμένον τὸν σταυρὸν ἐν αὐτῇ, ὑποσημαίνοντα ὡς διὰ τῆς εἰς τὸν σταυρὸν πίστεως τῆς γῆς ἐγκρατὴς γέγονε· σφαῖρα μὲν γὰρ ἡ γῆ, διὰ τὸ σφαιροειδὲς τῆς αὐτῆς· πίστις δὲ ὁ σταυρός, διὰ τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ σταυρῷ ἀναστηλωθέντα θεόν]. in the flesh. Yet Justinian was not the author of this invention; coins of Theodosius and others so marked exist long before him. Indeed, I observe that the Byzantine princes carried this cross in their own hand in public processions. John Curopalates: Of such ornaments the emperor carries whichever he wishes; but he always carries the cross in his right hand [Ἀπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν τοιούτων φορημάτων φορεῖ ὁ βασιλεὺς ὅ τι ἂν βούληται· τὸν δὲ σταυρὸν ἐν δεξιᾷ φέρει ἀεί]. And further: In his right hand he holds the cross, as it is customary for the emperor to hold it whenever he also wears the stemma, that is, the diadem [Καὶ τῇ μὲν δεξιᾷ χειρὶ κατέχει τὸν σταυρόν, ὡς σύνηθές ἐστι κρατεῖν τὸν βασιλέα ὅταν καὶ τὸ στέμμα φορεῖ]. From this custom that cross-bearing globe is still, among the insignia of that holy empire, infi-

units.la: Quod his elogiis cum Damasceno lubens merito afficio, Θυγὴς καὶ ὅπλον τῆς τρόπαιον καὶ τῆς διαβόλου, φθορᾶς εἰς μὴ Θίγη ἡμῶν ὁ ὁλοθρεύων, τῶν χειρῶν ἀνάστασις, τῶν ἐντῶν σὺν ἐλαγμα, ἀδάνων βασιλεία, ποιμένων ὁμιλητῶν ἀράδων, ἐπισεφόντων χαρᾶς γηγενῶν, σωτηρίου ἀντιλόντων τελείωσις, ψυχῆς σωτηρία
units.tr: With these epithets I gladly and rightly honour it, with Damascene: a shield and weapon and trophy against the devil, the destroyer of corruption who ruins us, the resurrection of the fallen, the staff of the weak, the kingdom of the eternal, the guide of ministers, the joy of those who sorrow, the perfection of salvation, the salvation of the soul [Θυγὴς καὶ ὅπλον τῆς τρόπαιον καὶ τῆς διαβόλου, φθορᾶς εἰς μὴ Θίγη ἡμῶν ὁ ὁλοθρεύων, τῶν χειρῶν ἀνάστασις, τῶν ἐντῶν σὺν ἐλαγμα, ἀδάνων βασιλεία, ποιμένων ὁμιλητῶν ἀράδων, ἐπισεφόντων χαρᾶς γηγενῶν, σωτηρίου ἀντιλόντων τελείωσις, ψυχῆς σωτηρία].

units.la: ϰαὶ σῶμα τῶ, πάντων τ κακῶν ὑπ τέ-πατων, πάντων τ ἀγαθῶν πηίξιν, ἁμαρτίας ἀναίρεσις, φυτὸν ἀναστάσεως, ξύλον ζωῆς αἰωνίς: Clypeus & armatura & tropæum contra diabolum, signaculum ne tangat nos eversor, jacentium erectio, stantium fulcrum, infirmorum scipio, pastorum virga, revertentium manuductio, prosicientium perfectio, anima conservatio & corporis, omnium malorum aversio, omnium bonorum conciliatio, peccati pernicies, stirps resurrectionis, lignum vitæ æterna. Da hanc nobis ô ÆTERNE.
units.tr: And body of the ... , the removal of all evils, the planting of all goods, the removal of sin, the plant of resurrection, the tree of eternal life [καὶ σῶμα τῶ, πάντων τ κακῶν ὑπ τέ-πατων, πάντων τ ἀγαθῶν πηίξιν, ἁμαρτίας ἀναίρεσις, φυτὸν ἀναστάσεως, ξύλον ζωῆς αἰωνίς]: "Shield and armour and trophy against the devil, a seal so that the destroyer may not touch us, the raising of the fallen, the support of those who stand, the staff of the weak, the rod of the shepherds, the guide of those who turn back, the perfection of those who advance, the preservation of soul and body, the turning away of all evils, the bringing together of all goods, the destruction of sin, the stock of resurrection, the tree of eternal life." Grant this to us, O Eternal One.
END OF BOOK III.
ON THE CROSS.
JUSTUS LIPSIUS
TO THE BOOKS
ON THE CROSS
NOTES.
ADDRESS.

units.la: AD textum etiam meum, Lector, visum fuit breviter hæc notare. Cur non in ipso? quia non pro omnium gustu hæc talia, & plerisque satis est capita rerum delibasse. Caussa etiam, quia placuit quædam explicatiùs aut firmiùs iterare. Debui sanè, ut hoc ævum est : in quo calumniæ, ut ille inquit. Quasi herba irrigua, succrescunt uberrimè.
units.tr: I thought it right to make a few brief notes here on my own text too, dear reader. Why not in the text itself? Because such things do not suit every taste, and for most readers it is enough to have skimmed the main heads of a subject. I also had reasons for wishing to repeat certain points more fully or more firmly. Indeed I ought to have expected this, given the age we live in, in which, as a certain writer puts it, slanders spring up most abundantly, like weeds in irrigated ground.

units.la: In culpâ sumus, sive quid commisimus, sive etiam omisimus: & plerisque pulchrum, non nisi * τὰς ἀκανθας τῶν βιβλίων ἐκλέγειν. Ego verò scio neminem esse tam felicem, qui non subjectus sit errori, & hoc non dementis esse proprium, verùm hominis. Itaque ne nunc quidem cùm caveo, satis cavero: utique in isto vario & diffuso scribendi genere, in quo, alius alio plura invenire potest, nemo omnia. Quo magis mirum, quod-
units.tr: We are at fault, whether we have committed something or even left something undone; and many think it fine to pick only the thorns out of books [τὰς ἀκανθας τῶν βιβλίων ἐκλέγειν]. For my part I know that no one is so fortunate as to be free from error, and that this belongs not to madness but to humanity. So even now, although I take care, I shall not have taken enough care, especially in this varied and diffuse kind of writing, in which one person may find more faults than another, but no one finds them all. All the more surprising, then, is it that some people insult us

units.la: * Spinas librorum eligere. quosdam nobis insultare: nec cogitare quàm multa ipsi fortasse non repperissent, si primi quaesissent. Non sum tam Lynceus, inquiunt, quàm mihi videor. Egóne? testor te summe Deus, non videor: & si quid olim in calidâ illâ œtate calidius, abiit, & veris me pretiis nunc æstimo & pendo. Quo longius in hac vitæ viâ progredior, magis magisque aspicio circumfusam animo caliginem, corpori imbecillitatem. Heracleitus, ut opinor, olim dicere solitus, Se cùm juvenis esset, nihil scire; cùm senex, nihil ignorare: mihi planissimè contrà evenit, & qui olim aliquid scire visus, nunc parum aut nihil. Et ô miseri, quid nos, doctrina, fama sumus? Ipsi pulvis, illa opinio, ista ventus. Atqui etiam tangunt quasi manum injecerimus scriptis alienis. Vellem parciùs: certè non merito meo fit, qui prolixè & libenter honorem ingeniis inventoribusque habitum ivi, nisi sicubi Dialogorum ratio & decorum rum id impedivit. Tale in Saturnalibus. neque negamus virum magnum multa ante nos in eo argumento observitasse : sed scripta ejus extant ; quid detraximus ? Illud tamen non arbitror, ibi aut alibi insigniorem notam aut correctiunculam malâ fraude in nomen meum transscriptam. Tetigit aliquis hanc aut illam materiam ? quid tum ? ego fortassis implevi. Et ut scerio loquar, lectionis aut collectionis tota ista res est : cur alteri imputemus ? Tot jam annos, imò lustra, in isdem illis scriptoribus versor, volvo revolvo in easdem curas: malè me hercules de industriâ ingenioque nostro sentit, quisquis aut non leƈta ea nobis censet, aut negleƇta. Ut è fonte quod haurimus, nostrum est, quisque tamen suo vase : sic quod è communibus illis scriptoribus, sed quisque pro judicii sui modo. Denique legere, aut colligere parum est : seligere, disponere, eloqui, poscit laudem.
units.tr: * To pick out the thorns of books. and never consider how many things they themselves would perhaps not have found, had they been the first to seek them out. "I am not as sharp-sighted as I think I am," they say. Am I? I call you to witness, highest God, that I do not think so. Whatever was too heated in that hot age of mine has cooled, and now I weigh and value myself by true standards. The farther I advance along the road of this life, the more I see a mist gathering around my mind and a weakness in my body. Heraclitus, I believe, used to say that when he was young he knew nothing, and when he was old he knew everything he had not known. My experience is quite the opposite: I who once seemed to know something now know little or nothing. Alas, what are we, learning and fame? Ourselves dust, that opinion, this a wind. Yet they also carp at us as if we had laid hands on other men's writings. I wish I had done so less. At any rate, it is not through my own fault that I have freely and generously given honour to men of talent and inventors, except where the nature of a dialogue and its fitting form prevented it. That is how it is in the Saturnalia. I do not deny that a great man observed many things on that subject before me, but his writings are still extant; what have I taken away from him? Yet I do not think that anywhere in that work, or elsewhere, a more notable mark or a small correction has been carried over under my name by bad faith. Has someone touched this or that subject? So what? Perhaps I have completed it. And, to speak frankly, this whole business is a matter of reading and collecting: why should we attribute it to another? For so many years, indeed for decades, I have lived among those same writers, turning and returning to the same concerns. Heaven knows, he has a bad opinion of my industry and talent who thinks either that these things were not read by me or that they were neglected. As with water drawn from a spring, what we draw is ours, though each of us draws it in his own vessel; so too with what we take from those common writers, each in the measure of his own judgement. In short, reading or collecting is not enough: selecting, arranging and expressing things is what deserves praise.

units.la: Hæc & talia satiare nos scriptionis poterant : melior ratio revocavit, & suasit publico prodesse quâ possum. Opes atque arma nostra, stilus. Quem tamen in alium numquam stringam aut proferam : absit : Christianum me commemini, id est, Sacerdotem pacis. Habet quidem gloria, ait Plinius, præsertim in studiis, quiddam * ἀχοινωνήτου; nolo in me expetat. & quandocumque moriar, feram mecum hanc conscientiam, tiam, nullius me famæ invidisse, quosdam meæ. Quod si ævum hoc parum etiam gratum sit : quid novi? Suum cuique pretium posteritas rependet. Tu Lector vale, & juvantem, aut certè volentem, ama.
units.tr: These and similar considerations might have been enough to satisfy me with writing; a better reason called me back and persuaded me to be of public service as far as I can. My resources and weapons are my pen. Yet I will never turn it against anyone, or bring out its points against another: far be it. I remember that I am a Christian, that is, a priest of peace. It is true, says Pliny, that glory, especially in scholarly pursuits, has something unsociable [ἀκοινωνήτου] about it; I do not want it to seek me out. And whenever I die, I shall carry with me this consciousness: that I have envied no one's reputation, and that some have envied mine. But if this age is also rather ungrateful, what is new? Each man's worth is repaid by posterity. Farewell, reader, and love the one who helps you, or at least the one who is willing to.

units.la: JVSTI LIPSII NOTÆ AD LIB. I.
units.tr: Notes of Justus Lipsius on Book I.
CHAPTER II.

units.la: PAg. 4. lin. 9. GABALVM] Exoticam vocem esse per me suspicabar, didici & Hebræam origine à Mart. Antonio Delrio, doctissimo & amicissimo viro. nam illis Gab, excelsum: Gabal, terminus, aut rectus stipes in agris. Quid nisi tale crux, quæ erecta, & in excelso? Reperio & in Persicarum vocum indice (à Franc. Raphelengio nostro habui) Gali notare excelsum. Jam nostras vox quantulum abit, qui patibulum Galgam appellamus? Sed nec Gallica valde abludit.
units.tr: Page 4, line 9. GABALVM: I had suspected this to be a foreign word, and I have learned from Martin Antonio Delrio, a most learned and dear friend, that it is also Hebrew in origin. For in that language Gab means high, and Gabal means a boundary, or an upright post standing in the fields. What is a cross but something upright and set on high? I also find in the index of Persian words (which I had from our friend Franciscus Raphelengius) that Gali means high. And how far is our own word from this, when we call a gallows a Galga? Nor does the French word differ much.

units.la: Pag. 6. lin. 8. & 9. Cruces Caucasorum.] Potes pro ipsis suppliciis accipere, & cruciaria morte. te. Aufonius de hac quoque Prometheâ: Sic inter rupes Scythicas fletit alitibus crux. Unde Prometheo de corpore sanguineus ros.
units.tr: Page 6, lines 8 and 9. Cruces Caucasorum. You may take this as referring to the punishments themselves, and to death by torture. Ausonius also speaks of this Promethean torment: So among the Scythian rocks the cross wept for the birds. Hence the bloody dew from the body of Prometheus.

units.la: Junius Bassus apud Senecam libro I. Controv. III. Nihil amplius putabam adjici posse, quàm quod in illa cruce Vestam nominaverat. Nusquam sane crux, sed virgo dejicienda de saxo erat, Vestam invocavit, & cecidit illæsa.
units.tr: Junius Bassus, quoted by Seneca in Controversiae Book I, Controversy III: I thought nothing more could be added than what he had named on that cross, Vesta. Clearly there was no cross at all; a virgin was to be thrown from a rock. She invoked Vesta, and fell unharmed.
ON CHAPTER III.

units.la: Pag. 8. lin. 5. Confixum esse Christo dicit.] Est illud Pauli ad Romanos cap. VI. ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη.
units.tr: Page 8, line 5. Confixum esse Christo dicit. This is that passage of Paul to the Romans, chapter VI: Our old man was crucified with him [ὁ παλαιὸς ἡμῶν ἄνθρωπος συνεσταυρώθη].

units.la: Pag. 9. lin. 5. & 6. Cruciarius] Quo modo & Verberonem, Flagrionem, Mastigiam dicimus, verbere, flagro, mastige dignum
units.tr: Page 9, lines 5 and 6. Cruciarius. Just as we say verberonem, flagrionem, mastigiam, for a man deserving the lash, the whip, the scourge.

units.la: Tertullianus aliter hac voce utitur. Febris per cruciarios & mortiferos exitus erogat hominem: id est, cruciantes. Quâ mente & Vinum crucium in Lucilio Festus observat, insuave, acerbum.
