units.tr: Tertullian uses this word in another sense: Fever wears out a man through cruciarii and deadly ends, that is, through torments. In the same sense Festus also notes vinum crucium in Lucilius, meaning harsh, sour wine.
ON CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Pag. 10. lin. 7. & 8. Σταυρὸς Σκόλοψ.] Nec tamen nego pluribus etiam verbis in hanc rem uti. Ecce & Ῥχξίον appellant crucem. Scriptor anonymus apud Suidam: Ἰχθὺς Ἰουδαῖοι τὸν Σωτῆρα σταυρώσαντες [?]: Ligno recto Judai Servatorem affixerunt. Sunt qui ita hoc verbi explicent & vertant in Thucydidis vitâ quam scripsit Marcellinus: Ἰχθὺς ἐπὶ τὸ ταῦρον [illegible, ~12 letters] Ait quosdam opinari Thucydidem peregrè & in exsilio mortuum. Lignum enim sive Tabulam super sepulchrum ejus positum esse. Hoc autem inanis & honorarii tumuli patrium signum & follenne Attıcum haberi, in iis qui tali infortunio obiissent, nec Athenis sepulti essent. Sunt, inquam, qui Crucem aut Furcam vertant, nec mihi probant. Magis est, ut Ἀρχίου hic lignum navale sit (peregrinantis, aut absentiæ indicium, quoniam mari ferè ex Attica abitur) de quo Hesychium vide. Ille idem Grammaticus addit: Ἀρχίου σαυλ-ἁμμα, ἢ ξύλον ἐν ᾧ κακὸς ἐγοι ξιοντες. Melius διοντες. id esset, lignum sive axis in quo malefici ligantur.
units.tr: Page 10, lines 7 and 8. Σταυρὸς Σκόλοψ. Yet I do not deny that they also use several other words for this thing. Look, they also call a cross [Ἀρχίον]. An anonymous writer in Suidas: The Jews, having crucified the Saviour [Ἰχθὺς Ἰουδαῖοι τὸν Σωτῆρα σταυρώσαντες [?]]: The Jews fastened the Saviour to an upright piece of wood. There are some who explain and translate this word thus in the Life of Thucydides written by Marcellinus: Ἰχθὺς ἐπὶ τὸ ταῦρον [illegible, about twelve letters]. He says that some think Thucydides died abroad, in exile. For a plank or tablet was placed over his tomb. This is regarded as the customary and solemn Attic sign of an empty, honorary tomb, for those who had died in such misfortune and were not buried at Athens. There are, I say, some who render it cross or gallows, and I do not approve of this. It is more likely that Ἀρχίου here means a ship's timber (a sign of one who is abroad or absent, since people mostly leave Attica by sea), on which see Hesychius. The same grammarian adds: Ἀρχίου, a plank, or a wooden beam on which evildoers are bound. The better reading would be διοντες, meaning a beam or axle to which criminals are bound.

units.la: Atque ita Eustathius in Iliad. x. Σανίς, ἐν ᾗ τὰς κακούργας ἔδει. Asser, in quo maleficos ligabant. Item Aristophanes: Βασανίζων πάντα τὰ ὀπτὰ, ἐν πίνακι δήσας: Omni modo torquens, in assere ligans. Reperio & in Eusebio Ἀρχίου pro cruce, & supra adduxi, lib. II. cap. XII. Σανίδα in
units.tr: So too Eustathius on the Iliad X: A board on which the wrongdoers were to be placed; an asser, on which evildoers were bound. Likewise Aristophanes: Βασανίζων πάντα τὰ ὀπτὰ, ἐν πίνακι δήσας [tormenting all the roasted meats, binding them to a board]: torturing in every way, binding to a plank. I also find Ἀρχίου for a cross in Eusebius, and I have cited above, Book II, chapter XII, Σανίδα in

units.la: hac re dixit Herodotus in extremâ Calliope: Α᾽παξαγόντες ὁ ἀντὸν ἐς τὴν ἀκτὴν, σανίδα ἀφαρπαγαλίσαντες ἀνεχρέμασαν. Quod vertunt : Adductum hunc in litus depaftis humi afferibus fuspenderunt. Vide an non σανίδι legas potius, hoc noftro sensu : Abducentes eum ad litus, asferi affigentes fuspenderunt. Esset affixio in stipite simplex.
units.tr: this matter, as Herodotus said in the last part of Calliope: Leading him to the shore, they hung him up, having fastened him to a plank [σανίδι]. They translate it: Having brought him to the shore, they hanged him on boards laid on the ground. See whether you should not rather read σανίδι, in our sense: Leading him to the shore, they hanged him, fixing him to a plank. The fastening would then be to a single upright post.

units.la: Pag. 13. lin. 6. Κεῖμεν. Ita palàm Plutarchus in Cæfare, de piratis : Πολλάκις ἡπειλησε κεφαλὴν ἀυτὸς ; Sæpe minatus crucifigere eos, ut Latini omnes loquuntur & narrant. Est & Antiochi regis edictum, quo philofophos regno pellit, & poenam etiam affectantibus ponit iftam; Τῶν δὲ νεωτέρων ὅσοι ἐπὶ ἀλίσκωνται πρὸς τὰς ψυχὰς, διότι κεφαλάσοιντο, ἡ οἱ πατέρες αὐτῶν ἐν αἰτίᾳ ἴσοι) μιγίσταις : Juvenum vero quicumque reperientur apud iftos, ii fuspendentur, & patres eorum harebunt in maximâ noxâ. Ita
units.tr: Page 13, line 6. Κεῖμεν. Thus Plutarch openly says in the Life of Caesar, about the pirates: He often threatened to crucify them [Πολλάκις ἠπείλησε σταυρώσειν αὐτούς], as all the Latin writers also speak and relate. There is also the edict of King Antiochus, by which he expels the philosophers from the kingdom and also sets this penalty for those who aspire to them: Of the younger men, whoever are caught in these matters, if they are found to be disciples of the philosophers, shall be hanged, and their fathers shall be held in the greatest guilt [Τῶν δὲ νεωτέρων ὅσοι ἐπὶ ... ]. Thus

units.la: Athenæus recitat lib. xii. sed utrùm de hac nostrâ in cruce suspensione, an de aliâ in trabe accipimus ? in trabe, inquam, ad verberandum flagellandumque. quem morem Græcis Latinisque fuisse, comœdiæ atque alia docent.
units.tr: Athenaeus recites it in Book XII. But do we understand this as hanging on a cross, as in our sense, or as on a beam, for beating and whipping? On a beam, I say, for beating and flogging. Comedies and other writings show that this custom existed among both Greeks and Romans.

units.la: Pag. 15. lin. 12. & 13. Aliorum inanes logos.] Ita verè, inanes. Nam Alciati quale est? Ait Histiæum Milesium intelligi, quem Sardibus prapositum Artaphernes & Harpagus cruci fixerunt, capite desecto & ad regem misso. Ita Herodotus, inquit, libro sexto. Quod verum est: sed quid Histiæo, cum Achæo? Respondet, ideò sic vocari à poëtâ, quia Histiæus Milesius fuit, Milesii coloni Ionum, Iones Achæi. Ergo à patria, Achæus. Quis color in hoc sermone? Sed nec amicum nostrum audio sine auctore scribentem: Achæum intelligi Lydiæ regem, qui ob avaritiam necatus in Pattoli aquis pependit.
units.tr: Page 15, lines 12 and 13. Aliorum inanes logos. Truly, empty. For what is Alciatus' view? He says that Histiaeus of Miletus is meant, whom Artaphernes and Harpagus placed in charge at Sardis, and who was fixed to a cross, with his head cut off and sent to the king. So says Herodotus, he writes, in Book VI. This is true enough, but what has Histiaeus to do with Achaeus? He answers that the poet so called him because Histiaeus was of Miletus, Miletus was a colony of the Ionians, and the Ionians were Achaeans. So from his country, Achaeus. What plausibility is there in this argument? Nor do I hear that our friend writes without an authority: that Achaeus is meant as the king of Lydia, who, killed out of greed, hung in the waters of the Pactolus.
ON CHAPTER V.

units.la: Pag. 18. lin. 5. & 6. Memorem Veneris Proserpina Adonim.] Ausonius fabellam aspicit, quæ est ista. Venus jam olim puerum hunc deamaverat, & ut sola fruretur, clàm depositurat apud Proserpinam. Sed hæc mox in eadem flammâ : ac repetenti Veneri negat dare. Lis est, itur ad Jovem. Ille rem sic componit, ut Adonis, quod ad usum, in tres anni partes secaretur. Primâ, ut Adonis, Adonidis esset: secundâ, Veneris: tertiâ, Proserpinæ. Acquieverunt. sed enim Adonis pronior in Venerem, suum quoque trientem illi tribuit. Hæc Apollodorus lib. III. Bibliothecæ. Ergo istud est, quod Proserpina nunc cruce vindicat. Theocritus & ipse huc aspexit. Eidyll. xv.
units.tr: Page 18, lines 5 and 6. Proserpina reminds Adonis of Venus.] Ausonius has in mind the story that follows. Venus had long ago fallen in love with this boy, and, wishing to enjoy him alone, secretly entrusted him to Proserpina. But Proserpina soon burned with the same flame, and when Venus asked for him back, she refused to give him up. They quarrelled and went to Jupiter. He settled the matter so that Adonis, as far as his use was concerned, should be divided into the three parts of the year: in the first he would belong to Adonis himself, in the second to Venus, and in the third to Proserpina. They agreed. But Adonis, being more inclined towards Venus, gave her his own third as well. This is in Apollodorus, Library, book III. So this is what Proserpina now claims by the cross. Theocritus also looked to this, Idyll xv.
Ἐξ-

units.la: Ἐ͂ξπεας, ὦ φίλ' Ἀδῶνι, ᾗ ἐνθάδε κ'εἰς Ἀ'χίεοῦσα Ἠμιθέων, ὡς φασι, μοναχαλ ᾧ.
units.tr: Ἔξεις, ὦ φίλε Ἄδωνι, ἢ ἐνθάδε κ' εἰς Ἀχέροντα, ἡμιθέων, ὡς φασι, μοῦνος ἁ ... [Ἔξεις, ὦ φίλε Ἄδωνι, ἢ ἐνθάδε κ' εἰς Ἀχέροντα, ἡμιθέων, ὡς φασι, μοῦνος ἀ...]

units.la: Migras, ô bone Adoni, isthuc & ad infera regna, Semideum, ut dicunt, solus.
units.tr: You go, dear Adonis, even there, to the kingdom below, alone, as they say, of the demigods.

units.la: Nam vult non alteri concessum, ut modò ad inferos, modò ad superos iret, & alternis copiam sui faceret duabus deabus.
units.tr: For he means that it was not granted to another to go now to the dead below, now to the living above, and to make himself available to the two goddesses in turn.

units.la: Pag. 19. lin. 8. Arbores recisas leviter.] Ad has, vel ad nudum alium stipitem, allusit Quintius in epigrammate quo poëtam Græculum facetè est ultus. Ille Philippum & Macedones insigni victoriâ fregerat, cujus laudem ad Ætolos transferre Alcæus quispiam voluit Græcâ levitate. Scilicet quia in auxiliis Romanis fuerant Ætoli. Scripserat igitur.
units.tr: Page 19, line 8. Trees lightly cut.] Quinctius alluded to these, or to a bare stump, in an epigram with which he gently avenged himself on a little Greek poet. That poet had broken Philip and the Macedonians with a remarkable victory, and some Alcaeus wanted to transfer the praise for it to the Aetolians, with Greek lightness. Clearly this was because the Aetolians had been among the Roman auxiliaries. So he had written:

units.la: Ἀ'κλαυσοι ἡ ἀδακρύσι, οἶ ἐπιοῖς, τῷ ἀλ' ἐπὶ τύμβῳ.
units.tr: Ἄκλαυστοι ἀδάκρυτοι, ἄταφοι, ἐπὶ ... ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τύμβῳ ...
Θεσ-

units.la: Θεσσαλίας, πεισαι κέρμεθα μυ-ελάδες, • Αἰολᾶν ἐμηθέντες ὑπ' Ἀγεσῶ, ἀδὲ Λατίνων, Οὓς Τίτῳ ἐυξέης ἤγαγ' ἀπ' Ἰταλίας. Indefleti, inhumati, his campis ecce jacemus Theffalia, cæsi millia ter decies, Ætolo domiti sub Marte, & Marte Latino, Quos Titus è latâ duxerat Italiâ.
units.tr: Θεσσαλίας, πεδίοις κείμεθα μυρίαδες, Αἰτωλῶν ὑπ' Ἄρεος ἐμηθέντες, ἠδὲ Λατίνων, οὓς Τίτος εὐρείης ἤγαγ' ἀπ' Ἰταλίης. [Θεσσαλίας πεδίοις κείμεθα μυρίαδες, ... Λατίνων ...] Unburied, unwept, unmourned, here in these Thessalian plains we lie, thirty thousand slain, beaten down by Aetolian and by Latin Mars, whom Titus had led from broad Italy.

units.la: In Ætolos Romanis præpositos, & quasi hi accessio illorum. Momordit Titum, & ultus est, sed versus versu, Rescripsit alludens: Αἰφλοι Θ ἐφυμῷ, ὀδοιπόςς, πὶ ἀ' ἐπὶ νάτῳ Αλκαίῳ ταωξὸς πὴ [?] ἡλίσατῷ :
units.tr: This is aimed at the Aetolians placed under the Romans, as if they were an addition to them. He bit at Titus, and took revenge, but verse answered verse; he replied in allusion: Αἰτωλοί ... ὁδοιπόρε ... Ἀλκαίου ... σταυρὸς ἀερία [Αἰτωλοί, ὀδοιπόρε, ... Ἀλκαίου ... σταυρός ...]
I Cor-

units.la: Corticibusque & fronde carens, hac monte, viator, Alcæo crux defigitur aëria.
units.tr: Stripped of bark and leaf, traveller, on this mountain the aerial cross of Alcaeus is fixed.

units.la: Quibus versibus significat crucem defixam ibi stare, quæ hominem illum exspectet. Plutarchum in Quinctio lege: & simul nota, altam hic Crucem poni, quasi in scelere insigni suo loco à nobis dictum.
units.tr: By these verses he means that a cross fixed there stands waiting for that man. Read Plutarch in his Life of Quinctius; and at the same time note that a high cross is set up here, as I have said elsewhere, in its proper place, for a notorious crime.

units.la: Pag. 21. lin. 17. Ipsidem vero Cererem. Ipse Tertullianus hoc affirmat, de Corona militis: Prima Isis repertas spicas capite circumtulit.nam quæ hæc Isis quæ spicas repperit, nisi Ceres?
units.tr: Page 21, line 17. Ceres herself indeed. Tertullian himself affirms this, in his De corona militis: Isis first carried the ears of corn she had found around her head. For who is this Isis who found the ears of corn, if not Ceres?
ON CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Pag. 24. lin. 19. & 20. Nescio an Mæcenati descripta. Ambiguè profero, quia etsi Mæcenatis verba nobis faciunt, vix tamen Senecæ, qui velut interpretans subdit: Suffigas licet, & acutam sesuro (ita legendum, non sensuro) crucem subdas, est tanti vulnus suum prepremere & patibulo pendere districtum. Atqui pendere, & patibulo quidem, vix est ut conveniat in nostram Acutam. Nisi si tamen patibulum etiam de uno ligno, in quo homo quomodocumque expansus : quod haud nimis velim sperni. Si displicet : alia interpretatio quærenda sit crucis hïc acuta. An ideò talis, quia cum dolore acri necat ? ut morbi quidam acuti medicis. Lente probem : & mavelim opinari genus aliquod crucium triste, rarum, in quo stipes, cui homo acclinatur, stimulis clavisque acutus sit præfixus.ut cùm acquiescere vellet(sesfuri vox in Seneca) pungeretur ac scinderetur in corpore averso. Nihil super hoc legi,fateor: commentum est merum, nisi si quid juvat illa Reguli machina, quæ sic armata, & in eam ipse inclusus. Quæ etsi nostra crux non fuit (aumarium potiùs quoddam & arca (tamen & crucem Seneca appellavit epistolâ xcv i i i. itemque libro de Providentiâ cap. i i i. Certè quidem Acuta vocem in Mæcenatis versibus non sic leviter & in ventum additam, ipse indicat Seneca, qui eam attollit ac repetit (tu vide) quasi in eâ sententiæ momentum.
units.tr: Page 24, lines 19 and 20. I do not know whether it was written down by Maecenas.] I put this forward with doubt, because although the words are Maecenas's, they hardly seem to be Seneca's, who, as if interpreting them, adds: Though you fix me to it and set beneath me the sharp cross (read sensurus, not sesuro), it is worth it to suppress one's own wound and hang stretched out on the gibbet. But that "hang" and "gibbet" hardly fit with our "sharp". Unless, indeed, the gibbet was also a single piece of wood on which a man was stretched out in some way; I would not very much like that to be dismissed. If that does not please, another interpretation must be sought for "sharp" in this cross. Is it perhaps called so because it kills with sharp pain, as some acute diseases do for doctors? I would rather not approve this lightly; I would prefer to suppose some sad and rare kind of crucifixion, in which the upright post to which the man is bent is sharpened with spikes and nails, so that when he wished to rest (sesfuri is the word in Seneca) he was pierced and torn in the body turned away. I admit I have read nothing on this; it is pure invention, unless perhaps the machine of Regulus helps, which was so armed, and in which he himself was shut up. Although this was not our cross (it was rather a kind of chest or coffin), Seneca nevertheless called it a cross, in Epistle 98 and likewise in book On Providence, chapter 3. Certainly Seneca himself shows that the word acuta in the verses of Maecenas was not added lightly and for nothing, since he picks it up and repeats it (look for yourself), as if the weight of the sentence lay in it.

units.la: Pag. 24. lin. 21. & 22. Jam olim sic legimus.] Nempe in curis secundis : idque e libris tantùm? imò ante me Pincianus, vir fidei & judicii bonus. Muretus tamen aliter : sed qui bene examinat, stabit à nostrâ. cujus sententia, Hanc vitam mihi sustine & proroga, etiam sedenti in acutâ cruce.
units.tr: Page 24, lines 21 and 22. We have read it thus for a long time.] Namely in the Secondary Notes; and that from books only? Indeed, before me Pincianus, a man of good faith and good judgment, did so. Muretus, however, reads otherwise; but whoever examines carefully will side with ours, whose opinion is: Sustain and prolong this life for me, even when I am sitting on the sharp cross.
ON CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Pag. 26. lin. 16. & 17. Ipsi vertunt ξύλον διδυμον.] Quod ipsum pro cruce posuit incertus scriptor apud Suidam: Ε‘κεὰν ὃ Ι’ʹΜΕΣΤΟΝ φθο-γίη, ςκεῖμενον ἐπὶ διδύμῳ ξύλῳ : Invenens niens Illustrum corruptorem, suspendit in gemino ligno. Id est cruce: etsi Suidas interpretatur, τὴν πεξὰ Γ'ω-μαίοις φᾶξιαν. Vide ipsum in voce Αἰδυμον, & Γ'λξ [?].
units.tr: Page 26, lines 16 and 17. They render it "a double wood" (ξύλον δίδυμον). The unknown writer quoted by Suidas uses this same phrase for the cross: "Having found the corrupter of the Illustrious, he hung him on a double wood." [Ἐκεὰν ὃ ... ἐπὶ διδύμῳ ξύλῳ] That is, the cross, although Suidas explains it as "the Roman fasces" [τὴν παρὰ Ῥωμαίοις φᾶξιαν]. See the passage itself under the word Δίδυμον, and Γλὼξ [?].

units.la: Pag.28.lin.22.&23. Vt Christum deformantes.] Puto scribendum, ut chi deformantes. Intelligo X. litteram Græcanicam, quæ verè figura manuum illarum fuit.
units.tr: Page 28, lines 22 and 23. As those who deform Christ. I think it should be written ut chi deformantes. I understand the Greek letter X (chi), which truly was the figure of those hands.
ON CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Pag.32.lin.17.&18. Penulæ aut manui.] In penulâ aut veste Monachorum crux, imò & cruces, si rectè capio Nicephorum Gregoram, qui sic de Imp. Andronico monacho novello: Λ'τω μὲν ἐχυδηδὴν πεσούθηκε τὸν τῆ Θέᾳ ϛαυρῆ τύ-πον, κάτω ἡ μέλαινα: Superne rubrum prætulit divina crucis signum, inferne nigrum. Duas diversi coloris cruces appositas videtur dicere: nisi tamen unam intelligit, sic distinctam. Quod manu autem tulerint, hodieque in Æthiopibus sive Abyssinis ille moş, uti vulgus reliquum cruces è collo pendulas gestet, monachi hoc ampliùs etiam manu. Auctor Damianus à Goës in illorum rebus. Illud etiam mihi novitium lêgi, miseros oppressosque cruces prætulisse, haud aliter quàm olim infulas & velamenta. Ligurinus lib. viii. de Italis hoc notat, qui jus auxiliumque poscebant ab Imp. Frederico: ex omnibus undique multi Vrbibus ac vicis aderant, queruloloque ferebant Innumeras clamore cruces. hoc quippe querelas More solent aperire suas.
units.tr: Page 32, lines 17 and 18. On the cloak or on the hand. On the cloak or garment of the monks there was a cross, indeed crosses, if I understand Nicephorus Gregoras rightly, who says this of the emperor Andronicus, a novice monk: "Above he had placed a red sign of the divine cross, below a black one" [Ἄνω μὲν ἐρυθρὸν ... κάτω δὲ μέλαιναν]. He seems to say that two crosses of different colours were placed one above the other, unless he means one cross, so marked. As for their carrying it in the hand, that custom survives today among the Ethiopians, or Abyssinians. The rest of the common people wear crosses hanging from the neck, but the monks carry them even more in the hand. Damian à Goës writes of their affairs. I have also read something new to me: that wretched and oppressed people carried crosses before them, much as in former times they bore fillets and veils. Ligurinus, book 8, on the Italians, notes this, when they sought law and help from the emperor Frederick: "From all sides many came from the cities and villages, and with loud complaint they bore countless crosses; for in this way they are accustomed to lay open their grievances."

units.la: Pag.33. lin.1. & 2. Cum anulo vel ansulâ. ] Ansulam Becanus facit, & interpretatur (ita ingenuum & scopus viri fuit) μυρινῶς, quasi moneamur apprehendere
units.tr: Page 33, lines 1 and 2. With a ring or a little ring. Becanus takes the little ring (ansula) and explains it, as was his nature and aim, as "a sign of the hand" [μυρινῶς], as if we were being reminded to grasp

units.la: crucem, & eam tenere. Quid si oculum esse dicam? Juvat aliquid Macrobius, qui inter notas Ægyptiacas refert, & significare ait Solem. Lib. I. Saturn. cap. xxI. Osirim Ægyptii ut Solem esse asserant, quoties Hieroglyphicis litteris suis exprimere volunt, insculpunt sceptrum, inque eo speciem Oculi exprimunt, & hoc signo Osirim monstrant: quia Solem, Iovis oculum, appellavit antiquitas. Et sanè quia signum hoc Tau Vitam venturam designavit: nónne appositè Sol ascriptus, qui auctor vitæ?
units.tr: the cross and hold it. What if I say it is an eye? Macrobius helps a little, who lists it among Egyptian signs and says it signifies the Sun. Book 1 of the Saturnalia, chapter 21: "The Egyptians, whenever they wish to express Osiris in their hieroglyphic letters, assert that he is the Sun. They carve a sceptre and in it represent the likeness of an eye, and by this sign they show Osiris, because antiquity called the Sun the eye of Jupiter." And surely, since this Tau sign designated the life to come, is not the Sun appropriately added, who is the author of life?
ON CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Pag. 36. lin. 14. Unicornis enim cornua.] Curiosè & pænè dixerim morosè explicat Justinus. simplicius multò Tertullianus adversf. Jud. cap. x. Tauri decor ejus, cornua unicornis cornua ejus, in eis nationes ventilabit pariter usque ad summum terræ. Non utique I 4 Rhi-
units.tr: Page 36, line 14. For the horns of the unicorn. Justin explains this in a curious, and I might almost say a tiresome, way. Tertullian, in Against the Jews, chapter 10, is much simpler: "His beauty is that of a bull, his horns the horns of a unicorn; with them he will winnow the nations together to the ends of the earth." Not indeed that
Page 36, line 14.

units.la: Rhinoceros destinabatur unicornis, nec Minotaurus bicornis: sed Christus in illo significabatur: cujus cornua essent crucis extrema. Nam & in antenna navis, quâ crucis pars est, hæc extremitates hujuscornua vocantur; unicornis autem medii Stipitis palus.
units.tr: the rhinoceros was meant as the unicorn, nor the Minotaur as the two-horned beast; but Christ was signified in it, whose horns were the ends of the cross. For also on the yard of a ship, which forms part of a cross, its ends are called the horns; the unicorn, however, is the post of the central stake.

units.la: Pag.41.l.11. * Αλων μὲν τῇ τροπαίων. ] Mutilus locus: & aptant quidem hæc ad tropæa vulgaria, sive monumenta victoriæ: ego cum in verba intendo, ambigo: & nescio quid de fascibus potiùs subolet dictum. Per illos (ita verterim τὶ ὧν) progressus in publicum fiunt: illi verè signa imperii & potestatis. Atque cum infertâ securi, crucem referunt planissimè. Nónne etiam Tropæa? inquies. Quis nescit? sed præivit fortasse aliquid de Tropæis illis: hic magis de fascibus (mihi quidem) dixisse videtur. Nec moveor quod Τροπαίων voce utatur: nónne & suprà Malum in navi sic vocavit? & Eusebius etiam Labarum
units.tr: Page 41, line 11. "Other things are for the trophies" (Ἀλλων μὲν τὰ τροπαίων). The passage is mutilated. They apply it indeed to ordinary trophies, or monuments of victory; but when I attend to the words, I am uncertain, and something about the fasces seems rather to be meant. "Through these" (so I would translate τὶ ὧν) "progress into public view": these are truly the signs of empire and power. And since they carry an axe fixed in them, they very plainly resemble a cross. Will you say also trophies? Who does not know? But perhaps he had something earlier about those trophies; here he seems to me to speak rather of the fasces. Nor am I troubled that he uses the word trophies (Τροπαίων); did he not also call the mast of a ship a trophy? And Eusebius too calls the

units.la: Irum illum militarem. Possunt & verba alia excidisse. Nec pono tamen ista, sed propono.
units.tr: Labarum that military standard. Other words may have dropped out. I do not, however, assert these things, but only put them forward.

units.la: Pa.41.l.15. A'νλοκραλέ-ων ἀπoθνησκόντων τὰς εἰκό-νας. Quæ illę sunt? quis me docet? In Nummis, in statuis nihil tale video, nec usquam in cruce propositos Principes defunctos. Subdubitabam an ad aquilas respiceret, quæ volantium habitu, & in cælum tendentium passis aliis conspiciuntur in Nummis, & additum Consecratio. Scilicet quasi Jovis illa ales animam defuncti ferret in gremium Jovis. Certè quidem eam formam crucis esse & Patres monent & res ipsa docet. Sed non placet. Hoc nunc magis, intelligere eum imagines defunctorum Principum, quæ ordine innexæ in militaribus signis. Nec enim vivorum solùm illìc effigies, sed magis mortuorum. De isto ipso ævo Constantini Eusebius, lib. II. De vitâ ejus, cap. XVI. Describit Licinii milites in pugnam, more veterum, id est, gentilium exeuntes: οἱ δὲ, inquit, πολυπληθίᾳ θεῶν θαρρῶντες σὺν πολλῇ δωμάτιι χιλιὸς τρωτὸν ἐπήσεσαν, νικᾶν ἴδωλα δαιμόνων ἐν ἀψύχοις ἐγκλήμασι ἀπεσπλαγχνίσι. Hi quidem numero deorum freti cum multâ manu militari ingruebant, mortuorum imagines in signis inanimatis præferentes. Et scripsi de hoc more in Militia Romanâ. Ergo hoc Justinus exprobrat, Vos, inquit, cruces colitis, cùm Imperatorum & quidem Divorum imagines proponitis in hastis & vexillis, quid nisi in crucibus? Nam ea illis figura. Respexi etiam aliquando ad Tertullianum, in Apologetico: Quod non simulacrum prius argilla deformat, cruci & stipiti superposiposita? Sed hoc diffusum nimis est, nec tangit Imperatores tantum.
units.tr: Page 41, line 15. "Of the images of those who died" (ἀποθνησκόντων τὰς εἰκόνας). What are these? Who will teach me? On coins and in statues I see nothing of the kind, nor anywhere do dead emperors appear placed on a cross. I wondered whether he was looking at the eagles, which appear on coins in the form of birds flying and rising to heaven with outspread wings, with the addition Consecratio. Evidently that bird of Jupiter carried the soul of the dead man into Jupiter's bosom. Certainly the Fathers remind us, and the thing itself shows, that this is indeed the form of the cross; but I do not like it. It is better now to understand him as meaning the images of dead emperors, which were joined in order on the military standards. For there were displayed there not only the likenesses of the living, but still more those of the dead. Of this very age of Constantine, Eusebius, book 2 of his Life of Constantine, chapter 16, describes the soldiers of Licinius going into battle in the manner of the ancients, that is, the pagans: "They, trusting in the multitude of their gods, advanced with a large military force, bearing in their standards the images of dead demons, lifeless emblems." [οἱ δὲ ... ἐπήσεσαν ... ἀπεσπλαγχνίσι]. I have written about this custom in my Roman Military. Therefore Justin reproaches them thus: "You worship crosses, when you display the images of emperors, and indeed of deified ones, on spears and banners; what are these but crosses? For that is their shape." I once looked also to Tertullian in the Apology: "What image does not form the clay placed over a cross and stake?" But this is too wide a matter, and does not touch the emperors alone.
ON CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Pag. 50. lin. 10. & 11. Caput obnubito.] Quod plerisque puniendis factum, præsertim si gladio. Hegesippus lib. v. c. XLVII. Dum percussor moratur, clausis jam fasciola oculis, sese proripuit ad Romanos. In vita Cypriani: Postea vero B. Cyprianus manu sua oculos sibi texit. Sed & cum ducerentur ad carcerem, aut ad mortem, caput tegebatur. Tacitus IV. Annal. Trahebatur damnatus, quantum obducta veste & adstrictis faucibus niti poterat clamitans. Ammianus lib. XIV. Carnifex rapinarum sequester, & obductio capitum, & bonorum ubique multatio. Imo & torquendis hoc factum. In Curtio lib. VI. de Philota. Dum obligantur oculi, dum vestis exuitur, deos patrios, gentium jura invocabat.
units.tr: Page 50, lines 10–11. Caput obnubito. This was done to most of those who were to be punished, especially those beheaded. Hegesippus, book 5, ch. 47: While the executioner delayed, with a little cloth already bound over his eyes, he broke away to the Romans. In the Life of Cyprian: Afterwards, however, the blessed Cyprian covered his eyes with his own hand. But also, when they were led to prison or to death, the head was covered. Tacitus, Annals book 4: The condemned man was dragged along, shouting as loudly as he could with his garment drawn over him and his throat constricted. Ammianus, book 14: The executioner, the agent of plunder, and the covering of heads, and the fining of goods everywhere. Indeed, this was also done to those being tortured. In Curtius, book 6, on Philotas: While his eyes were being bound and his clothing stripped off, he called upon the gods of his fathers and the laws of the nations.

units.la: Proprie autem de crucifigendis, vetus illud carmen quod jam explico : & in libro Esther, cùm Aman ad crucem rapitur, Statim operuerunt faciem ejus.
units.tr: But properly speaking, of those being crucified, there is that old verse which I am now explaining; and in the book of Esther, when Haman is dragged to the cross: They at once covered his face.

units.la: Pag. 50. lin. 12. & 13. Populariter & ad caussam Cicero dixerit.] Quòd historicâ fide, non opinor. Plinius non ei fautor libro xxxvi. cap. xv. Novum & inexcogitatum antea posteaque remedium invenit ille rex (Tarquinius superbus) ut omnium ita defunctorum figeret crucibus corpora, spectanda civibus, simul & feris volucribusque laceranda. Nam liquet eum loqui de mortuis & iis qui se interficerent laborum taedio, quos ille crucifixit. Ad non id in vivis usurpavit primus, ut ait, ultimusque.
units.tr: Page 50, lines 12–13. Cicero spoke in a popular way, and in a legal case. That this is true to historical fact, I do not think. Pliny is no supporter of it, book 36, ch. 15: That king (Tarquin the Proud) devised a new remedy, unthought of before or since: to fix the bodies of all the dead to crosses, to be viewed by the citizens and at the same time torn apart by wild beasts and birds. For it is clear that he is speaking of the dead, and of those who killed themselves from weariness of life, whom that king crucified. He did not, as Pliny says, first and last use it on the living.

units.la: Pag. 51. lin. 6. Arboribus suspendunt.] Haud injuriâ ambigo, ad utram poenam referam, laquei, an Crucis. Nam nec verba ba alterutrum evincunt, nec alia exempla. Lego in Martyrologio, die xiv. Martii, de duobus Monachis, quos Longobardi suspendio necaverunt in arbore. In ipsis Longobardorum Legibus, Tit. cap. xiv. Si servus regis Morth fecerit, ita decrevimus ut componatur ipsa persona sicut adpreciatus fuerit : & servus ipse super fossam mortui appendatur, & in eum vindicta detur, & sit caussa finita. Plurium (antiquorum quidem) nunc non memini : & hæc ipsa incerta, nec dijudicaverint litem.
units.tr: Page 51, line 6. They hang them on trees. I am not without doubt as to which punishment I should assign it to, the noose or the Cross. For neither the words nor other examples settle the matter one way or the other. I read in the Martyrology, on 14 March, of two monks whom the Lombards put to death by hanging on a tree. In the Laws of the Lombards themselves, Title ..., ch. 14: If the king's slave Morth commits (a crime), we have decreed that the person himself be compensated at the value he was assessed; and that the slave himself be hanged over the grave of the dead man, and vengeance be given against him, and the case be ended. I do not now recall more examples from the ancients; and these very examples are uncertain, nor have they decided the dispute.

units.la: JUSTI LIPSII NOTÆ AD LIB. II.
units.tr: Notes of Justus Lipsius on Book II.
CHAPTER III.

units.la: PAg. 71. lin. 6. & 7. A'τεχ-γαλωλὰς μάστιγας.] Addo, si nosse lubet, quasdam etiam dictas τεχγ[αλωτὰς, istis haud absimiles, contortas scilicet & nodosas Suidas: τεχγ[αλιῶδες, διεσεχμμένον. Καὶ τεχγ[αλωτὴ μάστιξ. Addit deinde verba incerti scriptoris: Οἱ δὲ εὐ-λίνσιν αὐτὸν μαστιγῶς τῆς τεχγ[αλωτῆ μάστιγι.
units.tr: On p. 71, lines 6 and 7: [τεχγαλωτὰς] μάστιγας. If you care to know, I add that some scourges were also called τεχγαλωτάς [techgalōtas], much like these, that is, twisted and knotted. Suidas: τεχγαλιῶδες [techgaliōdes], "split apart." And τεχγαλωτὴ μάστιξ [techgalōtē mastix], "knotted scourge." He then adds the words of an unnamed writer: "Others scourged him with the knotted scourge" [τῆς τεχγαλωτῆ μάστιγι].
ON CHAPTER V.

units.la: Pag. 78. lin. 13. & 14. Quid opus erat auxiliatore & subsequa, qui adlevassēt?] Ita vulgata quidem opinio est, dumtaxat adlevasse. At D. Hieronymus in Matthæum censet etiam tulisse, sed seorsim & post Christum. Nam cum Joannes aperte scribat Christum tulisse, alii tres Evangelistæ Simonem Cyrenæum: ipse conciliat, & hoc intelligendum est, inquit, quod egrediens de Prætorio Iesus ipse portaverit Crucem suam: postea obvium habuerint Simonem, cui portandam crucem impososuerunt.
units.tr: On p. 78, lines 13 and 14: "What need was there for a helper and a follower, who would have lifted it?" The common opinion is that he merely lifted it. But Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, thinks that Simon also carried it, but separately and after Christ. For while John plainly writes that Christ carried the cross, the other three Evangelists name Simon of Cyrene. Jerome reconciles them: "This must be understood thus," he says, "that Jesus himself, going out of the Praetorium, carried his own cross; afterwards they met Simon, on whom they laid the cross to be carried."
ON CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Pag. 82. lin. 11. & 12. Super lignum se ipsum extendit.] Quid is de transversario tantum ligno capias, in eo figi solitos, & deinde subduci atque appendi? Pugna omnis cessetl; & breviter fortasse rem dixi.
units.tr: On p. 82, lines 11 and 12: "He stretched himself upon the wood." Should you take this as referring only to the transverse beam, to which they were usually fixed and then drawn down and hung up? All the dispute then falls away. Perhaps I have stated the matter briefly.
ON CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Pag. 87. lin. 5. Clavis aut sunibus.] Nescio an Lucanus non utrosque memoret in his occultioris sententiæ versibus: qui quoniam toti ad crucem, ponamus, & retegamus. Lib. 6. de magâ Thessalâ, — Laqueum nodosque nocentes Ore suo rupit, pendentia corpora carpsit, Abrasitque cruces, percussaque viscera nimbis Vulsit, & incoctas admisso Sole medullas: Incertum manibus chalybem, nigramque per artus Stillantis tabi saniem, virusque coactum Sustulit, & nervo morsus retinente pependit.
units.tr: On p. 87, line 5: "Nails or ropes." I do not know whether Lucan does not mention both in these verses of a rather hidden meaning, which, since they all refer to the cross, let us set out and explain. Book 6, on the Thessalian witch: "With her own mouth she broke the noose and the guilty knots; she tore at the hanging bodies and scraped the crosses, and from the storm-struck flesh she pulled the inner marrow baked by the sun. The iron, not known to her hands, and the black pus of the dripping rot through the limbs, and the forced poison, she took up, and hung there, while the sinew held the bite."

units.la: Quod ait laqueum & nodos nocentes: alii nocentum edunt: atque ita haud incommodè ad vincula aptes, quibus noxii ad cruces astricti. Tamen in aliquot scriptis libris, recentes. & id malim: credamque ad suspendiosos dumtaxat referendum, & qui seipsos illaqueaverunt. Reliqua jam de Cruce: & percussa viscera nimbis, & incoctas sole medullas. signanter dixit de corporibus quæ (ut lib. II. cap. xv. scripsi) in crucibus relicta, situ marcida & tabida fiebant, quatenus volucres non laniarent. Jam Incertum manibus chalybem, clavos intelligi liquebit, si emendes Insertum. Nam hos quoque appetitos ad Magicas artes Apuleius ostendit, in describenda feralí illâ officina, lib. III. Hic nares & digiti, illic carnosi clavi pendentium. Sed & amplius de his funibus addo. Videri, quorundam judicio, necessarios fuisse in omni fixione. Nam volunt manus ligatas, ne se subducerent ad ictum aut commoverent. tum etiam ut firmius & cum adminiculo pendérent. deinde & alterum funem ad pectus, corpus ambiisse sub ipsas alas, eoque sublevatum hominem & attractum in summam crucem. Id porrò factum admotis utrimque scalis. Ejus sententiæ vir stirpe & moribus antiquis Joannes Boisso-
units.tr: As for his words laqueum et nodos nocentes ("the noose and the guilty knots"), others print nocentum ("of the guilty"), which fits fairly well with the bonds by which the guilty were tied to the crosses. Yet in some manuscripts it is recentes ("fresh"), and I would prefer that reading, and I believe it refers only to those who were hanged and who had entangled themselves. As to the rest, now about the cross: percussa viscera nimbis ("the flesh struck by storms") and incoctas sole medullas ("the marrow baked by the sun"), he spoke pointedly of the bodies which, as I wrote in Book II, chapter 15, were left on the crosses, and became withered and rotten through neglect, so that birds would not tear them. Now, that Incertum manibus chalybem ("the iron unknown to her hands") means the nails will be clear if you emend it to Insertum ("inserted"). For Apuleius also shows that these were sought for magical arts, in his description of that grim workshop, Book III: "Here noses and fingers, there the fleshy nails of the hanging men." But I add more about these ropes. It seems, in the judgment of some, that they were necessary in every fixing. For they want the hands bound, so that they would not withdraw from the blow or move; then also so that they hung more firmly and with support. Next, another rope went round the chest and body just beneath the armpits, and by this the man was raised and drawn up to the top of the cross. This was done, moreover, with ladders set up on both sides. Of this opinion is Joannes Boissotus, a man of ancient lineage and manners, who kindly suggested it to me.

units.la: Boisotus est, qui amicè hoc suggessit. Et sanè de scalis, apponere eas pænè necessarium videtur, utique ad Erectam crucem. Quomodo aliàs subduxeris, aut fixeris? Etiam de funibus sunt quæ suadeant, præter ante dicta. ut Hilarius de Trinitate lib. x. Penduli in cruce corporis pœna, & colligantium funium violenta vincula, & adactorum clavorum vulnera. Jungit simul & funes & clavos, ut Lucanus. Etiam illud Christi vaticinium in Petri mortem, poscit funes. Joannis cap. xix. Extendet manus tuas, & alius te cinget. Cinctio ista vinculorum in cruce est, Theophylactus: Τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ σταυρῷ ἐκτασιν ... διὰ τὰ δεσμὰ δηλοῖ: Extensionem in cruce & vincula notat. Tertullianus in Scorpiaco: Tunc Petrus ab altero cingitur, cùm cruci adstringitur. Videndum an non in Ausonii Cupidine simile, qui adstrictus describitur, & mox addit
units.tr: Boisotus is the one who kindly suggested this. And indeed, about ladders: it seems almost necessary to set them up, certainly for raising the cross upright. Otherwise how would you have drawn him down, or fixed him? There are also things about ropes that support this, besides what was said above: as Hilary says in On the Trinity, Book 10: "The punishment of a body hanging on the cross, and the violent bonds of the ropes that bound it, and the wounds of the nails driven in." He joins ropes and nails together, as Lucan does. Also Christ's prophecy of Peter's death calls for ropes: John 21: "Another shall gird you, and you shall stretch out your hands." This binding is, according to Theophylact, on the cross: [Τὴν ἐπὶ τῷ σταυρῷ ἐκτασιν ... διὰ τὰ δεσμὰ δηλοῖ] "He signifies the stretching out on the cross ... by means of the bonds." Tertullian in Scorpiace: "Then Peter is girded by another, when he is bound to the cross." It should be considered whether there is not something similar in Ausonius's Cupid, where he is described as bound, and immediately adds

units.la: Marginal note fragments at the left, partly covered by the plate: "A" / "fchyl[?]" / "μασ[?]" / "λισ[?]" / "appel[?]" / "lat[?]" / "Prom[?]" / "theo[?]". dit, cAdfigunt. Atque ecce in tabulâ formam duplicem fixionis, pro duplici subductione.
units.tr: Fragments of marginal notes at the left, partly covered by the plate: "A," "fchyl[?]," "μασ[?]," "λισ[?]," "appel[?]," "lat[?]," "Prom[?]," "theo[?]." ... "they fasten him." And see, in the plate, a twofold form of fixing, corresponding to the twofold lowering.

units.la: Pag. 90. lin. 14. Tres reperit. ] An & duas latronum transtulit, non cultus sed memoriæ causâ? Videtur ex Suidâ, si tamen ex meo nunc sensu corrigendus. In voce φόρος inquit : Κάτωθεν τῆς φόρας κεχωρισμένοι ὑπὸ ἐχθρῶν δύο σταυρηγοὶ τῶν δύο λῃστῶν, καὶ βίαιον μόρος ὢ ἡλέψαλο ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ πολλὰ ἐπὶ σημειοφορικά, τιθεῖσθαι μὲν παρὰ Κωνσταντίνῳ τῷ μεγάλῳ, ἀφανισθέντα ὑπὸ τῆς μεγάλης Θεοδοσίου :
units.tr: On p. 90, line 14: "He finds three." Did he also transfer two of the robbers, not for ornament but for the sake of memory? It seems to come from Suidas, if it is to be corrected by my present understanding. Under the word phoros he says: [Κάτωθεν τῆς φόρας κεχωρισμένοι ὑπὸ ἐχθρῶν δύο σταυρηγοὶ τῶν δύο λῃστῶν, καὶ βίαιον μόρος ὢ ἡλέψαλο ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ πολλὰ ἐπὶ σημειοφορικά, τιθεῖσθαι μὲν παρὰ Κωνσταντίνῳ τῷ μεγάλῳ, ἀφανισθέντα ὑπὸ τῆς μεγάλης Θεοδοσίου] "Below the forum, separated by enemies, were two crosses of the two robbers, and the vessel of unguent with which Christ was anointed, and many other signs, set up by Constantine the Great, and removed under the great Theodosius."

units.la: Nam puto legendum δύο σταυροί. Qui verò fuerint σταυρηγοί, sive duces duorum latronum? nec id sit idonei ullius sensus. Vertam igitur : Infra forum defossa erant duæ cruces duorum latronum, & vasculum unguenti quo Christus unctus, & alia multa insignia, posita quidem à Constantino magno, sublata verò sub Theodosio magno. Admonitus postea per litteras sum à Joanne
units.tr: For I think δύο σταυροί ("two crosses") should be read. But who the σταυρηγοί were, or whether they were "leaders of the two robbers," is unclear, and it makes no sense in any case. I shall therefore translate: "Below the forum were buried the two crosses of the two robbers, and a small vessel of ointment with which Christ was anointed, and many other notable objects, placed there by Constantine the Great and removed under Theodosius the Great." Later, having been reminded by letter by our friend Joannes

units.la: Livineio amico nostro, serió & sine ambitione docto, vitium esse ab imperitia transcriptorum qui cum in autographo repperissent ῥε̃ι, quod compendiaria scriptura ῥωμεῖ erat, fecerunt flagitiosè ῥεμ-πηγοί.
units.tr: Livineius, a man learned in earnest and without ostentation, I learned that the fault came from the ignorance of copyists. When they found in the autograph ῥεῖ, which in compendious writing stood for ῥωμεῖ, they shamefully wrote ῥεμπηγοί [rempēgoi].
TO CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Pag. 92. lin. 1. ᾿Αμιτεμτὰ δὲ.] Ita benè & doctè Franc. Nansius, cùm antea essent ὀμ.τεμτα. Et sanè clavi isti grandes: atque ita ipse Nonnus idemtidem σιδήρια κίντρα appellat Stimulos ferreos.
units.tr: Page 92, line 1: "Amitemta de [Ἀμιτεμτὰ δέ]." Thus well and learnedly Franciscus Nansius, when the text previously read "omtemta [ὀμ.τεμτα]." And indeed these are large nails, and so Nonnus himself repeatedly calls them iron goads [σιδήρια κέντρα].

units.la: Ibid. lin. 16. & 17. Contrà tendunt alii & suggerunt quaternos.] Atque ego, etsi negavi me decidere, pronior sum in hanc partem. In templis Græciæ hodie intelligo passim Christum cruci affixum, disparatis pedibus sic pingi. Vidimus id ipsi Venetiis in gentis ejus templo, tum & alibi in antiquioribus picturis. Audio & Treviris clavum qui asservatur, diserte in memoriis antiquis scribi clavum pedis dextri. Addo autem, Constantinum Imperatorem quosdam ex his clavis (id quoque multitudinem suadet) inseruisse capiti statuæ quam suo nomine Constantinopoli posuit.
units.tr: Ibid., lines 16 and 17: Others on the contrary argue for four nails. I, although I said I had not given way, am more inclined to this side. In the temples of Greece today I notice everywhere that Christ fixed to the cross is painted with his feet set apart in this way. We saw this ourselves at Venice, in the temple of that people, and also elsewhere in older pictures. I hear too that at Trier the nail which is preserved there is plainly recorded in ancient memorials as the nail of the right foot. I add that the Emperor Constantine inserted some of these nails into the head of the statue which he set up at Constantinople in his own name (the number also supports this).

units.la: Zonaras : O’δὲ Θεόδοσιος— Αὐτοκράτως εἰς οἰκίαν ὀνομα τὸ ἄγαλμα (τῆς Αὐτόλ-λων) ἔστησε, τὴν κεφαλὴν τότε τινὰς τῆλαι ἐκ ἐμοσάμφῳ, ὅτι τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Κυρίου προσῆλωσεν.
units.tr: Zonaras: But Theodosius, the Emperor, set up the statue in the house (of Autolycus?), and then some people (hung?) its head, because it had nailed the body of the Lord [Ὁ δὲ Θεοδόσιος ... Αὐτοκράτως εἰς οἰκίαν ... ἔστησε ... ὅτι τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Κυρίου προσῆλωσεν].
TO CHAPTER X.

units.la: Pag. 94. l. ult. Extensus ambas manus.] Proprium hoc Crucis, extendi. Itaque Euangeliorum vetus Gothica translatio (Auctor Antonius Morillonus) vertit idemtidem Crucifigere, Ɓstraemen/quasi dicas extendere, & quidem proprie de pannis, quos in palis vallisq; distendit fullo. Ea extensio ad manus maximè refertur. Artemidorus lib.I. cap. LXXVIII. Ἐι δέ τις ὑψηλὸς ἐπί τιν᾽ ὀχοῖτο, ὡς φόβον καὶ δίκην πιστεύτω. κακὸς ἔγω᾽ ὁ ὤν, σωθήσεται, διὰ τὸ ὕψος καὶ τὴν τ᾽ χειρῶν ἔκτασιν: Si quis sublimis in loco quopiam saltet, in periculum & metum incidet. maleficus autem existens, crucifigetur, ob altitudinem & manuum extensionem. Epictetus apud Arrianum, ab hac caussa comparat falsè eos qui in balneis se distendunt & lavandos fricandosque præbent, cum crucifixis; libro IV. Dissertat. cap. xxvi. Γ᾽ν᾽ ἐν τῇ βαλανείῳ ἐκδυσάμενος, καὶ ἐκτείνας σεαυτὸν, ὡς οἱ ἐσταυρωμένοι, τρίζῃ ἐνδὲ καὶ ἐνδὲ: Ut in balneo exutus & teipsum distendens, ut solent crucifixi, fricêris hinc atque illinc.
units.tr: Page 94, last line: Extended both hands. This is a peculiar feature of the cross: extension. Hence the old Gothic translation of the Gospels (author Antonius Morillonus) repeatedly renders "to crucify" by a Gothic word meaning to stretch out, as one might say; and it is used properly of cloths which the fuller stretches on poles and posts. That extension refers chiefly to the hands. Artemidorus, book 1, chapter 78: "If anyone, being high up, climbs onto some height, he will fall into danger and fear; but if he is a wrongdoer, he will be crucified, because of the height and the stretching of the hands." [Εἰ δέ τις ὑψηλὸς ἐπί τιν᾽ ὀχοῖτο ... καὶ τὴν τῶν χειρῶν ἔκτασιν]. Epictetus, in Arrian, for this reason falsely compares those who stretch themselves out in the baths and let themselves be rubbed and anointed with the crucified; book 4, Dissertation 26: "When you have undressed in the bath and stretched yourself out, as the crucified do, you are rubbed this way and that." [Γυμνωθεὶς ... ἐκτείνας σεαυτὸν, ὡς οἱ ἐσταυρωμένοι].

units.la: Pag. 100. lin.15. & 16. Vestigium hujus tabellæ exstare audio.] Imò & video: ac misit ad me Dionysius Villerius vir veteri doctrinæ & mihi valdè amicus ectypon nummi Græcanici veteris, qui aureus asservatur in monasterio Lætiensi in Hannoniâ, quem ecce habes.
units.tr: Page 100, lines 15 and 16: I hear that a trace of this little tablet survives. Indeed, I also see it. Dionysius Villerius, a man learned in the old learning and very friendly to me, sent me an impression of an old Greek coin, which is preserved in gold in the monastery of Lobbes in Hainaut. Here it is.

units.la: Inscriptio in eo est : Κόσμε τὸ λύτρον, αἷμα τῆς Θεῖς Λόγῳ : Mundi redemptio, sanguis Dei Verbi. Missus is nummus cum aliis sacris donariis est ab Henrico Imperatore, tunc Constantinopoli, anno Christi MCIↃ.CC.VIII.
units.tr: The inscription on it reads Redemption of the world, the blood of the Word of God [Κόσμε τὸ λύτρον, αἷμα τῆς Θεῖς Λόγῳ]: the redemption of the world, the blood of God the Word. This coin was sent, with other sacred gifts, by the Emperor Henry, then at Constantinople, in the year of Christ 1208.
TO CHAPTER XI.

units.la: Pag. 102. lin. 9. & 10. Πεϱιαχ-ϑεὶς κύκλῳ τᾶ ἀμφιθιάτρες.] Id di-cunt Circumduci; sicut Traduci, cùm ostentui dumtaxat per ora populi ducebantur, & sæpe alibi puniendi. Suetonius in Tito, cap. vii. Hos (Delatores) novissime traductos per amphitheatri arenam, partim subjici in servos ac vanire præcepit, partim in asperrimas insularum avehi. Nescio an Martialis versus, qui jamdiu cubat in morbo, sic sanandus, lib 1. de his ipsis Delatoribus & Titi facto: Turba gravis paci placidaque inimica quieti, Quæ semper miseras sollicita-bat opes: Traducta est titulis, nec cepit arena nocentes, Et delator habet quod dabat exsilium. Titulis enim vult traductos Delatores. quomodo ? nónne omnium unus est communis ? non hic: quia additum, quos & quàm illustres quisque detulisset. Exempli causâ: Hic est Titius qui Camerinum detulit. Hic, qui Lateranum, & talia. In libris legitur: Traducta est Gætulis, in aliis, Tradita Gætulis : & emendarunt , Traducta est Gyaris, quod ego & ratio facilè refellant.
units.tr: Page 102, lines 9 and 10: Πεϱιαχ-ϑεὶς κύκλῳ τᾶ ἀμφιθιάτρες. They call this led around in a circle, as also traduced, since they were led through the mouths of the people merely for display, and often punished elsewhere as well. Suetonius, in Titus, chapter 7: "These informers, last of all, led through the sand of the amphitheatre, he ordered partly to be sold as slaves, and partly to be carried off to the most desolate islands." I do not know whether Martial's verses, which have long lain sick, can be healed in this way. Book 1, on these very informers and Titus's deed: "A heavy crowd, hostile to peace and placid quiet, which always troubled poor wealth with anxiety, was led through by name; the arena did not take the guilty, and the informer has what he gave, exile." For he means informers led through by their titles. How so? Is it not one name common to all? Not here, because it was added whom and how illustrious each man was whom he had informed against. For example: "This is Titius who informed against Camerinum. This is one who informed against Lateranus," and such things. In some books it is read "Traducta est Gaetulis," in others "Tradita Gaetulis," and they emended it to "Traducta est Gyaris," which I and reason can easily refute.

units.la: Pag. 102. lin. 10. Πίναξ αὐ- τὸν πεοάγοντ.] In tabellâ enim hæc talia scribi solent : sicut & Titulus Servatoris. Cyprianus de montibus Sinâ & Sion : Pontius Pilatus impulsâ mente à Deo accepit Tabulam, & titulum scripsit tribus linguis : & in capite ligni clavis tribus Tabulam cum nomine Regis Iudæorum confixit. Ex cujus verbis vides etiam Tabulam non super lignum (ut multi repræsentant & pingunt) sed in ipso supremo ligno clavis fixam.
units.tr: Page 102, line 10: Pinax [Πίναξ] leading him [αὐτὸν προάγοντ.]. For on a tablet such things are usually written, just as the title of the Saviour was. Cyprian, on the mounts Sinai and Sion: "Pontius Pilate, his mind impelled by God, received a tablet and wrote a title in three languages, and at the top of the wood he fixed the tablet bearing the name of the King of the Jews with three nails." From his words you see that the tablet was fixed not upon the wood (as many represent and paint it) but in the very top of the wood, with a nail.

units.la: Pag. 103. lin. 14. De quo more alii.] Inter eos P. Faber libris Semestrium, ubi & sparsim plura de Cruce, & quædam selecta atque edecumata.
units.tr: Page 103, line 14: Concerning this custom, others. Among them is Petrus Faber in his books of the Semestria, where many things about the cross are scattered, and some selected and digested.
On Chapter XIV.

units.la: Pag. 110. lin. 1. & 2. Disparata hæc supplicia.] Notavit & publicè ante nos monuit Cæsar Baronius, vir sacra profanaque doctus, in Martyrologio. Sed cur frangebant iis, quos statim mortuos vellent, crura? An non caussa in Plinio? Ille lib. xi. cap. xlv. notat in iis vitalitatem esse: atque addit: Nam in ipsa genus utriusque commissura, dextra lavaque a priore parte, gemina quædam buccarum inanitas inest: quâ perfossâ, ceu jugulo, spiritus fugit. Aliud autem est à fragio crurum, Exsecare crura: quod in Am-miani miani lib.xxi i. leges, in oratione Juliani: Quisque agmine cohærens incedat, sciens quod, si remanserit usquam, exsectis cruribus relinquetur. Hoc enim proinde est, quasi dixisset, nervis aut suffraginibus incisis. Vetus sævitia, & Annibali usurpata in Romanos. Ennius: His pernas succidit iniqua potentia Pæni. Potentia Pœni more Græco, est Pœnus. Livius de eâ ipsâ re, in clade Cannensi: Quosdam jacentes vivos succisis feminibus poplitibusque inventos fuisse. nempe ne attollerent se, & ut desolati morerentur. Usurpatum est Tyrannis in Christianos. Sozomenus lib. i. cap. x. de Paphnutio & Maximo: quos, inquit, Μαξιμῖνος ἐν τοῖς μετάλλοις ἐργάζεσθαι καταδίκασε, τὰς δεξιὰς αὐτῶν ἐκόψας ὀφθαλμούς, καὶ τὰς ἀριστερὰς ἀχρείους ἀπολέσαι· Maximinus ad opus metalli condemnavit, dextros eorum
units.tr: Page 110, lines 1 and 2. These disparate punishments.] Caesar Baronius, a man learned in sacred and profane matters, noted this and publicly warned of it before us, in his Martyrology. But why did they break the legs of those whom they wanted to die at once? Is the reason not in Pliny? He, in book 11, chapter 45, notes that vitality lies in these parts, and adds: For in the very joint of each knee, on the right and on the left at the front, there is a certain twin hollowness of the hollows; when this is pierced, the breath escapes as through a throat-cut. But breaking the legs is one thing, and cutting off the legs is another, which you will read in Ammianus, book 21, in Julian's speech: Let each man march in the column keeping close, knowing that if he lags behind anywhere, he will be left with his legs cut off. For this is just as if he had said, with the sinews or hamstrings severed. It is an old cruelty, and Hannibal used it against the Romans. Ennius: On these the unjust power of the Carthaginian cut off the legs. "Potentia Poeni," in the Greek manner, means "the Carthaginian." Livy, on this very matter, at Cannae: Some were found lying alive, with their thighs and hamstrings cut, namely so that they could not raise themselves and might die forsaken. It was also used by tyrants against Christians. Sozomen, book 1, chapter 10, on Paphnutius and Maximus, whom, he says, [Μαξιμῖνος ἐν τοῖς μετάλλοις ἐργάζεσθαι καταδίκασε, τὰς δεξιὰς αὐτῶν ἐκόψας ὀφθαλμούς, καὶ τὰς ἀριστερὰς ἀχρείους ἀπολέσαι] "Maximinus condemned them to work in the mines, gouging out their right

units.la: oculos excutiens, & sinistri pedis suffragines abscindens. Eusebius ostendit aduri etiam solere, lib. VIII. cap. XII. ubi quorumdam meminit τὰς λαιὰς ποδὰς κατὰ τὰν ἀγκυλᾶν κωλῆγσιν ἀχεισμένας: qui sinistris pedibus, circa poplites, ferro adustis, inutiles facti essent.
units.tr: eyes and rendering the left feet useless." Eusebius shows that they were also commonly burned, book 8, chapter 12, where he mentions certain men who, with their left feet burned with iron around the knees, [τὰς λαιὰς ποδὰς κατὰ τὰν ἀγκυλᾶν κωλῆγσιν ἀχεισμένας] had been made useless.

units.la: Pag. 112. lin. 17. Liberi non immunes.] Lego in Eusebii lib. VI. cap. XIX. de Apollonio Martyre, cùm is sub Commodo Principe delatus esset ut Christianus, accusatori, ex lege crura fracta fuisse. Verba huic rei: Ὅτι μὴ ζῆν ἐξὸν ἦν, ἐξ τὸν βασιλικὸν ἐγον, τὰς τοιαύτας μηνύσας, ἀντίκα κατάγγυντ τὰ σκέλη: quoniam vivere nefas, juxta legem Principis, talium delatores, statim crura et fracta sunt. Sed cujus Principis haec lex tam commoda in Christianos? Non opinor ipsius Commodi. Numquid M. Aurelii ? de quo Tertullianus Apolog. c. v. Qui sicut palàm ab ejusmodi hominibus (Christianis) pœnam dimovit ; ita alio modo palàm dispersit, adjectâ etiam accusatoribus damnatione, & quidem tætriore. Et quod ait de damnatione tætriore, possis vel ad Crurifragium istud referre: vel ad Vivicomburium, quo affici accusatores Christianorum jubet ejusce Principis epistola apud Onufrium in Fastis expressa.
units.tr: Page 112, line 17. Free men not exempt.] I read in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 19, about the martyr Apollonius, that when under the Emperor Commodus he was denounced as a Christian, the accuser had his legs broken, according to the law. The words on this matter are [Ὅτι μὴ ζῆν ἐξὸν ἦν, ἐξ τὸν βασιλικὸν ἐγον, τὰς τοιαύτας μηνύσας, ἀντίκα κατάγγυντ τὰ σκέλη]: since, according to the emperor's law, it was not lawful for such people to live, their informers had their legs broken at once. But whose law was so convenient against Christians? I suppose it was not Commodus' own. Was it that of Marcus Aurelius? Of him Tertullian says, in Apology chapter 5: Who, as he openly removed punishment from such men (Christians), so in another way openly scattered them, adding also a condemnation for the accusers, and that a more grievous one. You could refer what he says of a more grievous condemnation either to this breaking of legs or to burning alive, to which an edict of that emperor, set out by Onuphrius in the Fasti, subjects the accusers of Christians.
On chapter XV.

units.la: Pag. 114. lin. 16. A Sole ac pluviâ corrumpi. ] Exemplum huic rei etiam in libris sacris, ut Reg. 11. cap. xxi. Dedit eos (septem viros) in manus Gabaonitarum, qui crucifixerunt eos in monte coram Domino. Tollens autem Respha filia Aia cilicium substravit sibi supra petram ab initio messis, donec stillaret aqua super eos de calo, & non dimisit aves lacerare eos per diem, neque bestias per noctem. Hoc de pluviâ: de sole, in Artemidoro lib. v. Ἔ̓δοξέ τις λαμπράδας ἀπὸ τῆς ἱερίας μὴ δύνασ̓θαι ἀνάψαι, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἡλιακῆς ἀνάψαι, ἱεραρχῶς. καὶ ἡ τοῦτο τὸν πρόσωπον τῆς ἡλιακῆς πυρὶ ἰδιάλωσιν: Visus aliquis faces è foco non posse accendere, & à cælo eas accendi. crucifixus est. atque hoc modo igne cælesti concalefactus.
units.tr: Page 114, line 16. To be spoiled by sun and rain.] An example of this also occurs in the sacred books, as in Reg. 11, chapter 21: He gave them (seven men) into the hands of the Gibeonites, who crucified them on the mountain before the LORD. But Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest, until water dropped upon them from heaven; and she did not suffer the birds to tear them by day, nor the beasts by night. This is about rain; about the sun, in Artemidorus, book 5: [Ἔ̓δοξέ τις λαμπράδας ἀπὸ τῆς ἱερίας μὴ δύνασ̓θαι ἀνάψαι, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἡλιακῆς ἀνάψαι, ἱεραρχῶς. καὶ ἡ τοῦτο τὸν πρόσωπον τῆς ἡλιακῆς πυρὶ ἰδιάλωσιν] A certain man seemed unable to light torches from fire, but to have them lit from the sun. He was crucified, and in this way warmed by heavenly fire.
CHAPTER III.

units.la: Ag.126. lin. 2. & 3. VERBERATVM patibuloque confstrictum. ] An ergo huc referas Dionis etiam illud lib. XLIX. de Antonii sævitiâ in Judææ regem Antigonum? Τὸς δ᾽ Ἀντίγονον, inquit, ἐμαστίγωσε φωρὰ σαυρόσυσας (ὁ μηδὲν ἄμεινον βασιλεὺς ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων ἐπεπόνθει) καὶ μὴ τοῦτο καὶ ἀπέκτεινε: Antigonum flagellavit crucи sive furcæ alligans (quod nemo alius Rex à Romanis unquam passus erat) ac postea interfecit. Verba ita præferre videntur: nec abhorreat ab Antonii impotentiâ, ut serviliter sævierit etiam in Regem. Tamen verius puto ut capias vertasque Palum. Ut palo, inquam, alligatus fuerit, solenni
units.tr: Ag.126. lin. 2. & 3. Beaten and fastened to a post. ] Should one then also refer here that passage of Dio, book XLIX, on Antony's savagery against Antigonus, king of Judaea? "Antony," he says, "scourged Antigonus, tying him to a cross or fork [ἐμαστίγωσε φωρὰ σαυρόσυσας] (a king who had suffered nothing worse at the hands of the Romans), and afterwards put him to death." The words seem to suggest that he did not shrink from Antony's violence, so that he raged slavishly even against a king. Yet I think it truer that you take and render it as stake. I mean that he was tied to a stake, in the solemn Roman manner, and then struck down with an axe.

units.la: Romanis more,& tum securi percuffus. Quod ipsum huic Antigono factum, etsi Dio non expressit, notavit Strabo, citante Jofepho (nam hodie non exstat) lib. xv.i. Antiq. cap. i. Ἀντώνιος δὲ Ἀντίγονον Ἰουδαῖον ἀχθέντα εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν πελεκίζει, καὶ ἰδοξε μὲν ἔτ᾽ αὐτῷ Ῥωμαῖοι βασιλέα πελεκισθῆναι: Antonius Antigonum Iudaum Antiochiam perductum securi persutit, & visus est primus Romanorum securi subjecisse regem. Idem Plutarchus in Antonio.
units.tr: Romans' manner, and then struck with the axe. Strabo noted that this very thing was done to this Antigonus, although Dio did not express it; Strabo is cited by Josephus (for he does not survive today), book XV of the Antiquities, chapter 1: "Antony had Antigonus the Jew, brought to Antioch, beheaded with an axe [Ἀντώνιος δὲ Ἀντίγονον Ἰουδαῖον ἀχθέντα εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν πελεκίζει], and he seemed to be the first of the Romans to subject a king to the axe." The same is found in Plutarch, in his Life of Antony.

units.la: Pag. 128. lin. 16. Patens hæc transversaque pars sic dicta. Strictè & proprie inquam. Alias quis nescit totam crucem sæpe venire in hoc nomen? Salluftius utro modo acceperit haud dixerim, in loco vitiato. Fragmentum est apud Nonium e iv. Hiftor. In quis notissimus quisque aut malo dependens verberabatur, aut immutilato copore improbi patibulo eminens assiaffigebatur: Lego mutilato corpore: quia mos ille frequens Orientalibus, ut priusquam crucifigerent admutilarent, aut etiam per tormenta necarent. Exempla habes in hoc libro, cap.xii. & alibi. At illud improbi, qui reformandum ignoro. Tentavi olim in proris. An & improbe? quod sic compositum pro simplici, ut in ante & talia, apud Tertullianum reperies Exhortat. ad Castitat. Cap. x. An etiam improbe? ut sit corpus fuisse improbè mutilatum? Credo enim hæc narrasse de sævitiâ Mithridatis in Cyzicenos, quos terrâ marique obsedit.
units.tr: Page 128, line 16. This spreading and transverse part is so called. I mean strictly and properly. Otherwise, who does not know that the whole cross often comes under this name? In which sense Sallust took it I would not venture to say, since the passage is corrupt. It is a fragment in Nonius, from book IV of the Histories: "In which the most notorious of each were beaten, hanging from a stake, or, with a mutilated body, projecting from the gibbet of the wicked, were fixed." I read mutilated body, because that custom was common among Orientals, to mutilate before crucifying, or even to kill by torture. You have examples in this book, chapter XII, and elsewhere. But I do not know how to correct improbi. I once tried in proris. Or improbe? compounded in the way that a simple word is compounded, as in before and similar forms, which you will find in Tertullian, Exhortation to Chastity, chapter X. Or also improbe, so that the body was shamefully mutilated? For I believe he was narrating these things about the savagery of Mithridates against the people of Cyzicus, whom he besieged by land and sea.
ON CHAPTER V.

units.la: Pag. 133. lin. 1. Facie quâ nafirum hodie patibulum.] Quæ sententia fuit Antonii Morilloni, viri summi futuri si diutius vixisset. Argumenta habebat (vidi & legi in epistolâ ejus ad Lindanum, quam heredes adservant) quod id referret formam Jugi: ferre autem jugum, ignomina & quasi comminatio hujusce mortis. itaque illinc petenda forma. Amplius, Livius ait lib. i. Romanos spectasse furcis duodenos à terrâ spectacula alta sustinentibus pedes: eas furcas proclinantia utrimque ligna fuisse cum tertio transversario supernè immissò, quod genus Capreolos Latini vocant, & nos hodie Schragas: ergo hanc esse faciem furcæ. Tertiò Hebræos hodiéque suum Tau sic pingere: cum eo autem comparari passim: tale igitur esse. Credo etiam addere (non firmiter nunc commemini, sed addi potest) Ausonium cum Φ litterâ Græcâ Crucem comparare: at ea quoque istuc abiit. Sed hæc sententia, etsi arguta, proba mihi non est ob multas causas, atque
units.tr: Page 133, line 1. With the face on which the gibbet is today.] This was the opinion of Antonius Morillonus, a man of the highest distinction, who would have become more so had he lived longer. He had arguments (I saw and read them in his letter to Lindanus, which his heirs keep) that it refers to the shape of a yoke. To bear a yoke, however, is a disgrace and something like a threat of this kind of death; therefore the shape is to be sought there. Furthermore, Livy says in book I that the Romans watched from the ground twelve men on forks, which held up high platforms on their feet; these forks, the Latins say, were pieces of wood leaning out on each side, with a third crossbeam placed on top, a kind which the Latins call capreoli and we today schragae. Therefore this is the shape of the fork. Third, the Hebrews even today draw their Tau in this way, and it is compared everywhere with it; therefore it is of such a shape. I think I may add (I do not clearly remember it now, but it can be added) that Ausonius compares the cross with the Greek letter Φ; but that too has gone away. Yet this opinion, though ingenious, does not please me, for many reasons, and

units.la: [The line "atque" is right-aligned at the foot of the column.] atque hanc unicam firmissimam, quòd refellunt spectiones & monumenta omnia antiqua, omnia inquam consensu. Quid Christianis nobis fiet, si ipsa imago crucis aliter ubique non pingenda solùm, sed manibus cottidie deformanda? At enim jugum tale olim. Ita, sed quid ad rem? militaris saltem ignominia illa fuit: & liberorum ea hominum, non servorum, ut latura furcæ. De Livio, nihil impedit Furcas nostro vulgarique more intelligi, quibus ligna transversa injecta, & super ea asseres, ad spectandum insistendumque. Fit & hodie, & olim primas domos sic erectas ex Posidonii sententiâ puto Senecam alibi tradere, & uti pariter voce furca. De Hebræis, verum est, sed hodiernis. Priscas eorum literas alias & diversiformes fuisse, periti ejus linguæ atque ipse Hieronvronymus tradiderunt. Jam de Ausonii versu, is talis:
units.tr: [The word "atque" is right-aligned at the foot of the column.] and above all for this one, most firm: all ancient monuments and images refute it, all of them, I say, with one accord. What would become of us Christians if the very image of the cross were not only painted otherwise everywhere, but daily misshaped by hand? "But the yoke was such formerly." Yes, but what does that matter? That disgrace was at least a military one, and of free men, not slaves, as the fork would be. As for Livy, nothing prevents furcae being understood in our ordinary sense, on which cross-timbers are laid, with boards over them, for watching and standing on. This is done today, and was done formerly, in the first houses so erected; following Posidonius, I think Seneca reports this somewhere, and uses the word furca in the same way. As for the Hebrews, it is true, but of today's letters. That their ancient letters were different and of various forms, the skilled readers of that language and Jerome himself have handed down. Now as to the verse of Ausonius, it runs thus:
And in the figure of a cross the Palamedean letter is extended, Φ.

units.la: Lectionem non muto, etsi alii libri proferunt gruis : nec id male. Sed esto crucis: verissimum est in nostra etiam forma. quomodo? in cruce inquam vestita, & in qua homo appensus. Vide faciem & pendula a ligno brachia, est haec ipsa litterae forma. Subjicio & formam crucifixionis quam imaginabatur & delineabat Morillonus.
units.tr: I do not change the reading, although other books give gruis, nor is that bad. But let it be crucis: this is most true also of our form. How? In a cross, I mean, clothed, and on which a man is hung. Look at the face and the arms hanging from the wood; this is exactly the shape of the letter. I add also a figure of crucifixion, which Morillonus imagined and drew.
TO CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Pagin. 140. lin. 9. & 10. Impudicas ancillas sic puniri.] Et est sane ignava mors, & Feminea etiam Panegyristae dicta. Alteri manibus satellitum Britannorum gula domi fracta, & inusta feminea mortis infamia, mia, ut scilicet maluisse vir ferri amantissimus videretur laqueo perire quàm gladio. Victor postremum appellavit, vilissimamque, in Maximo : Pœnas mortis genere postremo, fractis laqueo cervicibus luit.
units.tr: Page 140, lines 9 and 10. Impudent maidservants are punished in this way.] Indeed it is a shameful death, and the panegyrist also calls it feminine. Another man's throat was broken at home by the hands of British soldiers, and the infamy of a woman's death was branded upon him, so that evidently a man most fond of the sword seemed to have preferred to perish by the noose rather than by the sword. Victor called it the last and most base death, in the case of Maximus: He paid the penalty of death in the last manner, his neck broken by the noose.

units.la: Pag. 140. lin. penult. Patibulum vulgò Furca dicitur. ] Quo ipso sensu inferiores Græci dixerunt φυλίζειν in furcam agere, asperiore illâ litterâ mutatâ. Cedrenus in Justiniano Rinotmetâ : Ἐν τῇ τέχει πάντας ἐφάλκισεν. quod vertendum est, In muro omnes de furcâ suspendit. Docet Zonaras qui in eâ ipsâ re : Ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῖς τείχεσιν ἀπηὼξεν: In lignis apud muros suspendit. Credo autem hanc Furcam primò non nisi dimidiatum Patibulum fuisse, id est, facie adhuc aliquâ Furcæ; paullatim, & quò plures appendi possent, immutasse.
units.tr: Page 140, last line but one: The patibulum is commonly called the furca.] In this very sense the later Greeks said φυλίζειν, to drive to the furca, with the rougher letter changed. Cedrenus, on Justinian Rhinotmetus: Ἐν τῇ τέχει πάντας ἐφάλκισεν [Ἐν τῇ τέχει πάντας ἐφάλκισεν], which must be rendered he hanged them all on the gallows in the wall. Zonaras, who tells the same story, says: Ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῖς τείχεσιν ἀπηὼξεν [Ἐν ξύλοις παρὰ τοῖς τείχεσιν ἀπηὼξεν], he hanged them on wooden posts beside the walls. I believe, however, that this furca was at first only a half patibulum, that is, still having some appearance of a furca, and that it was gradually changed, so that more people could be hanged on it.
TO CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: Pag. 145. lin. 6. Injectis per crura funibus. An magis placet hic sensus, Funes ipsos per crura eorum trajectos & transmissos ? Tale in Curtio legó Alexandrum usurpasse in Batin quendam lib. iv. Per talos spirantis lora trajecta sunt, religatumque ad currum traxere circa urbem equi. Id factum à rege exemplo Achillis, qui Hectorem sic fœdavit, ut Curtius inibi notat. Sed tamen Ammianus Injectos ait, non Trajectos, nec id supplicii credam vulgò usitatum.
units.tr: Page 145, line 6. Injectis per crura funibus. Does this sense seem more likely: that the ropes themselves were passed through and across their legs? I have read that Alexander used such a method on a certain Batis, in Curtius, book 4: Thongs were passed through the ankles of the man still breathing, and the horses, tied to a chariot, dragged him around the city. Curtius notes that the king did this after the example of Achilles, who disgraced Hector in the same way. But Ammianus says Injectos, not Trajectos, and I do not think this was the usual form of punishment.
AD CAP. X.

units.la: Pag. 147. lin. 12. & 13. Moriturum in ipsis, non per ipsas. Præter exempla quæ dedi, hoc rarum videatur in Philippo, de quo Eusebius in Chronico, anno xii. Claudii: Philippus Apostolus Christi apud Hierapolim Asiæ civitatem, dum Euangelium populo nunciaret cruci affixus, lapidibus opprimitur. Quasi in ipsâ cruce lapidibus obrutus esset. Atque hoc quidem in vulgatis libris, in veteri & probo meo manuscripto vestigium non est horum verborum.
units.tr: Page 147, lines 12 and 13. He will die in them, not through them. Apart from the examples I have given, this seems a rare case in Philip, of whom Eusebius writes in his Chronicle, in the twelfth year of Claudius: Philip, the Apostle of Christ, at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, while he was preaching the Gospel to the people, was fixed to the cross and stoned. As if he had been buried under stones on the cross itself. Yet this phrase is found in the printed books, and it is not in my old and trustworthy manuscript.
AD CAP. XIII.

units.la: Pag. 157. lin.4. & 5. Viri fide digni afferunt. Inter eos eximius Theologus Alfonsus Ciacco, qui de signis Crucis nunc nuper accuratè scripsit.
units.tr: Page 157, lines 4 and 5. Men worthy of trust report. Among them is the distinguished theologian Alfonso Ciacco, who recently wrote carefully on the signs of the cross.

units.la: Pag. 157. lin. penult. Iam illa Amanis praealta. De quâ accipienda quæ in Codice Justinianæo leguntur, De Judæis & cælic. ubi scribuntur Judæi quodam festivitatis suæ solenni, Aman ad pœna quondam recordationem incendere, dere, & sanctæ crucis adsimilatam speciem in contemptum Christianæ fidei exurere, atque id facere deinceps vetantur. Totidem pænè verbis in Codice Theod. lib.xvi. tit. vii. Ex quibus vides Judæos Amanis inimici sui mortem annuâ memoriâ repræsentasse, & in cruce suspensum cum eâ ipsâ combussisse : speciem Amanem, re & mente Servatorem & nostram crucem. Ideò meritissimò interdicti.
units.tr: Page 157, second last line. Now that lofty story of Haman. To this must be referred what is read in the Justinian Code, under "On the Jews and the Caelicolae," where it is written that the Jews, at a certain solemn festival of theirs, kindle a likeness of Haman, once the object of punishment, and that they burn in contempt of the Christian faith a figure made like the holy cross; and they are forbidden to do this from now on. Almost the same words occur in the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 7. From these you see that the Jews, by an annual observance, represented the death of their enemy Haman, and burned him together with the cross on which he was hanged, a figure of the Saviour and of our cross, in fact and in intention. Therefore they were rightly forbidden.

units.la: Pag. 160. lin. penult. Novus etiam orbis. ] In quo sanè hoc mirum, cruces repertas fuisse plurisariam in templis atque in sepulchris. De Indiâ Occiduâ loquor. Quâ origine aut fine? nescimus, nisi si jam tunc providus ille Deus exstare voluit omen & signum dominaturæ illic crucis.
units.tr: Page 160, second last line. The New World also. In this there is indeed something remarkable: crosses were found in many places, in temples and in tombs. I am speaking of the West Indies. By what origin or for what purpose, we do not know, unless perhaps that providential God already wished there to be a sign and token of the cross that was to rule there.
AD CAP. XIV.

units.la: Pag. 162. lin. 4. Edicto prohibitum manet.] Atqui in Panegyricâ oratione, sanè disertâ, quæ Theodosio dicta, mentio etiam crucis quasi licitæ & manentis. Et post hanc tu vocem, non illum in crucem tulli, non culleo insui, non discerpi in frusta jussisti. Et fieri sanè potest ut apud gentiles, & Christo adversos, supplicium etiam manserit. sicut de Slavis in Helmoldi Chronico scriptum lib. I. In illis diebus Slavi quendam Danum suffixerunt cruci. In ignominiam scilicet divinæ crucis.
units.tr: Page 162, line 4. It remained forbidden by the edict. And yet in the Panegyric addressed to Theodosius, a speech certainly eloquent, there is also mention of the cross as if it were still lawful and continuing: And after this, you said, "Let him not be carried to the cross, let him not be sewn into a sack, let him not be torn into pieces." And it is quite possible that among the gentiles, and those opposed to Christ, the punishment remained too. As is written about the Slavs in the Chronicle of Helmold, book 1: In those days the Slavs fixed a certain Dane to a cross. Clearly as an insult to the divine cross.
AD CAP. XV.

units.la: Pag. 165. lin. 14. Ἐκ χευσῆς χειδιάσας σωτὴρ.] Quem suo ævo exstitisse in Palatio Socrates asseverat, Eccl. Hist. lib. I. cap. I. Τότε πιϑὶς τῆ χρηςμῷ, καταςκευάζει μὲν τὸ ςαυροειδὲς τρόπαιον, ὅ μίχρι νῦν ἐν τοῖς βασιλείοις φυλάττεται: Huic oraculo fidem habens, confecit fimile illud cruci tropæum, quod usque nunc in regia servatur. Idem Cedrenus: Τότε ςαυρὸν χρυσῆν χειδιάζας, ὃς ἐςι μίχρι νῦν: Tunc crucem auream efformans, quæ etiamnunc exstat. Non opinor tamen hanc esse, de quâ Suidas: Σταυρὸς ἐπὶ τὸ βόρειον τῆς Φόρης μέρος ἵςατο, ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὸν Κωνσταντῖνος, χρυ-σίμπλας ἐν τοῖς ἀκρωτηριαχοῖς τοῖχ- γύλοις, μήλοις, ἵνα καὶ αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτῆ καθιερώνυτο χρυσίμβαφοι: Crux ad partem Borealem foristabat, ut vidit eam Constantinus, auro illita in extremis rotundis pomis, ubi & ipse & filii ejus conspiciebantur aurati.
units.tr: Page 165, line 14. [Saviour, fashioning] from gold. Socrates asserts that this stood in the palace in his own age, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 1: Trusting this oracle, he made that cross-shaped trophy, which is kept in the palace even now. Cedrenus likewise: Then, fashioning a golden cross, which is still in existence. I do not think, however, that this is the one of which Suidas writes: A cross stood on the northern side of the Forum, when Constantine saw it, gilded on the rounded ends, where he and his sons were seen gilded.

units.la: Pag. 166. lin. 1. In hoc vin- ce.
units.tr: Page 166, line 1. In this conquer.

units.la: Nummis hoc pluribus expressum cernitur, atque etiam quibusdam uberiùs, In hoc signo vince. Sanè Christiani libenter appellarunt signum Dei, aut Christi quasi Crucem, ipsam Imperatoris illius tesseram aut vexillum. Justinianæo Codice vetatur, signum Salvatoris Christi humi vel in silice insculpi. Quid, quòd Græci interpretes sic legem Scævolæ accipiunt, xxxviii. De aur. arg. mund. Fieri volo jubeoque signum Dei ex libris centum. Accipiunt, inquam, & reddunt Crucem. An verè? minimè, scimus signum Dei statuam esse apud Scævolam sive Solis, sive indigenæ cujuspiam & familiaris dei. Sed pietas, non error, Græcos eò traxit. Monuit super hac interpretatiunculâ Petrus Oranus, juris & litterarum consultus, & germanum in modum mihi amicus.
units.tr: This is seen expressed on many coins, and on some more fully: In this sign conquer. Certainly Christians gladly called the sign of God, or of Christ, a cross, that emperor's own watchword or standard. The Justinian Code forbids that the sign of the Saviour Christ be carved on the ground or in stone. What of the fact that Greek translators take Scaevola's law in this way, book 38, on gold, silver and ornaments: I wish and order that a sign of God be made of a hundred pounds. They take it, I say, and render it as cross. Is this truly so? Not at all; we know that in Scaevola the sign of God is a statue either of the Sun or of some native and household god. But piety, not error, drew the Greeks to this interpretation. Peter Oranus, a learned jurist and scholar and a friend to me like a brother, pointed out this small mistake of interpretation.

units.la: Pag. 167. lin. 1. & 2. --gemmanti textus in auro Signabat labarum.] Dixi ipsi velo nomen intextum; & poëta hic aperte. Tamen ex descriptione Eusebii, videbis & supra velum sæpe ex auro statui : & exempla in nummis utriusque posituræ dedi. illius tamen magis crebra. Ipsa Labari vox qualis? vereor ut peregrina, certè novitia, & sub Trajani aut illud ævum nata. Vetustior Tertulliano, qui hodie exstant, non commeminit. Gregorius Nazianzenus,doctus & fortis Orator, ait καμάτων λυτήεσον ἀναγ , περὶ τῆ Γω-μαίης ὀνομάζεσθαι : Laborum levamen pausamque esse, & à Romanis sic appellari. Igitur à labore derivavit, eo proclivius, quia ipsi Græci λάξωγον scribebant. Sed nostri poëtæ nónne corripiunt? Quomodo etiam pausam laboris, non alià additione, vox ea significet? nisi forte, quia ubi laborabatur in acie, signum illud eò solet ferri. Longinquum est, & perseverò externam vocem esse.
units.tr: Page 167, lines 1 and 2. --on the gold a standard marked with a jewelled text. I have said that the name was woven into the veil, and the poet here plainly says so.
