Yet from Eusebius's description you will also see that the standard was often set up of gold above the veil, and I have given examples of both positions on coins, though the former is the more frequent. What is the word labarum itself? I fear it is foreign, certainly new, and arose under Trajan or in that age. Older writers than Tertullian, whose works survive today, do not mention it. Gregory Nazianzen, a learned and vigorous orator, says: It is a relief from toils and a pause, and is so called by the Romans. So he derived it from labor, the more readily because the Greeks themselves wrote labarum. But do not our poets lengthen the first syllable? And how does that word signify a pause from toil without some other addition? Unless perhaps because the standard was usually carried where men were labouring in battle. It is a long way off, and I persist in thinking the word is foreign.

units.la: Pag. 167. lin. penult. Duæ litteræ Christi nomen exprimentes.] Ita est, & conspicuæ sunt in Nummis. Ipsum etiam Chi solitarium, signabat Christum. In Antiochenorum dicteriis recenlet Julianus, Misopogone: Τὸ Χῒ, φασιν, ἐδὲν ἰδίκησε τὴν πόλιν, ἐδὲ τὸ Κάππα. & addit: Ἡμεῖς ὁ ἰδιδάχθημεν ἀρχὰς ὀνομάτων εἶναι τὰ χεράμματα, δηλῶν δ' ἰδέλειν τὸ μὲν Χεῖρ, τὸ δὲ Καισαρτίνον. Chi, inquiunt, & Kappa nihil injuria intulerunt civitati. Nos autem didicimus initia nominum esse has litteras, & significare velle illud quidem Christum, hoc Constantinum. Ita Julianus, qui has ipsas litteras è Labaro postea conatus removere. Frustrà, & vicit nomen quod æternum vivit & vincet.
units.tr: Page 167, second last line. Two letters expressing the name of Christ. So it is, and they are conspicuous on the coins. The single letter Chi also signified Christ. Julian, in his Misopogon, lists among the Antiochenes' jokes: "The Chi," they say, "has done the city no wrong, nor the Kappa." And he adds: We were taught that these letters are the beginnings of names, and that the one signifies Christ, the other Constantine. So Julian, who later tried to remove these very letters from the standard. In vain: the name that lives forever has conquered and will conquer.
TO CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Pag. 173. lin. 9, Ω᾽ξύλοι μάχαι- {*}σεσιν. ] Verè, quia nos per illud μάχαιρις. Atque ita σεβασμιώτατον καὶ τίμιον, adorandum & venerabile, Imperator appellat novellâ quintâ. Eaque caufsâ vetitum, in lapidibus fculpi, quæ in folo. Lex extat in Codice Justinianæo : & apud Paullum Diaconum sic Tiberius : Crucem Domini quâ frontem nostram & pectora munire debemus, eam sub pedibus concul-camus ? Tale & Synodus habita in Trullo, can. lxxxiii. Quamquam autem è pavimentis templorum remota, non etiam è tectis. Fulfit jam olim ibi, clarum certumque symbolum Christiani cultus. Nicephorus Gregoras libro ix. in descriptione tempestatis quæ Constantinopoli : Τηνικαῦτα μὲν τοι πεπλώκασι καὶ πόλει
units.tr: Page 173, line 9, "O wood, battles-..." [Ὦ ξύλοι μάχαι-σεσιν]. Truly, because through that word we... most worshipful and honourable [σεβασμιώτατον καὶ τίμιον], adorable and venerable, the Emperor calls it in his fifth Novel. For this reason it was forbidden to carve it in stones that lie on the ground. The law is found in the Justinian Code. Tiberius, as Paul the Deacon reports, says: Shall we trample under our feet the cross of the Lord, by which we ought to fortify our brow and breast? The Synod held in Trullo says the same, canon 83. Although the cross was removed from the floors of churches, it was not removed from their roofs. Long ago it already shone there as a clear and certain sign of Christian worship. Nicephorus Gregoras, book 9, in his description of the storm at Constantinople: At that time indeed... to the city [Τηνικαῦτα μὲν τοι πεπλώκασι καὶ πόλει].

units.tr: Many of the iron crosses that stood on the earth, and that are customarily set upon churches, could not bear the force of the wind, and fell at that time [πολλοὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἱδρυμένων ἐκ σιδήρου σταυρῶν, ὑπενεγκεῖν δὲ μὴ δυνάμενοι τὴν τοῦ πνεύματος βίαν]. Then many crosses, which are customarily set upon temples and made of iron, fell, unable to withstand the violence of the wind.
THE END.
